pools.title: What a Sense Is For
pools.covers: reading §8.0 (the unnumbered Opening), §8.1.1 · lecture 8.1 slides what_module_7_set_aside, what_each_signal_carries, eyes_for_different_lives

items.stem: Before a pattern of activity caused by an eel’s smell can exist in a fish’s olfactory bulb, what has to happen?

options.text: Receptor cells in the fish’s nose have to turn molecules carried by the current into electrical signals.
options.why: Correct. A pattern in the olfactory bulb is made of electrical signals. Before it exists, molecules have to reach receptor cells, and those cells have to turn them into electrical signals.

options.text: Connections in the olfactory bulb have to be strengthened over many encounters, until one pattern stands for an eel.
options.why: Strengthening connections so that a pattern stands for an eel works on patterns that already exist. The step before any pattern is receptor cells turning molecules into electrical signals.

options.text: The fish has to swim upstream toward the eel, so that the molecules reach its nose in a steady stream.
options.why: Swimming does change what reaches the senses, but molecules reach a still fish too. No pattern exists until receptor cells turn them into electrical signals.

options.text: The fish has to see the eel first, so that its brain can tell which molecules in the water to attend to.
options.why: Smell works without sight, since molecules from an eel out of view still reach the nose. What smell needs first is receptor cells turning those molecules into electrical signals.

items.stem: A computer model of a frog catching flies is handed, as its input, a list giving the exact position of every fly near the frog. What does this input skip that a real frog’s senses have to do?

options.text: Turn light into electrical signals in receptor cells, signals that tell the frog some things about a fly and not others.
options.why: Correct. A real frog has no list. Receptor cells in its eyes have to turn light into electrical signals first, and light, like every kind of signal, carries some facts about the world and leaves out others.

options.text: Nothing, since the positions of nearby flies are exactly what a frog’s eyes deliver to its brain, directly and in full detail.
options.why: That treats sensing as direct. No sense hands over the world ready-made: receptor cells turn a physical signal into electrical signals, and what caused the signal has to be recovered from them.

options.text: Filter out flies too far away to catch, since passing on only what is within reach is the main job of a frog’s eyes.
options.why: Leaving out distant flies is something the model could still do with its list. What the list skips comes before any filtering: receptor cells turning light into electrical signals.

options.text: Move the frog’s tongue toward a fly, since aiming a strike is a job that the frog’s senses carry out by themselves.
options.why: Moving the tongue is action rather than sensing, and the model would still have to do it. The list skips the step where receptor cells turn light into electrical signals.

items.stem: A fish follows a smell upstream. As it swims, its lateral line reports a constant stirring of the water along its sides, and the scene keeps sweeping across its eyes. What causes much of this input?

options.text: The fish’s own swimming, since each beat of its tail and each turn of its body changes what reaches its senses.
options.why: Correct. A moving animal causes much of what reaches its own senses. Each tail beat stirs the water along the fish’s sides, and each turn sweeps the scene across its eyes.

options.text: An eel close by, since stirred water and a shifting scene are what a predator near the fish would produce.
options.why: An eel close by could stir the water too. But the fish produces the same kinds of input with every tail beat and turn, whether an eel is there or not.

options.text: The current of the stream, since a fish holding still in flowing water receives the same stirring and the same sweeping scene.
options.why: Flowing water does stir along a still fish’s sides. But a still fish makes no tail beats or turns, and those are what cause much of this input.

options.text: The smell it is following, since a strong smell sets off activity in the lateral line and the eyes as well as the nose.
options.why: Each sense begins with receptor cells that respond to one kind of physical signal. The lateral line responds to moving water and the eyes to light, not to molecules.

items.stem: A fish catches sight of an eel moving through the weeds ahead. Why can the fish not treat the place where it sees the eel as the place where the eel is now?

options.text: The signals that tell the fish where the eel is are already a little out of date by the time they arrive.
options.why: Correct. Signals about where something is are a little old by the time they arrive. By then a moving eel is somewhere a little different.

options.text: Light carries little about direction, so vision can say only that an eel is somewhere ahead, and not where it is.
options.why: Light carries direction with great precision, which is why vision is the sense that says where, exactly, something is. The trouble is that its report is a little old.

options.text: The fish’s lateral line takes over from vision once an eel is close, so whatever the eyes report is set aside.
options.why: The lateral line reports moving water within a body length or two, alongside vision rather than in place of it. The trouble with the eyes’ report is its age.

options.text: The eel’s smell in the water blurs the image of the eel, so the eel appears in a different place from where it is.
options.why: Smell and sight run on different signals, molecules and light, and molecules do not blur an image. The seen position is off because the signals are already out of date.

items.stem: An account of a fish’s escape from eels takes two shortcuts. It starts from a pattern of activity already present in the fish’s brain, and it treats the fish as if it were holding still. What do the two shortcuts leave out?

options.text: The senses that produce the pattern in the first place, and the movement of the animal that has those senses.
options.why: Correct. These are the two things a fuller account has to take up: how receptors produce the pattern in the first place, and what the animal’s own movement does to its senses.

options.text: The learning that links a pattern to an eel, and the memory of earlier encounters that the pattern is compared with.
options.why: An account that starts from a pattern can still ask what the pattern means and how that is learned. What it leaves out is where the pattern came from, and what movement does to it.

options.text: The eel’s own movement through the water, and the drift of the current that carries the eel’s smell downstream.
options.why: The eel and the current do move, but the shortcut is about the fish. Treating the fish as still leaves out its own movement, and starting from a pattern leaves out the senses.

options.text: The fish’s choice among routes of escape, and how quickly it can learn to flee from a predator it has not encountered.
options.why: Choosing a route and learning about a new predator come after a pattern exists. The two shortcuts leave out the senses that produce the pattern and the fish’s own movement.

items.stem: Why are perceiving and moving best understood together, rather than as two separate topics?

options.text: They are hard to separate, because much of what reaches a moving animal’s senses is caused by its own movement.
options.why: Correct. Each tail beat and each turn changes what reaches the fish’s senses. A sense cannot be understood apart from the movements that keep changing its input.

options.text: They are hard to separate, because the receptor cells that sense the world also send out the commands that move the muscles.
options.why: Receptor cells turn physical signals into electrical ones; they do not command muscles. The link is that the animal’s movement produces much of what its senses receive.

options.text: They are hard to separate, because a sense works only while its owner is moving, and falls silent when the owner holds still.
options.why: Moving does make some information available that a still animal lacks, but a still animal still senses the world. The link is that a moving animal’s own movement causes much of what its senses receive.

options.text: They are easy to separate, since a sense reports the world in the same way whether its owner is moving or holding still.
options.why: That is the simplification that has to be dropped. A moving animal’s senses report its own doings mixed with the world’s.

items.stem: A swallow hunts small insects on the wing, twisting and turning as it flies. In a few sentences, explain how the swallow’s own flight affects what reaches its eyes, and why the signals telling it where an insect is cannot simply be taken as where the insect is now.
items.answer: Every twist and turn of the swallow’s body sweeps the whole scene across its eyes. So much of the change in what reaches its eyes is caused by the swallow itself rather than by the world. The insect is moving too, and the signals that tell the swallow where an insect is are already a little out of date when they arrive. So the place where the swallow sees the insect is where the insect was a moment ago, not where it is now.
rubric: Says each twist or turn of the swallow’s body sweeps the scene across its eyes.
Says that much of what reaches the swallow’s eyes is therefore caused by the swallow itself rather than by the world.
Says the signals reporting where an insect is are already a little out of date when they arrive.
Says the insect keeps moving in the meantime, so its seen position is where it was, not where it is now.

items.stem: What does a sense do for an animal?

options.text: It helps the animal find out about things it is not touching, or cannot see inside, through a signal those things shaped.
options.why: Correct. An eel reflects light, disturbs the water, and sheds molecules. Each of those signals was shaped by the eel, and what caused the signal has to be recovered from it.

options.text: It delivers the things around the animal to its brain directly, so that nothing about what caused a signal has to be worked out.
options.why: That is the view of sensing as direct. None of a sense’s information is direct, so the cause of a signal always has to be recovered from the signal.

options.text: It stores what the animal has learned about the things around it, so that each one can be recognized when it appears again.
options.why: Storing what has been learned is memory, which works on what the senses deliver. A sense finds out about things through a physical signal they shaped.

options.text: It turns the animal’s intended actions into commands, sent from the brain out to the muscles that carry the actions out.
options.why: That describes a movement command, on the output side of the nervous system. A sense is on the input side: it finds out about things through a signal they shaped.

items.stem: Smelling an eel is plainly indirect: the fish smells molecules the eel left in the water, not the eel itself. Seeing an eel in clear, bright water can seem different, as if the eyes simply take in the eel. Is vision’s information about the eel any more direct than smell’s?

options.text: No, because what reaches the eye is light the eel’s surfaces have shaped, and what produced that light has to be recovered from it.
options.why: Correct. Light is a physical signal the eel shaped, just as the molecules are. None of a sense’s information is direct, so what caused the light has to be recovered from it.

options.text: Yes, because light travels fast and in straight lines, so what reaches the eye in clear, bright water is the eel itself, with nothing to recover.
options.why: Light does travel fast and in straight lines, which is why it carries layout and direction so precisely. But it is still a signal the eel shaped, not the eel, and its cause has to be recovered.

options.text: Yes, because where light falls on the retina already says which direction it came from, so nothing about what is there has to be worked out.
options.why: Where light falls does give direction relative to the eye with no further computation. But direction is not what the eel is, and what produced the light still has to be recovered.

options.text: No, because the image that an eye forms is upside down, and turning it the right way up is the work that makes vision indirect.
options.why: The orientation of the image is not what makes vision indirect. Light is a signal the eel shaped, and its cause has to be recovered from it, as for every sense.

items.stem: A deer stands in dense forest on a moonless night. Something moves behind a thick screen of bushes a few meters away. Which kind of signal is best suited to tell the deer that something is happening there?

options.text: Sound, because it bends around obstacles and works in the dark, so it carries news of events hidden from view.
options.why: Correct. Sound bends around obstacles, works in the dark, and arrives from every direction at once, which suits it to telling an animal that something is happening even when it cannot be seen.

options.text: Light, because it travels fast and in straight lines, so it carries the precise direction of whatever is moving there.
options.why: Light does carry precise direction, but anything in the way blocks it, and on a moonless night there is almost none of it.

options.text: Chemicals, because they drift and linger in the air, so they tell exactly where something is at this moment.
options.why: Chemicals do drift and linger, and that is why they carry what something is far better than where it is. They are poor at saying where, and slow to arrive.

options.text: Touch, because it reports pressure and vibration, so it can pick up movement anywhere close to the animal.
options.why: Touch reports only what is in contact with the body. Something behind the bushes is not touching the deer at all.

items.stem: Suppose a fish had many times more smell receptors than its neighbors, each one highly sensitive. Could smell then tell it where, exactly, an eel is waiting upstream?

options.text: No, because chemicals move slowly, linger, and drift with the current, so the signal itself carries little about where the eel is.
options.why: Correct. A sense can report only what its physical signal carries. More or better receptors cannot recover a location that drifting, lingering molecules do not carry.

options.text: Yes, because what a sense can report is limited only by its receptors, so enough sensitive receptors would locate the eel exactly.
options.why: Receptors are one limit, but the signal is the other. Molecules that linger and drift with the current carry what far better than where, whatever the receptors.

options.text: No, because chemicals carry neither what an eel is nor where it is, so smell can at most tell the fish that the water is moving.
options.why: Chemicals carry what something is very well, which is how smell tells the fish an eel has been somewhere upstream. What they carry poorly is where.

options.text: Yes, but only while the eel stays still, since a still eel sheds molecules that travel in a straight line from it to the fish.
options.why: Molecules do not travel in straight lines the way light does. Even from a still eel, they drift with the current and linger, so they carry little about where it is.

items.stem: From the next room, a listener hears two things dropped on the floor. The first rings on for a second or two after it lands. The second makes a short, dull sound that stops almost at once. What does the difference most likely tell the listener?

options.text: Something about what the two things are made of, since metal keeps ringing and wood goes quiet almost at once.
options.why: Correct. Sound carries information about the physical makeup of whatever made it. A dropped pan and a dropped book sound different because they are different things.

options.text: Exactly where each one landed, since sound travels in straight lines and carries the direction of its source precisely.
options.why: That describes light, which carries precise direction because it travels in straight lines. Sound bends around obstacles and arrives from every direction at once.

options.text: Only that something happened, since sound says that an event occurred out of sight but nothing about what caused it.
options.why: Sound does tell that something is happening out of sight, but it also carries the makeup of what made it. Ringing on and stopping at once are clues to the material.

options.text: How heavy each one is, since heavy things keep ringing for a long time and light things stop almost at once.
options.why: Weight shows in pitch: heavy things ring at low pitches. How long the ringing lasts is a clue to the material, since metal keeps ringing and wood goes quiet.

items.stem: What is the lateral line?

options.text: A line of sensory organs along each side of a fish’s body that respond to movements of the surrounding water.
options.why: Correct. The lateral line works like touch at a distance, reporting moving water within a body length or two of the fish.

options.text: A line of receptor cells along the inside of a fish’s nose that respond to molecules carried in by the current.
options.why: That describes smell receptors, which tell the fish what something is far better than where. The lateral line responds to moving water along the body.

options.text: A set of organs deep in a fish’s inner ear that respond to rotation of the head, to gravity, and to acceleration.
options.why: That describes the vestibular system, the organs of balance in the inner ear. The lateral line runs along the outside of the fish’s body and responds to moving water.

options.text: A set of receptors in a fish’s muscles, tendons, and joints that report the position and movement of its own body.
options.why: That describes proprioception, the sense of the body’s own position and movement. The lateral line responds to movements of the water around the fish.

items.stem: On a dark night in muddy water, a predatory fish glides past a smaller fish, about one body length from its side, without touching it. Which of the smaller fish’s senses is best placed to report the passing predator?

options.text: Its lateral line, which reports moving water within a body length or two, like touch reaching a short way out.
options.why: Correct. Touch reports only what is in contact with the body, and the lateral line extends something like touch a short way out. A predator gliding past one body length away stirs water the lateral line can feel.

options.text: Its sense of touch, which reports pressure and vibration from anything moving within a body length or two of its skin.
options.why: Touch reports only what is in contact with the body. The predator never touches the fish, so the sense that can report it is the lateral line, which extends something like touch into the water.

options.text: Its sense of smell, which reports where a predator is from the molecules it sheds, even in dark and muddy water.
options.why: Smell works in the dark, but chemicals carry what something is far better than where it is. Smell can tell that a predator has been somewhere upstream, not that one is gliding past right now.

options.text: Its eyes, which report the layout of nearby surfaces with great precision about direction, even when the water is muddy.
options.why: Light does carry precise direction, but anything in the way blocks it, and on a dark night in muddy water there is little light to carry anything.

items.stem: A fish has three ways to learn about an eel: smell, its lateral line, and vision. In a short paragraph, explain which job each of the three is suited to, and why, in terms of how its signal travels or how far it reaches.
items.answer: Smell tells the fish that an eel has been somewhere upstream. Chemicals move slowly, linger, and drift with the current, so they carry what something is far better than where it is. The lateral line tells the fish that something is moving close by. It reports moving water only within a body length or two, extending something like touch a short way into the water. Vision tells the fish where, exactly, something is. Light moves fast and in straight lines, so it carries precise direction at a distance, though anything in the way blocks it.
rubric: Says smell tells the fish what is or has been somewhere upstream, but little about where it is.
Explains smell’s limit by chemicals moving slowly, lingering, or drifting with the current.
Says the lateral line reports movement close by, within about a body length or two, like touch at a short distance.
Says vision tells where, exactly, something is, because light travels fast and in straight lines.

items.stem: Some flowers carry markings that show up only in ultraviolet light. The light reflected from such a flower includes that ultraviolet pattern, yet a person looking at the flower sees no markings. Which limit on what a sense can report does this illustrate?

options.text: A limit set by the receptors, since the human eye filters ultraviolet light out before it reaches them, so they cannot respond to it.
options.why: Correct. A sense reports only what its signal carries, and only to the extent its receptors respond to it. Here the signal carries the markings, but the human eye filters ultraviolet out before it reaches the receptors.

options.text: A limit set by the signal, since light reflected from a flower cannot carry markings, only the flower’s overall color and brightness.
options.why: Here the reflected light does carry the ultraviolet pattern, so the signal is not what falls short. The limit lies with the receptors, which the ultraviolet never reaches.

options.text: A limit set by the ill-posed problem, since many different flowers could have reflected the same light, so the markings cannot be recovered.
options.why: The ill-posed problem is real, but it concerns signals that fit many causes. The trouble here comes earlier: the ultraviolet pattern never reaches the human eye’s receptors.

options.text: A limit set by the light’s path, since ultraviolet light bends around the petals the way sound bends around obstacles and never reaches the eye.
options.why: Bending around obstacles is a property of sound. Light travels in straight lines, and here the ultraviolet does reach the person’s eye, which filters it out before the receptors.

items.stem: Early mammals were probably small animals active mostly at night. What would their eyes most have needed to deliver?

options.text: Sensitivity to dim light, which matters far more in the dark than telling one color from another.
options.why: Correct. For a small animal active mostly at night, catching what little light there is matters far more than color.

options.text: Sharp detail at the center of gaze, which an animal needs for picking fruit and insects out of the leaves.
options.why: Sharp central detail is what a primate picking fruit and insects in daylight needs. At night, with little light, sensitivity matters more.

options.text: Sight of ultraviolet light, which reveals markings and prey that an eye without it cannot see at all.
options.why: Seeing ultraviolet light suits many fish in shallow, sunlit water. An animal active at night needs sensitivity to dim light more.

options.text: Fine discrimination among many colors, which helps an animal pick out ripe food against a background.
options.why: Color matters little at night, when there is little light to compare. Sensitivity to dim light matters far more.

items.stem: Two related species of fish live in the same lake. One feeds near the sunlit surface on small, brightly colored insects. The other lives near the bottom of deep water, where very little light reaches. What difference in what their eyes have to deliver would be expected?

options.text: The deep-water fish needs sensitivity to dim light more than color, while bright light lets the surface fish use color and detail.
options.why: Correct. What a sense has to provide depends on how its owner lives. In dim light, sensitivity matters far more than color. Near the sunlit surface there is light enough for color and detail to help in picking out small, colored insects.

options.text: None, since both receive light under the same physics, and the physics of a signal alone settles what an eye has to deliver.
options.why: Physics sets what light can carry, but what an eye has to deliver also depends on how its owner lives. Two fish in one lake can need very different eyes.

options.text: The deep-water fish needs color more than the surface fish, since telling colors apart makes up for having little light to see by.
options.why: In deep water there is little light, and color matters little when light is scarce. Sensitivity to dim light is what matters there, as it did for early mammals active at night.

options.text: The surface fish needs sensitivity to dim light more, since bright light near the surface is too strong for its receptors to use.
options.why: Bright light is what makes color and detail usable near the surface. It is the fish in dim, deep water that needs sensitivity.

items.stem: A shallow-water fish that sees ultraviolet light, a small mammal active mostly at night, and a primate picking fruit in daylight need quite different things from their eyes. Which conclusion about eyes follows from comparing the three?

options.text: No one of them is the best eye in general; each is good for a way of life, so what an eye must deliver depends on its owner.
options.why: Correct. These are three different answers to the question of what an eye is for. Before asking how an eye works, we have to ask what its owner needs it to deliver.

options.text: The primate’s eye is the best of the three, since sharp detail at the center of gaze is what every eye would deliver if it could.
options.why: Sharp central detail serves a primate picking fruit in daylight. A small animal active at night needs sensitivity to dim light far more.

options.text: The fish’s eye is the best of the three, since it sees light that the other two eyes miss, and seeing more is always better.
options.why: Seeing ultraviolet suits a fish in shallow, sunlit water. Seeing more of the spectrum is not better in general; what matters is what the owner’s way of life needs.

options.text: The three eyes differ by chance, since what an eye must deliver is set by the physics of light, which is the same for all three.
options.why: Physics sets what light can carry, but what an eye must deliver also depends on how its owner lives. The differences track three ways of life, not chance.

pools.title: Never Enough Information, and the Same Thing Again

items.stem: What is an ill-posed problem?

options.text: A problem for which the available information does not settle a single answer, since more than one answer fits that information.
options.why: Correct. A flat image on the retina could have been produced by many different arrangements of objects, and nothing in the image alone settles which one was there. Every sense faces some version of this problem.

options.text: A problem with no answer to be found at all, since the signal reaching the sense carries no information about what caused it.
options.why: The signal does carry information about its cause. It just does not settle a single answer. Brains settle for what can be deduced from it, such as which of two points is nearer.

options.text: A problem of pairing each point in one eye’s image with the point in the other eye’s image that came from the same place in the world.
options.why: That is the correspondence problem, which stereo vision has to solve before it can measure disparity. An ill-posed problem is any problem whose available information does not settle one answer.

options.text: A problem whose answer the signal does settle, but only after a delay, so that the answer is out of date when it arrives.
options.why: That describes delay, a separate problem for a body that acts on old information. An ill-posed problem is not about timing: even with no delay, the information would not settle a single answer.

items.stem: Which term names a problem in which the available information leaves more than one answer open, as when one flat image could have come from many different three-dimensional scenes?

options.text: ill-posed problem
options.why: Correct. Every sense faces a version of it. In hearing, for example, many combinations of sources can produce the same summed wave at the ear.

options.text: correspondence problem
options.why: The correspondence problem is pairing each point in one eye’s image with its partner in the other eye’s image. It is one hard problem stereo vision faces, not the general idea of information that fails to settle an answer.

options.text: depth cue
options.why: A depth cue is a feature of the signal that, given an assumption usually true of the world, indicates how far away something is. Depth cues are one way vision copes with an ill-posed problem, not the problem itself.

options.text: auditory scene analysis
options.why: Auditory scene analysis is grouping the parts of one mixed sound wave into the sources that made them. It is the work of handling hearing’s ill-posed problem, not the name for that kind of problem.

items.stem: In a photograph, a toy car close to the camera takes up exactly the same part of the image as a real car farther down the street. Why can the image alone not settle which car was there?

options.text: A small object nearby and a large object far away can cast the same image, so more than one scene fits it.
options.why: Correct. This is vision’s ill-posed problem. A flat image could have been produced by many different arrangements of objects, and nothing in the image alone settles which arrangement was there.

options.text: An image leaves direction unsettled, so where the car sits has to be worked out before its size can be.
options.why: An image does carry direction: where the light falls already says which direction it came from. What a flat image leaves open here is distance, and with it the size of what was there.

options.text: The two cars sit at different distances, so their images must differ in size, and only blur in the photograph hides it.
options.why: Their images need not differ. A small car near the camera and a large car far from it can fill exactly the same part of the image, which is why the image cannot settle which was there.

options.text: A photograph taken from one place carries no information about the objects in it, only about the light.
options.why: A single image carries a great deal of information, about direction and layout among other things. The trouble is that it does not settle a single answer about size and distance.

items.stem: A single microphone left in a forest records a woodpecker drumming, wind in the leaves, and a stream running, all at once. A program is asked to recover each of the three sounds from the recording. Why is this problem ill-posed?

options.text: The microphone receives one wave, the sum of all three sounds, and many different combinations of sources could produce that same wave.
options.why: Correct. Like each ear, the microphone receives a single pressure wave with every source already added in. Since many combinations of sources produce the same wave, the wave alone does not settle what the sources were.

options.text: The stream is nearer the microphone than the woodpecker, so its sound hides the drumming and leaves no trace of the drumming in the wave.
options.why: That is how occlusion works in vision, where a near object hides the one behind it. In hearing nothing is hidden. Every source is spread across the whole mixture.

options.text: A single microphone cannot record differences in pitch, so the high drumming and the low rush of the stream come out sounding much alike.
options.why: A pressure wave carries pitch, and one microphone records it. The difficulty is that the three sources arrive added together, not that any one of them is missing.

options.text: The three sounds were made out of sight, and sound carries no information about what made it, only that something happened.
options.why: Sound does carry information about what made it: metal keeps ringing, and wood goes quiet almost at once. The problem is that the three sources arrive summed into one wave.

items.stem: Vision and hearing both have to recover separate things from a single signal. In pulling the separate things apart, what difficulty does hearing face that vision does not?

options.text: In vision a near object hides a far one, but the visible parts are usually intact; in hearing nothing is hidden, but every source is spread across the mixture.
options.why: Correct. In vision the parts of a scene that stay visible are usually intact. In hearing every source runs through the whole wave, so each one has to be pulled out of all of it.

options.text: In hearing a loud source hides a quiet one, leaving whatever is still heard of it intact; in vision nothing is hidden, but every object is spread across the whole image.
options.why: That reverses the two senses. Hiding belongs to vision, where a near object covers part of a far one. In hearing every source is spread across the whole mixture.

options.text: Recovering sources from a summed wave is ill-posed, while recovering objects from a flat image is not, since each flat image fits just one scene.
options.why: Hearing’s problem is ill-posed, but so is vision’s. Many different scenes can produce the same flat image, just as many combinations of sources can produce the same summed wave.

options.text: In hearing the sources arrive one after another and have to be held in memory, while in vision every object in a scene arrives at the same moment.
options.why: Sounds made at the same time arrive at the same time, added into one wave. The difficulty is not their order but that every source is spread through the whole of that wave.

items.stem: A passenger sits upright with eyes closed on a train that runs along a straight, level track. At which point in the trip do the inner ear’s sensors for gravity and acceleration give the same signal that tilting the head back would give?

options.text: While the train is speeding up after it pulls out of a station.
options.why: Correct. To any sensor that responds to acceleration, accelerating forward and tilting the head back produce the same signal. So while the train speeds up, these sensors alone cannot tell the passenger’s situation from a backward tilt.

options.text: While the train is cruising at a steady high speed between stations.
options.why: The sensors respond to acceleration, not to speed. At a steady speed on a straight, level track nothing is accelerating, so the signal is the same as sitting still.

options.text: While the train is standing still at a station with its doors open.
options.why: While the train stands still, the sensors respond only to the pull of gravity on an upright head. That is the signal of no tilt at all, not of a backward one.

options.text: While the train is slowing down as it pulls into the next station.
options.why: Slowing down is a change of speed too, but it pushes the passenger forward, away from the seat. A backward tilt matches speeding up, which presses a person into the seat.

items.stem: A motion-simulator ride tilts its seat slowly backward, and the rider feels pressed into the seat as if speeding forward. Why does tilting the seat produce this feeling?

options.text: To an acceleration sensor, a backward tilt and a forward acceleration give the same signal, and the ride’s makers use that on purpose.
options.why: Correct. The organs of balance contain sensors that respond to gravity and to acceleration, and those sensors alone cannot tell a backward tilt from a forward acceleration. The ride is built to exploit the ambiguity.

options.text: The seat presses on the rider’s back, and touch reports any pressure on the back as forward speed, whatever the head is doing.
options.why: Touch does report the pressure of the seat. But the feeling of speeding forward comes from the organs of balance, whose acceleration sensors give the same signal for a backward tilt.

options.text: The tilt is too slow for the inner ear to register, so the rider receives no signal at all and fills in the missing signal with a sense of speed.
options.why: The tilt does register. The sensors for gravity and acceleration respond to it, and what they report is the same signal a forward acceleration would produce.

options.text: The seat carries the rider forward a short way as it tilts backward, and the inner ear reports that real movement as fast travel.
options.why: The seat tilts rather than travels. The feeling of speed comes from the tilt itself, because to an acceleration sensor a backward tilt and a forward acceleration are the same.

items.stem: When the information in a signal cannot settle a single answer, what do brains recover from it?

options.text: What can be deduced from the signal, with what a sense delivers shaped by what the animal needs to do next.
options.why: Correct. Brains do not recover everything. They settle for what the signal can settle, and that is a sensible choice when what matters is the next action, such as fleeing an eel that is nearer than the weed.

options.text: Every property of the scene exactly, by combining the available cues until a single answer remains.
options.why: Brains do not recover everything. Even in a well-lit room with every cue available, people do not judge exact distances reliably.

options.text: Nothing dependable at all, so that an animal’s actions rest on guesses rather than on what its senses report.
options.why: People judge very reliably which of two points is nearer, and an object’s shape. What brains settle for is dependable. It is just not everything.

options.text: The exact distance of each object, which the signal states directly, while shape and order are left unknown.
options.why: That reverses the pattern. People judge order and shape reliably and exact distance poorly, because order and shape are what the signal settles well.

items.stem: In a well-lit room, people look at two cups on a desk. They are asked which cup is nearer, what shape each cup has, and how many centimeters away each cup sits. Which pattern of answers matches measurements of human depth perception?

options.text: Reliable about which cup is nearer and about each cup’s shape, but not reliable about either cup’s exact distance.
options.why: Correct. Judgments of which point is nearer, and of shape, are reliable, though a shape may be seen as somewhat deeper or flatter than it is. Exact distances are not, even in a well-lit room. In one researcher’s phrase, vision prefers “robustness over precision”.

options.text: Reliable about all three, since a well-lit room with every cue available lets vision settle exact distance too.
options.why: Exact distance stays unreliable even in a well-lit room with every cue available. Vision settles for what the signal can settle: order and shape.

options.text: Reliable about the exact distances, but not about which cup is nearer, since order is worked out from the distances.
options.why: That reverses the pattern. Order is judged very reliably, and exact distance is not, so order cannot be computed from the distances.

options.text: Not reliable about order, shape, or distance, since a flat image on the retina carries no information about depth.
options.why: A flat image does not settle depth, but it still carries information about it. People use that information to judge order and shape reliably.

items.stem: An engineer argues that a robot’s vision is failing unless it reports the exact distance, in centimeters, to every object in view. What reply follows from what brains recover when a signal cannot settle the answer?

options.text: A sense is better judged by whether it serves the next action, and reliable order and shape can do that without exact distance.
options.why: Correct. What a sense delivers is shaped by what the animal needs to do next. A fish needs to know that the eel is closer than the weed, and which way the eel is moving, not the eel’s distance in centimeters.

options.text: The engineer is right, since human vision reports exact distances whenever a scene is well lit and every cue is available.
options.why: Human vision does not. Even in well-lit rooms with every cue available, people do not judge exact distances reliably, though they judge order and shape well.

options.text: The engineer asks too little, since a good vision system should report exact distance and exact size, which a flat image settles.
options.why: A flat image does not settle distance or size: a small near object and a large far one can cast the same image. That is what makes the problem ill-posed.

options.text: Distance does not matter for action, so a vision system needs only to report what objects are, and never where they are.
options.why: That overcorrects. Where things are matters a great deal for action. What a sense needs is the part of it that can be deduced reliably, such as which object is nearer.

items.stem: A banana keeps looking yellow from noon to dusk, and a ringtone is recognized whether it rings inside a pocket or across an echoing room. What do the two cases share?

options.text: In each, one thing produces inputs that change a great deal, and yet it is still recognized as the same thing.
options.why: Correct. This is the hardest form of generalization, recognizing the same thing across variation that changes its inputs completely. Each sense faces its own version of it: color in vision, and the ringtone in hearing.

options.text: In each, the input stays nearly the same from one setting to the next, so recognizing the thing again takes no work.
options.why: The input changes a great deal. The light from the banana changes between noon and dusk, and the ringtone changes in loudness, muffling, and echo. Recognizing each as the same is the hard part.

options.text: In each, the observer’s own movement causes most of the change in the input, which must be told apart from the world’s.
options.why: That describes self-caused sensation, a different problem. Here the change comes from the world: the light falling on the banana, and the pocket and room around the phone.

options.text: In each, the input is the sum of several sources, which have to be pulled apart before the thing can be recognized.
options.why: That is hearing’s summed-wave problem. What these two cases share is different: one thing whose input varies a great deal is still treated as one thing.

items.stem: A person reaches into a coat pocket and recognizes their house key by touch, whether gripping it by the ring or by the blade, with bare fingers or through a thin glove. Which problem has the person’s sense of touch solved?

options.text: Touch’s own version of recognizing one thing across inputs that change a great deal, which vision and hearing also face.
options.why: Correct. The same key presses on very different parts of the skin, with very different force and texture, from one grip to the next. Recognizing it across that variation is touch’s version of the problem every sense faces in its own way.

options.text: Touch’s version of separating sources, the problem of pulling the key’s signal out of one sum of every object in the pocket.
options.why: The summed wave is hearing’s problem, since each ear receives every sound added together. What is hard here is that the same key feels very different from one grip to the next.

options.text: Touch’s version of finding direction, which it has to compute by comparing what the two hands feel at once.
options.why: Touch gets location almost for free: which receptors in the skin are pressed says where on the body the touch fell. The problem here is treating changing inputs as one key.

options.text: Touch’s version of finding an affordance, the opportunity for action that the key offers to this particular hand.
options.why: A key does offer the action of turning in a lock, but that is not what is being solved. Treating the feel of the ring, the blade, and the gloved key as one thing is the problem here.

items.stem: Which of these lists the sources of variation that make one object cast very different images on the eye?

options.text: Its angle, its distance, and the lighting, where daylight can be up to a billion times brighter than starlight.
options.why: Correct. An object seen from the front and the side, near and far, or in shade and sunlight casts quite different images. And the overall amount of light varies enormously.

options.text: Its angle and its distance, while lighting barely matters, since daylight is only about ten times brighter than starlight.
options.why: Tenfold is roughly the range one ganglion cell in the retina responds over at any one time. The overall amount of light varies far more: daylight can be up to a billion times brighter than starlight.

options.text: Its distance alone, since turning an object or changing the light on it leaves the image it casts unchanged.
options.why: Turning an object changes its image a great deal, as front and side views show. So does moving it from shade into sunlight.

options.text: Its angle and the lighting, but not its distance, since a near object and a far object cast the same image.
options.why: The same object near and far casts images of different sizes. It is a small near object and a large far one that can cast the same image.

items.stem: Someone proposes that a person recognizes a friend’s face by storing one exact image of it and checking each new image for an exact match. Why would this proposal fail?

options.text: The same face casts very different images at new angles and distances, in shade or sun, and as the amount of light varies enormously.
options.why: Correct. One object casts very different images with every change of angle, distance, and lighting, and daylight can be up to a billion times brighter than starlight. An exact match to one stored image would almost never occur.

options.text: The retina carries no information about direction, so a stored image could never be lined up with a new image of the same face.
options.why: The retina gives direction almost for free, since where light falls says which direction it came from. The trouble is that the face’s image itself changes enormously.

options.text: A stored image would match well, since the image of a face changes very little except when the friend’s expression changes.
options.why: A face’s image changes a great deal even when its expression does not: from the front and the side, near and far, in shade and in sunlight.

options.text: The image would match well in daylight, but in dim light the eye receives no image of a face at all, so nothing could match.
options.why: Dim light changes the image a great deal, but it does not remove it. And even in daylight, a new angle or distance gives an image that would not match the stored one.

items.stem: A white shirt looks white in sunlight at noon, and it still looks white under a yellowish lamp at night, though the light reaching the eye from it is quite different. What does this case show?

options.text: The shirt keeps its apparent color while the light from it changes, which is invariance applied to color.
options.why: Correct. This is color constancy. The light reaching the eye from a surface changes with the light falling on it, yet the surface keeps looking the same color, as a banana keeps looking yellow at noon, at dusk, and under a lamp.

options.text: The light reaching the eye from the shirt barely changes, so its color can simply be read off that light.
options.why: The light from the shirt changes a great deal between sunlight and a yellowish lamp. That the shirt still looks white despite the change is the whole point.

options.text: The person’s own movement changes the light from the shirt, and that change is canceled as self-caused.
options.why: Self-caused sensation is a different problem. Here the change in the light comes from the world, from the lamp that replaced the sunlight.

options.text: A white surface sends the eye the same light under any lamp, so only a white shirt would keep its color this way.
options.why: White is not special here. The light from the shirt does change under the yellowish lamp, and a banana keeps looking yellow at noon, at dusk, and under a lamp too.

items.stem: At sunset, a gray rock lit by reddish light sends the eye the same light that a reddish rock sends at noon. What follows about recovering a surface’s color from the light that comes from it?

options.text: That light mixes the surface with the light falling on it, and nothing in that light alone says how much is due to each.
options.why: Correct. Recovering a surface’s color is ill-posed. A gray surface in reddish light and a reddish surface in daylight can send the same light, so the light alone cannot settle which was there.

options.text: A more precise measurement of the light from the rock would show which rock it is, since the two lights must differ a little.
options.why: The two lights can be the same, so no amount of precision in measuring them would help. The problem is that more than one surface and lighting could produce that light.

options.text: The gray rock really is reddish at sunset, since the color of a surface simply is the light that reaches the eye from it.
options.why: A surface keeps its apparent color while the light from it changes, as a banana keeps looking yellow at dusk. The color of a surface is not the same thing as the light it sends.

options.text: The rock’s color can be recovered only by moving around it, since a moving observer sees the surface from many places.
options.why: Movement gives information about depth, as near things shift faster than far ones. It does not separate the surface from the light falling on it.

items.stem: Recovering the color of a surface is ill-posed in the same sense as recovering a scene from a flat image. What do the two problems share?

options.text: In each, the signal could have come from more than one combination of causes, and nothing in the signal alone says which.
options.why: Correct. The light from a surface mixes the surface and the light falling on it, and a flat image fits many arrangements of objects. In neither case does the signal alone settle the answer.

options.text: In each, a near thing hides part of a far one, so what lies behind has to be filled in before it can be recovered.
options.why: A near object hiding a far one is a feature of scenes, and it has nothing to do with the color of a surface. What the two problems share is a signal that more than one combination of causes could produce.

options.text: In each, the animal’s own movement changes the signal, so what the world did has to be separated from what the animal did.
options.why: Self-caused sensation is a different problem. Both of these problems arise even for an animal holding perfectly still.

options.text: In each, the signal arrives too late to act on, so the answer has to be predicted from what the signal reported earlier.
options.why: Delay is a separate problem for a moving body. These two would be ill-posed even if the signal arrived instantly.

items.stem: A phone’s ringtone sounds loud on a desk, muffled inside a purse, and echoing in a large room, yet a listener recognizes every instance at once as the same sound. Which problem does this show hearing solving?

options.text: Recognizing the same sound across inputs that change a great deal, which is invariance as it arises for sound.
options.why: Correct. Loudness, muffling, and echoes from the walls all change the ringtone’s sound enormously. Treating every instance as the same sound is the invariance problem, posed by hearing.

options.text: Recovering separate sources from one summed wave, since the ringtone reaches each ear added to every other sound.
options.why: That is hearing’s ill-posed problem of pulling sources apart. Recognizing that every changed version is the same ringtone is a different demand.

options.text: Computing the direction of the phone from the differences between what arrives at the two ears.
options.why: Hearing does have to compute direction that way, but the phone’s location is not what is asked about here. The question is how such different sounds are recognized as one.

options.text: Telling a sound the listener caused from one the world caused, as a voice is loudest in its owner’s ears.
options.why: Self-caused sound is a real problem, but the ringtone is caused by the phone. The problem here is recognizing one sound across very different inputs.

items.stem: A listener hears a friend’s ringtone in two settings. In a quiet bedroom it rings muffled under a pillow, the only sound there. At a loud party it rings in plain view on a shelf while music plays. Which describes the main difficulty in each setting?

options.text: In the bedroom, recognizing a sound that muffling has changed; at the party, pulling the ringtone out of one wave summed with the music.
options.why: Correct. Under the pillow the ringtone is the only source, but its sound has changed, which is the invariance problem. At the party it reaches each ear added to the music, and recovering it from that summed wave is ill-posed.

options.text: In the bedroom, pulling the ringtone out of one wave summed with the pillow; at the party, recognizing a sound that the music has changed.
options.why: That swaps the two problems. A pillow muffles the ringtone without adding a second source, and the music at the party is a second source, added into the same wave.

options.text: Each setting poses only the summed-wave problem, since a pillow adds a sound of its own to the ringtone, just as the music does.
options.why: A pillow makes no sound of its own. It changes the ringtone’s sound, which is a problem of recognizing one thing across changed inputs.

options.text: Each setting poses only the invariance problem, since music changes how the ringtone sounds in the same way that a pillow does.
options.why: The music does not change the ringtone itself. It adds a second source, and each ear receives the two summed into one wave.

items.stem: At a crowded party, one microphone records everyone talking at once, and one camera takes a photograph of the same crowd. In a few sentences, explain why recovering each person’s voice from the recording is an ill-posed problem, and in what way it is harder than picking out each person in the photograph.
items.answer: The microphone, like an ear, receives a single pressure wave, the sum of every voice reaching it. Many different combinations of voices could produce that same wave, so the wave alone does not settle what the separate voices were, which is what makes recovering them ill-posed. The recording is also harder than the photograph in one way. In the photograph, a person standing in front hides part of the person behind, but the parts that remain visible are usually intact. In the recording nothing is hidden, but every voice is spread across the whole mixture, so each one has to be pulled out of all of it.
rubric: States that the microphone receives one wave that is the sum of all the voices.
States that many different combinations of sources could produce the same wave, so the wave alone does not settle the answer.
States that in the photograph a nearer person hides part of a farther one, while the parts left visible are usually intact.
States that in the recording nothing is hidden, but every voice is spread across the whole mixture.

items.stem: A pilot is flying level at night through thick cloud, with no view of the ground, when the plane speeds up steadily. In a few sentences, explain why the speeding up could feel to the pilot like the plane’s nose tilting up. Say what the inner ear’s sensors for gravity and acceleration cannot settle on their own.
items.answer: The organs of balance in the inner ear contain sensors that respond to the pull of gravity and to acceleration. To any sensor that responds to acceleration, speeding up forward and tilting back produce the same signal. So when the plane speeds up, the pilot’s sensors give the same signal that a nose-up tilt would give, and the pilot can feel tilted back. These sensors alone cannot tell the two apart. The information they provide does not settle a single answer, which makes this one more ill-posed problem, like the one vision faces with a flat image.
rubric: States that the inner ear’s organs of balance contain sensors that respond to gravity and to acceleration.
States that to a sensor that responds to acceleration, speeding up forward and tilting back produce the same signal.
Concludes that these sensors alone cannot tell whether the plane is speeding up or tilting nose up.
Applies that conclusion to the pilot: steady speeding up in level flight can feel like a nose-up tilt.

items.stem: A red apple sits on a windowsill. At noon it is lit by daylight, and in the evening by a warm, yellowish lamp. In a short paragraph, explain what stays the same for a person looking at the apple, what changes in the light reaching the eye from it, why this is a case of invariance, and why recovering the apple’s color from that light alone is ill-posed.
items.answer: The apple keeps looking red at noon and in the evening. But the light reaching the eye from it changes a great deal, because that light depends on the apple’s surface and on the light falling on it, mixed together. Keeping the same apparent color across that change is invariance applied to color, the same demand as recognizing one object across very different images. And nothing in the light from the apple alone says how much of it is due to the apple and how much to the lamp. Different combinations of surface and lighting could send the eye the same light, so the light does not settle a single answer, which is what makes the problem ill-posed.
rubric: Says the apple keeps looking red, so its apparent color stays the same.
Says the light reaching the eye from the apple changes a great deal between daylight and the lamp.
Identifies keeping the same apparent color across that change as invariance applied to color.
Explains that the light mixes the surface with the light falling on it, and nothing in that light alone says how much is due to each, so the problem is ill-posed.

pools.title: Where Things Are, and Signals of One’s Own Making
pools.covers: reading §8.1.4, §8.1.5 · lecture 8.1 slides direction_comes_free, hearing_computes_direction, direction_on_the_eye, signals_of_ones_own_making

items.stem: For an eye, how do the direction of an object and its distance differ in what has to be done to recover them?

options.text: Direction comes with the image, since where light falls says where it came from, while distance is not laid out on the retina and has to be computed.
options.why: Correct. An eye forms an image, so direction needs no further computation. Distance is not laid out anywhere on the retina, so it has to be worked out by comparing views, from two eyes or from one eye that moves.

options.text: Distance comes with the image, since nearer objects fall on a different part of the retina, while direction has to be computed by comparing the two eyes.
options.why: Direction and distance are swapped here. Where an image falls says which direction the light came from, not how far it traveled, and distance is the one that has to be computed from differences between views.

options.text: Both come with the image, since where light falls on the retina says both which way an object lies and how far away it is from the eye.
options.why: Only direction comes with the image. Distance is not laid out on the retina at all, and has to be computed from differences between views.

options.text: Both have to be computed from differences between views, since a single image on its own says nothing about where anything is.
options.why: A single image already gives direction, because light from each direction falls on a different place on the retina. Only distance needs a comparison of views.

items.stem: A mosquito lands on the back of a person’s left hand while the person is looking the other way. How does the person’s sense of touch say where on the body the mosquito landed?

options.text: Which receptors in the skin are pressed already says where on the body the touch fell, so no further computation is needed.
options.why: Correct. Touch works the way the retina does here. Its receptors are laid out across the skin, so which ones respond gives the location for free.

options.text: The touch is compared between the two hands, and the difference in when each hand feels it gives the place, as two ears do for sound.
options.why: Comparing two sensors is how hearing has to get direction. Touch needs no such comparison, because which receptors are pressed already says where the touch fell.

options.text: The place on the skin has to be combined with where the eyes were pointing before the touch says anything about where on the body it fell.
options.why: Combining with where the eye was pointing is what vision needs to turn a place on the retina into a direction in the world. A place on the skin is already a place on the body.

options.text: The place is computed from differences between the touch now and the touch a moment ago, as a moving eye does for the distance of things.
options.why: Differences between views over time carry information about distance for a moving eye. Where a touch fell needs no such comparison, since which receptors are pressed says it.

items.stem: An animal with one eye covered sways its head from side to side before leaping across a gap. What does the swaying give it that a still eye does not have?

options.text: Views of the gap from different places over time, whose differences carry information about how far away the far side is.
options.why: Correct. Distance is not laid out on the retina, so it has to be computed from differences between views. A moving eye supplies those views one after another, where a second eye would supply them at once.

options.text: The direction of the far side of the gap, which a still eye cannot give, because direction has to be computed from movement.
options.why: Direction is what a still eye gives for free, since where light falls on the retina already says which direction it came from. What the swaying adds is information about distance.

options.text: A wider view of the scene around it, so that it can keep watching for predators while it judges the leap.
options.why: A wide view is what eyes on the sides of the head give. Swaying one eye gives views from different places, and the differences between those views carry information about distance.

options.text: A map of distance across its retina, since a moving eye lays distance out on the retina the way a still eye lays out direction.
options.why: Distance is never laid out on the retina, whether the eye moves or not. The swaying helps because it produces views from different places, and the differences between them carry information about distance.

items.stem: A grazing deer has eyes on the sides of its head, and a fruit-eating monkey has eyes that both face forward. What trade does this difference reflect?

options.text: The deer’s eyes cover a wide view, good for spotting predators, while the monkey’s overlap, which gives the most depth information within arm’s reach.
options.why: Correct. Forward-facing eyes give up much of the wide view. In exchange their fields overlap, so most of the scene is seen twice, and two such views say the most about depth close by, where a primate’s hands do their work.

options.text: The deer’s eyes overlap across most of the scene, good for judging distance, while the monkey’s cover a wide view, good for spotting predators.
options.why: The two arrangements are reversed here. Eyes on the sides of the head cover the wide view, and eyes that face forward overlap.

options.text: The deer’s eyes cover a wide view, while the monkey’s overlap, which gives the most depth information about things far off on the horizon.
options.why: The deer’s side is right, but overlapping fields carry the most depth information at close range, within arm’s reach, not at a great distance.

options.text: The deer’s eyes and the monkey’s give the same depth information, since in both, two eyes see the scene from slightly different places.
options.why: Two eyes see from slightly different places in both animals, but the scene is seen twice only where their fields overlap. Side-facing eyes overlap little, so they trade depth information for width.

items.stem: What is the cochlea?

options.text: The fluid-filled organ of hearing in the mammalian inner ear, laid out so that different frequencies vibrate different places along it.
options.why: Correct. The cochlea’s receptors form a map, but the map is by pitch. Which receptors respond says which frequencies are in a sound, not where the sound came from.

options.text: The organs of balance in the inner ear, which sense rotation and acceleration of the head rather than responding to any sound.
options.why: That is the vestibular system. It sits in the inner ear beside the cochlea, but it senses the head’s own movement, not sound.

options.text: A line of small sensory organs along each side of a fish’s body, which respond to movements of the water flowing around it.
options.why: That is the lateral line, which works like touch at a distance. Fish have no cochlea at all, and hear with other organs of the inner ear.

options.text: A sheet of receptors at the back of the eye, laid out so that light from different directions falls on different places on it.
options.why: That describes the retina, whose layout gives direction for free. The cochlea also lays its receptors out in a map, but by pitch, not by direction.

items.stem: The retina and the cochlea both lay their receptor cells out in a map. Why does the retina’s map give an animal the direction of a stimulus with no further computation, while the cochlea’s map does not?

options.text: The retina’s map is laid out by the direction the light came from, while the cochlea’s is laid out by pitch, which says what frequencies are present.
options.why: Correct. An eye forms an image, so where light falls already says which direction it came from. Which receptors in the cochlea respond says which frequencies a sound contains, and nothing about where it came from.

options.text: The retina has far more receptor cells than the cochlea does, and a map needs a great many receptors before it can carry any direction.
options.why: The number of receptors is not the difference. The difference is what each map is laid out by: direction for the retina, pitch for the cochlea.

options.text: Light reaches both eyes at the same moment, while sound reaches the near ear first, and that delay scrambles the layout of the cochlea’s map.
options.why: The difference in arrival time between the ears is where hearing’s information about direction lies, not something that scrambles it. The cochlea’s map was never a map of direction to begin with.

options.text: The retina’s map is laid out by distance, with nearer things on one part and farther ones on another, and direction follows from distance.
options.why: Distance is not laid out anywhere on the retina; it has to be computed from differences between views. What the retina’s layout gives for free is direction.

items.stem: A cricket hidden in the grass chirps at one steady pitch, first from a listener’s far left and then from the far right. Where must the information that lets the listener tell the two positions apart come from?

options.text: From differences between what arrives at the two ears, since the same pitch excites the same place in each cochlea, whichever side the cricket is on.
options.why: Correct. The cochlea is laid out by pitch, so a chirp of one pitch excites the same receptors from either side. For a mammal, left and right show up only in how the sound at one ear differs from the sound at the other.

options.text: From which receptors in each cochlea respond, since a chirp from the left excites a different place along the cochlea than one from the right.
options.why: The cochlea’s map is not a map of direction. It is a map of pitch, so a cricket of one pitch excites the same place from either side.

options.text: From the cochlea of the nearer ear by itself, since each ear of a listener is directional on its own, whatever pitch the cricket happens to chirp at.
options.why: Each ear is directional by itself in a lizard, whose eardrums are joined through its mouth. A mammal’s ears are isolated from each other, so left and right exist only in the difference between them.

options.text: From the image of the cricket on the retina, since hearing cannot recover direction at all and has to borrow it from vision.
options.why: Hearing does recover direction. It has to compute it, from differences between the two ears, rather than reading it off a receptor sheet the way vision does.

items.stem: A lizard’s two eardrums are connected through its mouth, while a mammal’s ears are acoustically isolated from each other. In a few sentences, explain where a mammal’s information about the direction of a sound has to come from, why it cannot come from either ear alone, and how small the differences involved can be.
items.answer: A mammal has to compute the direction of a sound from the differences between what arrives at its two ears. Because its ears are isolated from each other, neither ear on its own is directional, and left and right exist only in the difference between them. A lizard’s connected eardrums make each of its ears directional by itself. The differences a mammal works with are tiny. A sound straight off to one side reaches the far ear only about seven tenths of a millisecond after the near one, and a shift of one degree changes that difference by roughly ten millionths of a second.
rubric: States that direction has to be computed from differences between what arrives at the two ears.
Says that because a mammal’s ears are isolated, left and right exist only in the difference between them (unlike the lizard’s, where each ear is directional by itself).
Gives the scale of the arrival-time difference for a sound off to one side: under a millisecond (about seven tenths).
Says a one-degree shift changes the timing difference by only millionths of a second (about ten).

items.stem: After one beat of a fish’s tail, the image of an eel falls on different cells of the fish’s retina, although the eel has not moved. What follows about where an image falls on the retina?

options.text: It gives the eel’s direction relative to the eye, so it says where the eel is only once it is combined with where the eye was pointing.
options.why: Correct. Every movement of the eye, the head, or the body moves the image across the retina. A place on the retina is a fact about the eel and the eye together.

options.text: It gives the eel’s distance rather than its direction, so a change in where the image falls means the eel is now nearer or farther away.
options.why: Distance is not laid out on the retina at all. Where the image falls gives direction, and here the direction changed because the eye turned, not because the eel moved.

options.text: It gives the eel’s direction relative to the world, so a change in where the image falls must be an error in the fish’s eye.
options.why: If retinal position gave direction in the world, the image could not move while the eel stayed put. It gives direction relative to the eye, so turning the eye moves the image.

options.text: It gives nothing about the eel’s position until the fish holds still, since an eye forms an image of the scene only while it is still.
options.why: A moving eye still forms an image, and the image still gives direction. The trouble is that the direction is relative to the eye, so it has to be combined with where the eye was pointing.

items.stem: A person sits looking at a lamp. In one case, the person turns their head a little to the left. In another, the head stays still and someone carries the lamp a little to the right. Both times, the lamp’s image slides across the retina by the same amount in the same direction. What does the person need, besides the image, to tell the two cases apart?

options.text: Where the eye was pointing each time, since a place on the retina gives the lamp’s direction relative to the eye and not relative to the room.
options.why: Correct. The same slide of the image can come from the eye turning or from the lamp moving. Only combined with where the eye was pointing does the image say where the lamp is in the room.

options.text: How far away the lamp was each time, since a change of distance and a change of direction slide the lamp’s image across the retina in the same way.
options.why: Distance is not what separates the two cases. What separates them is whether the eye turned or the lamp moved, and only where the eye was pointing can settle that.

options.text: A second eye’s view of the lamp each time, since the differences between two views of the same lamp say whether the lamp itself has moved.
options.why: Differences between two eyes’ views carry information about distance. Both eyes turn with the head, so their images slide together and still leave the two cases looking alike.

options.text: Nothing further, since the image slides the same way both times, and so both times the lamp has moved to the same new place in the room.
options.why: In the first case the lamp did not move at all. The same change on the retina came from two different events, which is why the image alone cannot settle where the lamp is.

items.stem: A frog sitting on a lily pad sees a fly, and the fly’s image falls on one particular place on the frog’s retina. In a short paragraph, explain two different reasons why that place alone does not tell the frog where the fly is, and what further information each reason calls for.
items.answer: First, the place on the retina gives the fly’s direction only relative to the frog’s eye. Every movement of the frog’s eye, head, or body moves the image across the retina. So the place has to be combined with where the eye was pointing before it says where the fly is in the world. Second, the place says nothing about how far away the fly is, because distance is not laid out on the retina. Distance has to be computed. The information for it lies in differences between views: the views of the two eyes, which see the scene from slightly different places, or the views of one eye as it moves over time.
rubric: States that a place on the retina gives direction relative to the eye, not relative to the world.
Says the place has to be combined with where the eye was pointing, because movements of the eye, head, or body move the image.
States that distance is not laid out on the retina, so it has to be computed.

Names differences between views as where the information for distance lies, from two eyes at different places or from one eye moving over time. (A depth cue present in a single image is also acceptable.)

items.stem: What is reafference?

options.text: Sensation caused by the animal’s own movement, such as the sweep of the scene across its eyes when it turns.
options.why: Correct. Reafference is named by its cause. Whatever the sense, a change in input that the animal’s own movement produced is reafference.

options.text: Sensation caused by events in the world, such as the sweep of a moving shadow across its eyes while it holds still.
options.why: That is exafference, sensation caused by the world independent of what the animal is doing. Reafference is the self-caused kind.

options.text: The sense of the body’s own position and movement, such as knowing where a limb is, from receptors in muscles and joints.
options.why: That is proprioception, one of the senses that respond to the animal’s movement. Reafference is not a sense but a kind of sensation, picked out by what caused it.

options.text: A copy of a movement command, such as the command for a turn, kept so its expected effects can be compared with the senses.
options.why: That is an efference copy. It is a copy of a command, not a sensation. Reafference is the sensation the movement itself causes.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “Sensation caused by events in the world, independent of the animal’s own movement”.

options.text: exafference
options.why: Correct. Exafference is the world-caused kind of sensation. Its counterpart, reafference, is sensation caused by the animal’s own movement.

options.text: reafference
options.why: Reafference is the other kind: sensation caused by the animal’s own movement. The two are told apart by their cause, not by which receptors respond.

options.text: proprioception
options.why: Proprioception is a sense, the sense of the body’s own position and movement from receptors in muscles, tendons, and joints. Exafference is not a sense but a kind of sensation, picked out by what caused it.

options.text: efference copy
options.why: An efference copy is a copy of a movement command, kept so that the expected sensory effects of the movement can be compared with what the senses report. It is a signal from inside the animal, not a sensation the world causes.

items.stem: A cat walks slowly along a hallway, and its whiskers brush the wall as it goes. Later, sitting quietly, it feels its whiskers bent by a breeze from an open window. How should each sensation be classified?

options.text: The brushing is reafference, since the cat’s own walking caused it, and the bending is exafference, since the breeze caused it while the cat did nothing.
options.why: Correct. What decides is the cause of the change. The wall stayed put, and the cat’s own walking brought its whiskers against it. The breeze changed the whisker input with no movement from the cat at all.

options.text: The brushing is exafference, because the wall is part of the world, and the bending is exafference too, because the breeze is part of the world.
options.why: Here the sensations are sorted by what was touched rather than by what caused the change. The wall is part of the world, but it changed the input only because the cat walked into it, so the brushing is reafference.

options.text: The brushing and the bending are the same kind of sensation, because both of them bend the same whiskers and stimulate the same receptors at their roots.
options.why: The same receptors respond, which is exactly why the problem is hard, as with the crayfish walking into a rock or touched by a predator. The kind of sensation is decided by its cause, and the causes here differ.

options.text: The brushing is exafference, because the cat did not mean to touch the wall, and the bending is reafference, because the cat’s whiskers moved.
options.why: Whether the cat meant to touch the wall does not matter; its own movement caused the brushing. And whiskers moved by a breeze are moved by the world, which makes that sensation exafference.
