items.stem: An electric fish’s tail bend changes the electrical input along its body far more than nearby prey does. A primate’s eye jump sweeps the whole image across the retina. A voice is loudest in its owner’s own ears. What do these three cases have in common?

options.text: A signal caused by the animal’s own movement can be far larger than the signal from the world, and can drown it out.
options.why: Correct. In each case the self-caused change is bigger than the change the world produces: ten to a hundred times bigger, for the electric fish. That is the scale of the problem self-caused signals pose.

options.text: Self-caused signals are small next to those from the world, so they matter mainly when the world itself is very quiet.
options.why: The reverse is true in every one of these cases. A tail bend, an eye jump, and one’s own voice all produce changes larger than most of what the world produces.

options.text: Each sense is turned down while the animal moves, so the signal its own movement causes does not reach the rest of its brain.
options.why: Dimming a sense during movement is one way of handling self-caused signals, but these cases are about the problem, not a way of handling it. The self-caused signals in them are large and do arrive.

options.text: Each sense reports with a delay, so what the animal senses is about where things were a moment ago, not where they are now.
options.why: Delay is a real problem for a moving body, but it is a different one. These cases are about the size of self-caused signals compared with the world’s.

items.stem: A person eating crunchy cereal can barely make out a quiet conversation in the next room, yet hears it easily the moment they stop chewing. Which problem is this an example of?

options.text: The crunch the person makes is far louder at their own ears than the conversation, so a self-caused signal swamps one from the world.
options.why: Correct. Chewing is the person’s own movement, and the crunch it makes is much louder at their own ears than the faint voices. Self-caused signals can be far larger than the world’s and drown them out.

options.text: Hearing has to compute where a sound comes from, from differences between the two ears, and the conversation is out of sight in the next room.
options.why: Hearing does compute direction that way, whether or not the person is chewing. So direction cannot be why the conversation becomes easy to hear once the chewing stops.

options.text: A sound takes time to travel, so by the time the conversation reaches the person, what it says about the people talking is already out of date.
options.why: The delay is the same whether the person chews or not. What changes when the chewing stops is that a loud self-caused sound is no longer drowning out the world’s.

options.text: The cochlea lays its receptors out by pitch, so it can register only one sound at a time, and the louder sound takes the place of the quieter one.
options.why: The cochlea’s map by pitch says which frequencies are present, and many can be present at once. The trouble is the size of the self-caused sound, not a limit of one sound at a time.

items.stem: Someone claims that telling self-caused sensation from world-caused sensation is a problem that arose with the vertebrates. Which observation counts against the claim?

options.text: Crayfish and flies, animals without backbones, both treat their own movement differently from movement in the world around them.
options.why: Correct. The problem, and ways of handling it, came before the vertebrates. Its origin is placed in the Cambrian, when fast animals with jointed bodies and image-forming eyes began producing self-caused signals in floods.

options.text: An electric fish’s own tail bend changes the electrical input along its body ten to a hundred times more than nearby prey does.
options.why: That is a real case of a self-caused signal swamping the world’s, but an electric fish is a vertebrate. It fits the claim rather than counting against it.

options.text: A primate’s eyes jump about three times a second, and each jump sweeps the whole image of the world across the retina.
options.why: That shows how large self-caused signals can be, but primates are vertebrates. The observation that counts against the claim has to come from an animal without a backbone.

options.text: A person’s own voice is louder in their own ears than in the ears of anyone else listening to them from across the room.
options.why: That is a self-caused signal drowning out the world’s, but in a vertebrate. It leaves the claim about vertebrates untouched.

items.stem: According to the reading, what two sources of information does an animal have about its own movement?

options.text: The commands it sends to its muscles, and senses that respond to the movement itself.
options.why: Correct. One source is the commands the animal sends to its muscles. The other is the vestibular system and proprioception, which respond to the movement itself.

options.text: The sensations its own movement causes, and the sensations the world causes.
options.why: Those are reafference and exafference, the two kinds of sensation the animal has to tell apart. They are what the sources of information about movement are needed for, not the sources themselves.

options.text: The image on its retina, and the differences between what arrives at its two ears.
options.why: The retina and the ears report about the world, mixed with whatever the animal’s movement does to them. The two sources about the animal’s own movement are its commands and the senses that respond to the movement.

options.text: The vestibular system and the cochlea, the two organs of hearing and balance in the inner ear.
options.why: The vestibular system is one of the senses that respond to the movement itself, but the cochlea is the organ of hearing. The two sources are the commands to the muscles and the senses of the movement.

items.stem: A person turns their own head to look to the left. Later, a barber holding the same person’s head turns it to the left by the same amount while the person stays relaxed. Which source of information about the head’s movement does the person have in the first case but not in the second?

options.text: The commands sent to the neck muscles, since a head moved by someone else’s hands moves without any command from the person it belongs to.
options.why: Correct. The two sources are the commands an animal sends to its muscles and the senses that respond to the movement itself. The barber’s turn still moves the head, so those senses still respond. What is missing is the command.

options.text: The vestibular system’s report of the head’s rotation, since the balance organs respond to a turn of the head only when the person makes it.
options.why: The vestibular system senses rotation and acceleration of the head whatever turned it. The barber’s turn rotates the head just as much, so the balance organs respond both times.

options.text: Proprioception from the neck’s muscles and joints, since those receptors respond when the person’s own muscles do the work, and not otherwise.
options.why: Proprioception senses the body’s own position and movement, and the neck moves in both cases. Those receptors respond to the movement itself, whoever produced it.

options.text: Touch from the skin of the head and neck, since those receptors report a turn of the head when the person’s own muscles cause it, and not otherwise.
options.why: Touch reports what is in contact with the body, and the barber’s hands on the head give it more to report, not less. What the person lacks when the barber turns the head is a command.

items.stem: A person walking briskly through tall grass misses a small insect crawling on their ankle, yet notices it at once after stopping to stand still. In a few sentences, explain what makes the insect hard to notice while the person walks, and name the two sources of information the person has about their own walking.
items.answer: While the person walks, every step jolts the leg and brushes grass and clothing against the skin. Those sensations are caused by the person’s own movement, and they are far larger than the faint touch of the insect. A self-caused signal like that can drown out a signal from the world, which is why the insect is easy to notice once the walking stops. The person has two sources of information about their own walking. One is the commands they send to their leg muscles. The other is the senses that respond to the movement itself: the vestibular system in the inner ear, and proprioception from receptors in the muscles, tendons, and joints.
rubric: Says the sensations from walking (the jolts, the brushing grass and clothing) are caused by the person’s own movement, while the insect’s touch comes from the world.
Says those self-caused sensations are much larger than the insect’s touch and can drown it out.
Names the commands sent to the muscles as one source of information about the walking.
Names senses that respond to the movement itself (the vestibular system, proprioception, or both) as the other source.

items.stem: What is the vestibular system?

options.text: The organs of balance in the inner ear, which sense rotation of the head, gravity, and acceleration.
options.why: Correct. The vestibular system is one of the senses that respond to the animal’s own movement. It senses how the head is turning and accelerating, and the pull of gravity on it.

options.text: The fluid-filled organ of hearing in the inner ear, with different frequencies vibrating different places.
options.why: That is the cochlea. It sits in the inner ear beside the organs of balance, but its job is hearing, and its map is by pitch.

options.text: The sense of the body’s own position and movement, from receptors in the muscles and joints.
options.why: That is proprioception, the other sense that responds to the animal’s movement. Its receptors are in the muscles, tendons, and joints, not in the inner ear.

options.text: The line of small sensory organs along a fish’s sides, which respond to moving water.
options.why: That is the lateral line, which works like touch at a distance. It responds to moving water around the body, not to the turning of the head.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “The sense of the body’s own position and movement, from receptors in the muscles, tendons, and joints”.

options.text: proprioception
options.why: Correct. Proprioception, with the vestibular system, makes up the senses that respond to the animal’s own movement, one of its two sources of information about that movement.

options.text: vestibular system
options.why: The vestibular system also senses movement, but its receptors are the organs of balance in the inner ear, and it senses rotation and acceleration of the head.

options.text: reafference
options.why: Reafference is not a sense but a kind of sensation: whatever input the animal’s own movement causes, through any sense.

options.text: efference copy
options.why: An efference copy is a copy of a movement command, not a sense. The commands are the other source of information about movement, alongside senses like this one.

items.stem: Lying still in a dark room with eyes closed, a person can tell that one knee is bent and the other is straight. Which sense supplies this, and from where?

options.text: Proprioception, from receptors in the muscles, tendons, and joints that respond to the body’s own position.
options.why: Correct. The angle of a knee is part of the body’s own position, which is what proprioception senses, and its receptors lie in the muscles, tendons, and joints.

options.text: The vestibular system, from the organs of balance in the inner ear that respond to the position of each limb.
options.why: The vestibular system senses rotation and acceleration of the head. It says nothing about the angle of a knee.

options.text: Touch, from receptors in the skin of the legs that say where on the body something is pressing on them.
options.why: Touch says where on the body something is pressing, such as the bed against the skin. The bend of a joint is the body’s own position, which proprioception senses.

options.text: Reafference, from the sensations that bending and straightening the knee produced as the person moved.
options.why: Reafference is a kind of sensation, picked out by its cause, not a sense. And the person is lying still, so no movement is producing sensation now.

pools.title: A Slow Body, and Moving in Order to Perceive

items.stem: What is a saccade?

options.text: A quick jump of the eyes to a new target, lasting only tens of milliseconds from start to finish.
options.why: Correct. A saccade jumps the eyes to a new target and is over in tens of milliseconds, before any feedback from vision could arrive to correct it.

options.text: A fast turn of the eyes opposite to a turn of the head, keeping the image steady on the retina.
options.why: That is the vestibulo-ocular reflex, which steadies the eyes while the head turns. A saccade is a quick jump of the eyes to a new target.

options.text: The sweep of the whole image across the retina that a movement of the animal’s own eyes produces.
options.why: That sweep is reafference, sensation caused by the animal’s own movement. A saccade does produce such a sweep, but the saccade is the eye movement itself, a quick jump to a new target.

options.text: A copy of the command that moves the eyes, kept so that the expected image motion can be compared with what the eyes report.
options.why: That is an efference copy, a copy of a movement command kept for comparison with what the senses report. A saccade is the eye movement itself, a quick jump to a new target.

items.stem: A light appears off to the right of where a person is looking, and the person’s eyes jump toward it. While the eyes are still jumping, the light moves a little farther to the right. What happens to the eyes?

options.text: The jump ends where the light was, and a second jump is needed to reach the light’s new position.
options.why: Correct. A saccade lasts only tens of milliseconds, and news from vision takes about a tenth of a second to become a correction. The jump is over before any correction could arrive, so a second saccade is needed.

options.text: The jump bends partway toward the light’s new position, steered by what the eyes see while they are moving.
options.why: Steering the jump partway would need feedback from vision during it. A saccade is over in tens of milliseconds, long before that feedback could arrive, so the correction comes only with a second saccade.

options.text: The jump halts partway, and the eyes hold still there until vision reports where the light has gone.
options.why: A saccade does not pause to wait for news from vision. It is over too quickly for that news to arrive, so the eyes land where the jump was aimed and a second saccade follows.

options.text: The jump lands on the light’s new position, because the command for the jump is updated as the light moves.
options.why: Nothing updates the jump once it has begun. A saccade is over in tens of milliseconds, before news of the light’s move could arrive, so the eyes land where the light was and a second saccade follows.

items.stem: Why can keeping the eyes steady while the head turns not wait for vision?

options.text: News of an image slip takes about a tenth of a second to become a correction, so each correction would answer a slip that had already changed.
options.why: Correct. Feedback that arrives late tends to overshoot and oscillate, because each correction responds to a situation that no longer exists. Steadying the eyes by vision would always mean correcting an old error.

options.text: Vision is switched off whenever the head turns, so no news of the image slipping reaches the nervous system until the head has stopped turning.
options.why: The trouble is not that vision is turned off. News that the image has slipped does arrive, but about a tenth of a second late, and a correction based on it would answer a situation that had already changed.

options.text: A flat image on the retina fits many different scenes, so vision cannot settle how far the image has slipped as the head turns.
options.why: A flat image does fit many scenes, but that ill-posed problem concerns recovering the scene, not detecting a slip. Vision does report the slip. The trouble is that its news arrives about a tenth of a second late.

options.text: The eyeballs keep growing and the eye muscles tire, so a correction worked out from vision would soon stop fitting the eye.
options.why: A changing body is a separate problem, and it is why the mapping from command to outcome has to keep being relearned. Steadying cannot wait for vision because vision’s news of a slip arrives too late.

items.stem: Keeping the eyes steady while the head turns, and jumping the eyes to a new target, both run into the slowness of feedback from vision. How do the two cases differ?

options.text: During steadying, feedback from vision would arrive but late, and steering by it would tend to overshoot; a jump is over before any feedback could arrive.
options.why: Correct. News of an image slip takes about a tenth of a second to become a correction, which is too late to steer steadying by. A saccade lasts only tens of milliseconds, so it is finished before that news could arrive at all.

options.text: During steadying, feedback from vision arrives in time to hold the eyes on target as the head turns; a jump is over before any feedback could arrive.
options.why: The jump half is right, but steadying cannot wait for vision either. News of a slip arrives about a tenth of a second late, and feedback that late tends to overshoot and oscillate.

options.text: During steadying, feedback from vision would arrive but late, and steering by it would tend to overshoot; a jump is slow enough to be corrected partway.
options.why: The steadying half is right, but a saccade lasts only tens of milliseconds. It is over before feedback could arrive, so a target that moves during the jump calls for a second saccade.

options.text: During steadying, feedback from vision would arrive but late, and steering by it would be steady but slow; a jump is over before any feedback could arrive.
options.why: The jump half is right, but late feedback does more than slow a correction down. Each correction responds to a situation that no longer exists, so feedback a tenth of a second late tends to overshoot and oscillate.

items.stem: In an unfamiliar shower, hot water takes several seconds to travel through the pipe after the tap is turned. A person turns the tap toward hot, still feels cold water, and turns it farther. Soon the water is scalding, so the person turns it far back, and before long it is cold again. Why do the person’s corrections keep swinging between too hot and too cold?

options.text: The water reaching the skin reflects where the tap was set a while earlier, so each correction responds to a situation that no longer exists.
options.why: Correct. The swinging is the problem of delayed feedback that engineers know well. Feedback that arrives late overshoots and oscillates, which is also why steadying the eyes cannot wait for a report from vision a tenth of a second old.

options.text: The hand turning the tap keeps changing its strength from one turn to the next, so the same turn of the tap gives a different result each time.
options.why: That would be the problem of a changing body, which makes the mapping from command to outcome need relearning. The hand in the shower is the same throughout; the corrections swing because the water reports old news.

options.text: The feel of the water is given in the skin’s terms rather than the tap’s, so the person cannot work out which way the tap should be turned.
options.why: That is the problem of the wrong coordinates, which arises when a sensory report must become a motor command. The person knows which way is hotter; the trouble is that each correction acts on information seconds old.

options.text: The feel of the water on the skin cannot settle how hot the water in the pipe is, so each turn of the tap rests on a guess about an unseen cause.
options.why: Senses never fully settle their causes, but the person needs only the temperature of the water, and the skin reports it. The trouble is that the report arrives seconds after the turn that produced it.

items.stem: Why does the mapping from a movement command to its outcome have to keep being relearned?

options.text: The body keeps changing, as heads and eyeballs grow, muscles tire or weaken, and new glasses change how the world lines up on the retina.
options.why: Correct. A command that once produced a given outcome produces a different one once the body has changed, so the mapping between them has to keep being relearned.

options.text: Signals from the senses arrive about a tenth of a second late, so any outcome they report has already been altered by the next command.
options.why: That is the problem of delay, which is why some corrections cannot wait for feedback. Relearning is needed because the body that carries out the command keeps changing.

options.text: A place on the retina has to become angles at the shoulder, elbow, and wrist, and that conversion changes with every turn of the eyes.
options.why: That is the problem of the wrong coordinates. The conversion does depend on where the eyes and head point, but that changes from moment to moment whether or not the body changes. Relearning is needed because the body itself changes.

options.text: The world keeps changing as objects move about, so a command that reached an object a moment ago no longer reaches where it is now.
options.why: A moving target calls for aiming at where it will be, which is a problem of delay. Relearning the mapping is needed because the body keeps changing, so the same command stops producing the same outcome.

items.stem: In one year a twelve-year-old grows ten centimeters, and the arms lengthen along with the rest of the body. For a while, the child keeps knocking over cups when reaching for them, though the child’s eyesight is good and the cups are in plain view. What problem is the child’s nervous system facing?

options.text: The same command to the arm now carries the hand farther than it used to, so the mapping from command to outcome has to be relearned.
options.why: Correct. Growth is one of the ways the body keeps changing. When it changes, a command no longer produces the outcome it used to, and the mapping from command to outcome has to be learned again.

options.text: News of where the cup is arrives too late to guide the hand, so each reach is aimed at where the cup was a tenth of a second earlier.
options.why: Delay matters for a target that moves, but these cups sit still, so where they were is where they are. What has changed is the child’s body.

options.text: The cup’s place on the retina gives its direction relative to the eye, so the child cannot work out where the cup is relative to the body.
options.why: Turning a place on the retina into a command for the body is a real problem, but every reach poses it, at any age. What is new this year is the body, so the same command now has a different outcome.

options.text: The cup’s image on the retina fits many different scenes, so the child cannot tell how far away the cup is until the hand touches it.
options.why: Every sense faces an ill-posed problem, but that does not explain clumsiness that comes with a growth spurt. The arm is longer, so the old mapping from command to outcome no longer fits.

items.stem: A target is described in one way by where its image falls on the retina, and must be described in another way before it can be reached. How do the two descriptions relate?

options.text: The place on the retina must be turned into angles at the shoulder, elbow, and wrist, and the angles it calls for depend on where the eyes and head point.
options.why: Correct. One sensory map has to be turned into a different motor map, and the turning depends on where the eyes and head are pointing at the moment.

options.text: The place on the retina already gives the angles at the shoulder, elbow, and wrist, since the retina lays out directions in the same way the arm does.
options.why: A place on the retina gives direction relative to the eye, not a set of joint angles. The two descriptions are in different coordinates, so one has to be turned into the other.

options.text: The place on the retina must be turned into angles at the shoulder, elbow, and wrist, and each place on the retina always calls for the same set of angles.
options.why: The conversion is needed, but it is not fixed. Which angles a retinal place calls for changes with where the eyes and head are pointing.

options.text: The place on the retina gives no direction at all, so the angles at the shoulder, elbow, and wrist must be found by moving the arm until it touches.
options.why: Where light falls on the retina does give its direction, with no further computation. The trouble is that the direction is relative to the eye, and the reach needs joint angles.

items.stem: A seated person looking straight ahead sees a cup at the very center of gaze. Later, still seated facing the same way but with eyes and head turned well to the left, the person sees a second cup, also at the very center of gaze. The two images fall on the same place on the retina. Will the same angles at the shoulder, elbow, and wrist reach both cups?

options.text: No, because the same place on the retina calls for different joint angles depending on where the eyes and head are pointing.
options.why: Correct. A place on the retina gives direction relative to the eye. Turning it into joint angles depends on where the eyes and head point, and for the two cups they point in different directions, so the cups need different reaches.

options.text: Yes, because the same place on the retina always stands for the same direction, and so calls for the same joint angles.
options.why: The same retinal place stands for the same direction relative to the eye, not relative to the body. With the head turned, that direction lies elsewhere, and so do the joint angles.

options.text: No, because the second cup is seen after a head turn, and a head turn makes the signal about the cup arrive later.
options.why: Nothing about the head turn makes the signal about the second cup older than the signal about the first. The reaches differ because the same retinal place stands for a different direction once the eyes and head have turned.

options.text: Yes, because the two cups are at the center of gaze, where the image is sharpest and the direction of a target is known exactly.
options.why: The center of gaze gives a target’s direction relative to the eye. That direction must still be combined with where the eyes and head point before it says how to move the arm.

items.stem: A small fish strikes at a water flea drifting in the current. Why must the strike be aimed at where the flea will be, rather than at where the fish sees it?

options.text: The fish’s signals report only where the flea was, and the flea keeps moving while the signals reach the fish and the strike is carried out.
options.why: Correct. The fish acts on old information. Its signals report where the flea was, so the strike has to be aimed ahead, at where the flea will be when the strike arrives.

options.text: The fish’s eyes report the flea’s place relative to the eye, and the strike need only correct for that to land where the flea is now.
options.why: The eyes do report the flea relative to the eye, and that has to be converted. But the report is also old, and the flea keeps drifting, so aiming at where it is now would still miss.

options.text: The fish’s lateral line reports the flea sooner than its eyes do, so the strike is aimed by the faster sense rather than by what vision reports.
options.why: The lateral line does sense movement in the water close by, but no sense reports the flea’s present position. Every signal is already old when it arrives, so the strike is aimed ahead.

options.text: The fish’s own swimming pushes the flea through the water, so the strike has to allow for the shove the fish’s body gives the flea.
options.why: The fish’s movement does stir the water, but the flea drifts with the current whatever the fish does. The strike is aimed ahead because the fish’s signals report only where the flea was.

items.stem: A swallow flying fast snatches insects out of the air. Which description fits the problem its nervous system has to solve for each catch?

options.text: Old signals about where the insect was relative to the eye must become a current command, in the body’s terms, aimed at where the insect will be.
options.why: Correct. The swallow’s catch poses the same problem as the fish’s strike at a water flea. The signals are old and eye-centered, and the catch needs a current, body-centered command aimed ahead of the insect.

options.text: Old signals about where the insect was relative to the eye can be used as they are, since the swallow flies toward wherever the eye is pointed.
options.why: The signals cannot be used as they are. They report where the insect was, and they are in the eye’s coordinates, while the catch is made by the body.

options.text: Current signals about where the insect is relative to the body must become a command aimed at where it is, since vision reports with no delay.
options.why: No sense reports with no delay. The swallow’s signals are already old when they arrive, and they report the insect relative to the eye, not the body.

options.text: Old signals about where the insect was relative to the body must become a command aimed at where it was, since it moves little in so short a time.
options.why: The signals are old, and a fast swallow and a flying insect both cover ground while they travel, so aiming at where the insect was would miss. And the signals start out relative to the eye, so they still have to be turned into the body’s terms.

items.stem: A passenger on a moving train looks out the window. Fence posts beside the track sweep past quickly, while hills far away creep by slowly. What does the difference in speed give the passenger?

options.text: Information about which things are near and which are far, made available by traveling, which a passenger on a stopped train would not have.
options.why: Correct. Moving changes what reaches the senses in lawful ways: near things shift across the eyes faster than far ones. That lawful change is information a stationary observer lacks.

options.text: A disturbance caused by the passenger’s own movement, which carries nothing about the scene and has to be removed before the scene can be seen.
options.why: The sweep does come from the passenger’s own movement, but it is not empty. Because it changes lawfully with distance, it carries information about the scene that holding still would not.

options.text: An illusion of motion, since the posts and hills are standing still, and only a passenger on a stopped train sees the scene as it truly is.
options.why: The posts and hills do stand still, but their images move, and the difference in speed between near and far is lawful. It is information about distance, not an error.

options.text: An affordance, since how fast things sweep past tells the passenger which of them could be reached and touched from the window.
options.why: An affordance is an opportunity for action that a place or object offers to a particular body. The difference in speed says which things are near and which far, not which actions the scene offers the passenger’s body.

items.stem: A fish swims through still, murky water past a rock it cannot see. As it passes, the water flowing along its sides changes shape around the rock, and its lateral line responds. What is true of that signal?

options.text: It is caused by the fish’s own swimming, and it is also how the fish senses that the rock is there.
options.why: Correct. The flood of self-caused signals and the information gained by moving are one fact seen from two sides. The fish’s own movement produces the signal, and that signal is how much of the sensing gets done.

options.text: It is caused by the fish’s own swimming, so it carries nothing about the rock and has to be removed.
options.why: Self-caused signals can drown out the world’s, but the flow along the fish’s sides changes lawfully with what the fish passes. Moving makes the rock’s presence available as information.

options.text: It is caused by the rock alone, since a signal that tells the fish about the world cannot be self-caused.
options.why: Without the fish’s swimming there would be no flow along its sides to change shape. A signal can be self-caused and still carry information about the world.

options.text: It is caused by the rock alone, and the fish could sense the rock just as well while holding still.
options.why: A still fish in still water would have no flow along its sides for the rock to change. Movement makes information about the rock available, which a stationary animal lacks.

items.stem: What is an affordance?

options.text: An opportunity for action that a place or object offers to a particular body, such as a gap one animal can pass and another cannot.
options.why: Correct. An affordance depends on the place and the body together. The same drop is a small step to a large animal and a cliff to a small one.

options.text: A change in what reaches the senses that an animal’s own movement produces, such as near things shifting across the eyes faster than far ones.
options.why: That describes the lawful change that moving produces in the senses, which gives information a still animal lacks. An affordance is an opportunity for action a place offers to a particular body.

options.text: A process that works out the movement command needed to produce a wanted outcome, such as the joint angles that would reach a cup.
options.why: That is an inverse model, which runs from a wanted outcome to the command that produces it. An affordance is an opportunity for action a place or object offers to a particular body.

options.text: Movement or energy that an animal produces in order to sense, such as a fish stirring the water to feel the objects around it.
options.why: That is active sensing. An affordance is not something the animal produces, but an opportunity for action that a place or object offers to its body.

items.stem: A cat walks easily along the narrow top of a garden fence. A large dog that tries the same fence-top cannot keep its footing and jumps down. What does this case show about the fence-top as an affordance?

options.text: Walking along it is an opportunity the fence-top offers to the cat’s body and not to the dog’s, since it depends on fence and body together.
options.why: Correct. An affordance is an opportunity for action that a place offers to a particular body. A narrow fence-top is a path to a cat and not to a large dog, just as the same drop is a step to one animal and a cliff to another.

options.text: Walking along it is an opportunity the fence-top offers to every animal, and the dog fails only because it has not perceived that opportunity.
options.why: That confuses the affordance with perceiving it. Perceiving an affordance is a separate problem, but the fence-top’s affordance itself differs for the two animals, because the dog’s body does not fit it.

options.text: Walking along it is a property of the cat’s body alone, since the cat would keep its footing on any surface at all, however narrow it is.
options.why: An affordance depends on the place as well as the body. A surface narrow enough would defeat the cat too.

options.text: Walking along it is a fact about how the cat perceives the fence-top, since the cat sees the narrow top as wider than it really is.
options.why: Nothing suggests the cat misjudges the width. The fence-top really does offer walking to the cat’s body and not to the dog’s, whatever either animal perceives.

items.stem: A traveler puts on a wide backpack for the first time. At the first narrow doorway, the traveler walks straight in as usual, and the pack catches on the frame. By the end of the day, the traveler turns sideways at each narrow doorway, and only at the narrow ones, without thinking. What happened, in terms of affordances?

options.text: The pack changed what a narrow doorway offers the traveler’s body, and the traveler’s perception of that change took practice to catch up.
options.why: Correct. An affordance depends on the place and the body together, so a wider body changes what a doorway offers. Perceiving an affordance is a separate problem, and the traveler’s perception was recalibrated with practice.

options.text: A narrow doorway offered the traveler’s body the same passage as before, since the doorway never changed, and only the perception was wrong.
options.why: The doorway did not change, but the traveler’s body did. An affordance belongs to the place and the body together, so the pack changed what the doorway offers.

options.text: Practice changed what a narrow doorway offers the traveler’s body, widening the gap it could pass, while the perception stayed the same.
options.why: That reverses the two. The pack changed what the doorway offers, and practice changed the traveler’s perception of it, which is the part that can be recalibrated.

options.text: Neither the doorways nor the traveler’s perception of them changed, and the traveler simply formed a habit of turning sideways.
options.why: A habit alone would not pick out the narrow doorways. Turning sideways only at those means the traveler is judging which gaps the wider body can pass, a perceived affordance that practice recalibrated.

items.stem: In her first week using a wheelchair, a woman often stops short at gaps the chair could pass through. Within a few weeks she judges such gaps correctly at a glance. What changed?

options.text: Her perception of which gaps the chair can pass was recalibrated by practice, while the gaps offered the same passage all along.
options.why: Correct. Perceiving an affordance is a separate problem from the affordance itself. The gaps were wide enough from the start; what practice changed was her perception of which ones were.

options.text: The gaps came to offer passage to her chair as she practiced, while her perception of which gaps it could pass stayed the same.
options.why: The gaps were passable from the start. What changed was her perception of them, which is the part that practice recalibrates.

options.text: Her vision grew sharper with practice, so she could see the edges of each gap more precisely than she could in her first week.
options.why: Nothing about her eyes needed to change. What she learned was which gaps her chair and body could pass, a perceived affordance that practice recalibrated.

options.text: Her perception came to need no interpretation, since with practice the information in her senses came to settle what the gaps were.
options.why: The signals reaching the senses never fully settle what produced them, so perception has to go beyond them. Practice recalibrated her judgment of the gaps, which is a different thing.

items.stem: According to the reading, the idea of affordances is worth keeping, but not the further claim that perceiving the world needs no interpretation because the information in the senses is enough. Why is that further claim rejected?

options.text: The signals reaching the senses never fully settle what produced them, so perception has to go beyond what the signals alone contain.
options.why: Correct. The reason is the ill-posed problem. A flat image fits many scenes and one summed sound wave fits many sets of sources, so the information in the senses is not enough by itself.

options.text: Affordances depend on the body as well as the place, so the senses report only the place and leave the body’s part to be worked out.
options.why: Affordances do depend on the body, but that is the idea being kept, not the reason for rejecting the further claim. That claim is rejected because no signal fully settles what produced it.

options.text: A moving animal produces most of what it senses, so the information in its senses is mostly about itself rather than the world.
options.why: A moving animal does produce most of what it senses, but much of that is information about the world, as when near things shift faster than far ones. The claim is rejected because signals never fully settle their causes.

options.text: The senses report about a tenth of a second late, so the information in them is already out of date by the time anything is done with it.
options.why: Delay is a real problem for a moving body, but it has nothing to do with whether perception needs interpretation. The claim is rejected because the signals never fully settle what produced them.

items.stem: Someone argues that a moving observer gathers so much information that perceiving the world needs no interpretation at all. Which point answers that argument most directly?

options.text: The signals reaching the senses never fully settle what produced them, as when one summed sound wave fits many different sets of sources.
options.why: Correct. However the signals are gathered, they never fully settle what produced them, so perceiving has to go beyond them. That is the reason given for rejecting the claim that perception needs no interpretation, while keeping the idea of affordances.

options.text: As an observer moves, near things shift across the eyes faster than far ones, so moving makes information available that holding still does not.
options.why: That is true, but it supports the argument’s premise rather than answering it. Movement adds information without ever making the signals settle their causes completely.

options.text: What a place offers for action depends on the body as well as the place, so the same drop is a step to one animal and a cliff to another.
options.why: That is true, and it is the idea of affordances, which is kept. It says nothing about whether perceiving needs interpretation.

options.text: A saccade is over in tens of milliseconds, before any feedback from vision could arrive to correct where the eyes are going to land.
options.why: That is true, but it is a point about delay in moving. It does not bear on whether the information in the senses settles what produced it.

items.stem: A moving animal floods its own senses with self-caused signals, and it also gains information by moving. According to the reading, how are the flood of signals and the information gained by moving related?

options.text: They are one fact seen from two sides: a moving animal produces most of what it senses, which is a problem to solve and also how much sensing gets done.
options.why: Correct. The animal’s own movement produces most of what it senses. That makes a problem, since self-caused signals can drown out the world’s, and it is also how much of the sensing gets done.

options.text: They are two separate facts with separate causes: the flood comes from the animal’s movement, and the information comes from the world alone.
options.why: The information gained by moving comes from the animal’s movement too. Near things shift faster than far ones only because the animal moves, so the two have one cause.

options.text: They are opposite effects that cancel out: the information gained by moving makes up for the flood, so a moving animal senses as a still one does.
options.why: The flood and the information do not cancel. A moving animal has information a still animal lacks, and it also has a flood of self-caused signals to deal with, and both come from its own movement.

options.text: They belong to different senses: the flood reaches the balance organs and the muscles, and the information reaches the eyes and the lateral line.
options.why: The flood and the information reach the same senses. A turn of the fish sweeps the scene across its eyes, which is a flood, and the same movement makes near things shift faster than far ones, which is information.

items.stem: A fish sees a water flea drifting in the current and strikes at it. In a short paragraph, explain why the fish cannot simply aim its strike at the place where its eyes report the flea, naming two separate problems its signals pose.
items.answer: The fish’s signals about the flea are already old when they arrive. They report where the flea was, and the flea keeps drifting, so the strike has to be aimed at where the flea will be when the strike arrives. The signals are also in the wrong coordinates. The eyes report where the flea’s image falls on the retina, which gives its direction relative to the eye, but the strike is made by the body. Turning a place on the retina into a command for the body depends on where the eyes and head are pointing at that moment. So the fish has to turn old, eye-centered signals into a current, body-centered command.
rubric: Says the signals are old, reporting where the flea was rather than where it is now.
Says the strike has to be aimed at where the flea will be when the strike arrives.
Says the eyes report the flea’s position relative to the eye, while the strike needs a command in the body’s terms.
Says that turning the eye-centered position into a body-centered command depends on where the eyes and head are pointing.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain how an animal’s own movement can be both a problem for its senses and a source of information for them. Give one example of each, and say how the two are related.
items.answer: A moving animal causes much of what reaches its own senses, and those self-caused signals can drown out the signals from the world. Each turn of a fish, for example, sweeps the whole scene across its eyes, although nothing in the world has moved. But movement also changes what reaches the senses in lawful ways. As an animal moves, near things shift across its eyes faster than far ones, which tells it what is near and what is far, information a stationary animal does not have. These are one fact seen from two sides. A moving animal produces most of what it senses, and that is a problem to solve and also how much of its sensing gets done.
rubric: Says self-caused signals can drown out signals from the world, with an example (a turn sweeping the scene across the eyes, a tail beat stirring the water along the lateral line, an eye jump sweeping the image).
Says movement changes what reaches the senses in lawful ways, with an example (near things shifting faster than far ones, water changing shape around objects).
Says the lawful change gives information that a stationary animal does not have.
Says the problem and the information are one fact: a moving animal produces most of what it senses.

pools.title: Depth, Stereo, and Color
pools.covers: reading §8.2.1, §8.2.2, §8.2.3 · lecture 8.2 slides depth_from_assumptions, two_eyes_one_matching_problem, color_from_comparisons

items.stem: What is a depth cue?

options.text: A feature of the sensory signal that, given an assumption that is usually true about the world, indicates how far away something is.
options.why: Correct. A flat image does not settle depth by itself. Each depth cue indicates distance only because the world usually works a certain way, for instance that two similar objects are the same real size.

options.text: A feature of the sensory signal that indicates how far away something is with certainty, needing no assumption about the world at all.
options.why: No depth cue gives certainty, because a flat image fits many different scenes. Every depth cue indicates distance only given an assumption that is usually, not always, true.

options.text: A movement an animal makes, such as bobbing its head up and down, in order to judge how far away something is.
options.why: That describes active sensing, producing movement or energy in order to sense. The bobbing can make a depth cue available, but the cue is the feature of the signal, not the movement.

options.text: A problem for which the information available does not settle a single answer, such as recovering a scene from one flat image.
options.why: That is an ill-posed problem. Recovering depth from a flat image is one, and depth cues are how vision gets an answer to it anyway.

items.stem: In a dark room, a person looks with one eye and holds the head still. Two glowing balls hang in the dark and look alike in every way except the size of their images. In fact the two balls hang at the same distance, and one is twice as large as the other. What would the person tend to see?

options.text: The larger ball as nearer, since vision assumes the balls are the same real size and takes the smaller image as farther.
options.why: Correct. Relative size indicates distance given the assumption that two similar objects are the same real size. Here that assumption is false, so the larger image is taken as the nearer ball.

options.text: The two balls at the same distance, since vision works out each ball’s real size and corrects each image for it.
options.why: The relative-size cue does not measure real size; it rests on an assumption about it. A cue that could measure real size would need no assumption, and the dark room leaves nothing to measure it from.

options.text: No difference in depth at all, since a single eye held perfectly still in the dark receives no depth cues of any kind.
options.why: One still eye loses the comparison cues, but the single-image cues remain. Relative size is one of them, and here it gives a wrong answer rather than none.

options.text: The larger ball as farther, since a larger image is the usual sign of an object lying at a greater distance from the eye.
options.why: That reverses the cue. Of two objects assumed to be the same size, the one casting the smaller image is the one taken to be farther away.

items.stem: A photograph of a cratered landscape is taken with sunlight coming from the top of the frame, and the craters look like dents. When the photograph is turned upside down, the same craters look like domes. Which explanation fits this reversal?

options.text: Shading indicates shape only given an assumed direction for the light, and turning the photograph over makes the same shading read the other way.
options.why: Correct. This is the light-from-above assumption at work. The shading has not changed, but read with light assumed to come from above, a dent turned over has the shading of a dome.

options.text: A flat photograph carries no information about depth at all, so whether the craters look like dents or domes is a guess that can change at any moment.
options.why: A flat image underdetermines the scene, but it is not empty of cues. The reversal is systematic, not a guess, because the shading is read through a fixed assumption about the light.

options.text: Turning the photograph over changes which craters hide parts of which, so occlusion then indicates the reverse of the depth it indicated before.
options.why: Turning a picture over does not change which outlines cut into which. What flips is where the lit side of each crater sits, which matters because shading is read with the light assumed to come from above.

options.text: Turning the photograph over reverses which way the texture grows finer, so the ground that looked far away now looks near and the craters change shape.
options.why: Reversing which way the texture grows finer would change which part of the ground looks farther away, not turn each crater from a dent into a dome. The shape of each crater is carried by its shading.

items.stem: A person views a single photograph of a long city street with one eye closed and the head held still. Which source of information about depth is still available to the person?

options.text: The two curbs converging toward the horizon, which indicates that their far ends lie a great distance away from the camera.
options.why: Correct. Parallel lines converging is a single-image cue. It is present in one flat image and needs neither a second eye nor any movement.

options.text: Nearer lampposts drifting the opposite way from farther buildings as the person moves the head from side to side.
options.why: That is motion parallax, a cue that compares views over time. The head is held still, and a photograph does not change as the head moves.

options.text: The mismatch between where each lamppost falls in the left eye and where the same lamppost falls in the right eye.
options.why: That is binocular disparity, which compares the two eyes. With one eye closed, and a flat photograph besides, there is no such mismatch to use.

options.text: The place on the retina where each building’s light falls, which gives its distance as directly as it gives its direction.
options.why: Where light falls on the retina gives direction almost for free, but distance is not laid out on the retina. It has to be computed from cues.

items.stem: What is motion parallax?

options.text: The differences in how fast and in which direction objects at different distances seem to move when the observer moves.
options.why: Correct. When an observer moves while looking at one point, nearer things drift the opposite way, faster the nearer they are, and things beyond that point drift along with the observer.

options.text: The difference between the positions of a point’s images in the two eyes, which depends on how near or far the point is.
options.why: That is binocular disparity, which compares the two eyes at one moment. Motion parallax compares the views of a single observer over time, as the observer moves.

options.text: The movement of an object’s image across the retina when the object itself travels through a scene that is otherwise still.
options.why: That is motion in the world, which reaches the senses whether or not the observer moves. Motion parallax arises from the observer’s own movement past things at different distances.

options.text: The sweep of the whole image across the retina each time the eyes jump quickly to look at a new target.
options.why: That is the effect of a saccade, a self-caused change that sweeps everything at once. Motion parallax is about objects at different distances moving at different speeds and in different directions.

items.stem: A passenger on a train moving to the right keeps their gaze on a cow standing in a field at middle distance. A fence runs close beside the track, and hills lie far beyond the cow. As the train moves, how do the fence and the hills seem to move?

options.text: The fence sweeps quickly to the left, and the hills drift to the right, along with the train.
options.why: Correct. With gaze held on the cow, things nearer than the cow drift opposite to the observer’s movement, faster the nearer they are, and things beyond it drift along with the observer.

options.text: The fence sweeps quickly to the right, and the hills drift to the left, against the train.
options.why: That reverses both directions. Nearer things drift against the observer’s movement and things beyond the fixated point drift with it.

options.text: The fence sweeps quickly to the left, and the hills drift to the left as well, only more slowly.
options.why: That is right for the fence, which is nearer than the cow, but not for the hills. With gaze held on the cow, things beyond the cow drift the same way the train is moving.

options.text: The cow seems to drift to the left, while the fence and the hills both stay where they are.
options.why: The cow is the point the gaze is held on, so its image stays put. It is the things nearer than the cow and beyond it, the fence and the hills, that drift.

items.stem: Texture growing finer with distance and motion parallax are both depth cues. What is the difference between them?

options.text: Texture can be read from one image, while motion parallax compares views over time and so exists only for a moving observer.
options.why: Correct. Texture is a single-image cue, present in a still photograph. Motion parallax is a comparison cue, and its second image comes from the observer having moved.

options.text: Motion parallax can be read from one image, while texture compares views over time and so exists only for a moving observer.
options.why: That swaps the two. In one still image of a tiled floor the tiles already shrink with distance, while drifting at different speeds requires movement.

options.text: Texture compares the images in the two eyes, while motion parallax compares the views that one eye has as the observer moves.
options.why: Texture growing finer needs only one image, from one eye. The comparison between the two eyes is binocular disparity, a different cue.

options.text: Texture indicates how far away a surface is, while motion parallax indicates which way an object in the scene is moving.
options.why: Motion parallax is also a depth cue. The drift it involves comes from the observer’s movement, and its speed and direction indicate how near or far each thing is.

items.stem: What is active sensing?

options.text: Producing movement or energy in order to sense, as when a fish senses distortions in an electric field it generates itself.
options.why: Correct. The animal produces something, a movement or a field, so that the senses receive information they otherwise would not.

options.text: Sensation caused by the animal’s own movement, whether or not the animal made that movement in order to sense anything.
options.why: That is reafference. Much reafference is a problem to be removed, such as the water a fish’s own tail beat stirs along its lateral line. Active sensing is movement or energy produced in order to sense.

options.text: An opportunity for action that a place or object offers to a particular body, such as a gap that one animal can pass through.
options.why: That is an affordance. It concerns what a body can do in a place, not movement or energy produced in order to gain information.

options.text: Combining estimates from several senses about the same thing, weighting each estimate according to how reliable it is.
options.why: That is cue combination, a way of using signals that have already arrived. Active sensing is about producing the movement or energy that makes the signals available.

items.stem: Which of these is a case of active sensing?

options.text: A bat that emits high-pitched calls and listens to the echoes coming back from insects flying nearby.
options.why: Correct. The bat produces energy, in the form of sound, in order to sense. Its calls are to the bat what the electric field is to the weakly electric fish.

options.text: A person talking on a busy street whose own voice, loudest in the person’s own ears, drowns out a quieter voice nearby.
options.why: That is reafference, self-caused sensation that here gets in the way. The person produces sound in order to talk, not in order to sense, so the voice is not active sensing.

options.text: An owl perched on a branch that hears the rustle of a mouse moving through dry leaves on the ground below.
options.why: The owl senses energy the mouse produced, which is exafference. Nothing the owl produces is used to gain the information, so this is not active sensing.

options.text: A rider on a motion-simulator ride who feels pressed back into a slowly tilting seat as if speeding forward.
options.why: That is the balance organs’ ambiguity between tilt and acceleration, which the ride’s designers exploit on purpose. The rider is not producing movement in order to sense.

items.stem: An octopus bobs its head up and down before it strikes, which lets it judge distance with one eye. How do active sensing and motion parallax each apply to this behavior?

options.text: The bobbing is active sensing, a movement made in order to sense, and motion parallax is the depth cue that the movement makes available.
options.why: Correct. The two terms name different things here. Active sensing names what the octopus does, and motion parallax names the information that its doing it produces.

options.text: The bobbing is motion parallax, a movement made in order to sense, and active sensing is the depth cue that the movement makes available.
options.why: That swaps the two terms. Motion parallax is a feature of the changing image, while active sensing is the producing of movement in order to sense.

options.text: The bobbing is active sensing, but it gives no motion parallax, since that depth cue needs a second eye to compare views with.
options.why: A second eye gives binocular disparity. Motion parallax compares the views of one eye over time, which is exactly what bobbing provides.

options.text: The bobbing gives motion parallax, but it is not active sensing, since that term covers only animals that produce energy, such as a field.
options.why: Active sensing covers producing movement as well as producing energy. In the reading, an octopus bobbing its head is given as a case of active sensing.

items.stem: Some depth cues come from comparing two images of a scene. In a few sentences, explain what any such comparison requires of an animal, how an animal with only one working eye could still get a comparison cue, and why that requirement means that recovering the world and moving through it are not separate problems.
items.answer: A comparison cue needs two images of the same scene taken from slightly different places. Those can come from two sensors at once, such as two eyes, or from one sensor that moves and takes its views one after another. An animal with one working eye can still compare views if it moves that eye, for instance by bobbing its head up and down as an octopus does. For cues of this kind, then, moving is part of how depth gets recovered, so recovering the world and moving through it are not separate problems.
rubric: States that a comparison cue needs either two sensors or one sensor that moves.
Says that an animal with one working eye can compare views over time by moving, for instance by bobbing the head or shifting it from side to side.
Concludes that recovering depth and moving through the world are not separate problems, because for these cues the movement supplies the second view.

items.stem: What is binocular disparity?

options.text: The difference between where a point’s images fall in the two eyes, which depends on how much nearer or farther it is than where the eyes point.
options.why: Correct. A point at the distance the eyes are pointing at falls on corresponding places in the two retinas. Nearer and farther points do not, and the size and direction of the mismatch carry depth.

options.text: The problem of pairing each point in one eye’s image with the point in the other eye’s image that comes from the same place in the world.
options.why: That is the correspondence problem. It has to be solved before binocular disparity can be measured, but it is not the disparity itself.

options.text: The difference in the time a sound takes to reach the two ears, which helps indicate which direction around the head a sound comes from.
options.why: That is the interaural time difference, a comparison between the two ears that carries direction. Binocular disparity compares the two eyes and carries depth.

options.text: The differences in how fast and in which direction objects at different distances seem to move across the view as the observer moves.
options.why: That is motion parallax, which compares the views of one moving observer over time. Binocular disparity compares the two eyes’ views at the same moment.

items.stem: A person looks at a doorframe across a room while holding up a thumb a short way in front of the face. The thumb appears doubled, while the doorframe looks single. Why does the thumb appear doubled?

options.text: The thumb is nearer than where the eyes are pointing, so its images fall on places in the two retinas that do not correspond.
options.why: Correct. Only a thin band of depth around the point being looked at fuses into one image. The thumb lies well in front of that band, so its two images are seen apart.

options.text: The thumb’s images have been paired at the wrong partners, as happens when a repeating pattern such as wallpaper is fused.
options.why: A wrong pairing makes a pattern seem to float at the wrong distance. The doubled thumb needs no pairing error; it lies outside the band of depth that fuses.

options.text: The thumb falls on corresponding places in the two retinas, and points that fall on corresponding places are the ones seen double.
options.why: That reverses it. Corresponding places are where the fixated doorframe falls, and it looks single. Places that do not quite correspond are what produce doubling.

options.text: The thumb’s image falls outside the fovea, and anything seen outside the fovea is seen double rather than in sharp detail.
options.why: Outside the fovea, detail is poor, but poor detail is blur, not doubling. The thumb doubles because it is nearer than the doorframe the eyes are pointing at.

items.stem: Each eye is shown its own field of random dots. In one field, a ring-shaped band of dots has been shifted slightly sideways, and viewed alone, each field looks like nothing but scattered dots. Viewed together, one field per eye, a ring floats above the background. What can be concluded about stereo vision?

options.text: It does not require recognizing any object first, since the ring exists only in the disparity between the fields.
options.why: Correct. Neither eye’s field contains a ring to be recognized. The ring appears only once the two fields are compared, so here the shape is found only through the comparison.

options.text: It works by first finding the ring in each eye’s field, and then comparing where the two rings lie in the two eyes.
options.why: Neither field, viewed alone, contains a ring. A process that had to find the ring in each eye first would have nothing to find.

options.text: It relies on a single-image cue here, since the shifted dots form a texture that grows finer than the rest.
options.why: Shifting a patch sideways leaves its dots the same size and spacing. The ring appears only when the two fields are viewed together, which a single-image cue would not need.

options.text: It finds the correct pairing easily here, since in random dots every dot is easy to tell apart from every other.
options.why: In a random-dot field every dot looks like every other dot. That makes pairing hard, with many possible pairings and most of them wrong.

items.stem: How are binocular disparity and the correspondence problem related?

options.text: Disparity is the mismatch that carries depth, and the correspondence problem is the pairing that must come before any disparity is measured.
options.why: Correct. A mismatch can be measured only between two things known to be partners. So each point must first be paired with its partner in the other eye.

options.text: Disparity is measured first, and the correspondence problem is then solved by using each point’s disparity to find its partner point.
options.why: That reverses the order. A disparity is a mismatch between a point and its partner, so it cannot be measured until the partner has been found.

options.text: The two terms are names for one and the same thing, the mismatch between where a single point falls in the left and right eyes.
options.why: They are two different things. The mismatch is the disparity, while the correspondence problem is working out which point in one eye goes with which in the other.

options.text: Disparity concerns the two eyes, while the correspondence problem concerns matching one eye’s views over time as the observer moves.
options.why: Both concern the two eyes. Comparing one eye’s views over time gives motion parallax, a different depth cue.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “The problem of pairing each point in one eye’s image with the point in the other eye’s image that comes from the same place in the world, which must be solved before binocular disparity can be measured”.

options.text: correspondence problem
options.why: Correct. Pairing points between the eyes is the correspondence problem, and it is what makes stereo hard, since many pairings are possible and most of them are wrong.

options.text: ill-posed problem
options.why: An ill-posed problem is one where the available information does not settle a single answer. The correspondence problem is hard in a related way, but the term for pairing points between the eyes is narrower.

options.text: auditory scene analysis
options.why: Auditory scene analysis is grouping the parts of a mixed sound wave into the sources that produced them. It is a sorting problem in hearing, not a pairing between the two eyes.

options.text: depth cue
options.why: A depth cue is a feature of the signal that indicates distance, given an assumption. Disparity is used as one once the pairing problem has been solved.

items.stem: A person stands close to a chain-link fence whose diamond-shaped openings all look alike, and lets the eyes relax. Suddenly the fence seems to float at a distance different from where it really stands. Why could this happen?

options.text: The diamonds offer many equally good pairings, and a pairing at the wrong partners gives a wrong disparity.
options.why: Correct. This is the wallpaper case. When every diamond looks like every other, a diamond in one eye can be paired with the wrong diamond in the other, and the wrong pairing gives a wrong depth.

options.text: The fence falls on corresponding places in both eyes, so there is no disparity left to measure at all.
options.why: If every point of the fence fell on corresponding places, the fence would be seen at the distance the eyes are pointing at, not at a wrong one.

options.text: The diamonds each have to be recognized as objects first, and recognizing so many at once overloads stereo.
options.why: Stereo does not need objects recognized first; in a random-dot stereogram neither eye’s field holds any object. The trouble lies in pairing points between the eyes, not in recognizing them.

options.text: The relaxed eyes stop moving altogether, so the fence’s image fades and its depth can no longer be judged at all.
options.why: A perfectly still image does fade, but fading removes the image rather than moving it to a wrong distance. The misplaced fence comes from a wrong pairing.

items.stem: How does the brain solve the correspondence problem, according to the reading?

options.text: The solution is still debated, and the proposals so far are models of how it might be done rather than known mechanisms.
options.why: Correct. The correspondence problem is well defined, and solving it is known to be necessary for stereo, but how the brain does so remains open.

options.text: By recognizing each object in the two eyes’ images first, and then pairing each object with its partner in the other eye.
options.why: In a random-dot stereogram neither eye’s field contains an object to recognize, yet a shape still floats in depth. So the pairing cannot wait for objects to be recognized.

options.text: By sliding one image over the other until the parts line up, which is now the well-established mechanism.
options.why: Sliding one image over the other is a way to picture the problem. It is not established as how the brain solves it; that is still debated.

options.text: By pairing points within each eye’s retina, before any of the signals have left the eye for the brain.
options.why: No single retina receives the other eye’s image. The two eyes’ signals first come together in the visual cortex, the first place disparity can be computed.

items.stem: A classmate argues that stereo vision has to work by first finding the objects in each eye’s image and then comparing where each object falls in the two eyes. In a few sentences, describe a demonstration that counts against this view, and explain why it does.
items.answer: A random-dot stereogram counts against that view. Each eye is shown its own field of random dots, and in one field a square patch of dots has been shifted slightly sideways. Viewed alone, neither field contains a square; each looks like scattered dots. Viewed together, one field per eye, a square floats in front of the background. Since there was no square in either image to find, the square exists only in the disparity between the two images, so stereo cannot require recognizing objects first.
rubric: Names or describes the random-dot stereogram: each eye sees its own field of random dots, with a patch shifted sideways in one field.
Says that neither field, viewed alone, contains a square or any other object.
Says that when the two fields are viewed together, one per eye, a square floats at a different depth from the background.
Concludes that stereo does not require recognizing objects first, because the square exists only in the disparity between the two images.

items.stem: A simple light sensor reports only how much light it has caught. It gives exactly the same response to a dim blue light and to a brighter yellow one. What follows for a creature that has only this one kind of sensor?

options.text: It cannot tell the two lights apart by wavelength, which needs a comparison across sensors tuned to different wavelengths.
options.why: Correct. One kind of sensor confounds wavelength with amount of light. Comparing the responses of sensors tuned to different wavelengths is what separates the two.

options.text: It can tell the two lights apart by how bright each one is, since brightness and wavelength are reported separately.
options.why: The sensor reports a single number, the amount of light caught, and both lights give the same number. Nothing in its response separates brightness from wavelength.

options.text: It can tell the two lights apart if it compares each with the rest of the scene, since that comparison supplies wavelength.
options.why: Comparing a surface with the rest of the scene is a proposal about color constancy, and it starts from color signals already available. It does not supply wavelength to a sensor that cannot report it.

options.text: It can tell the two lights apart if it moves, since moving gives it two views of each light to compare with each other.
options.why: Moving gives views from different places, which is useful for depth. Each view would still give the same single number for both lights.

items.stem: Two comparisons bear on how color is recovered: comparing receptors tuned to different wavelengths, and comparing a surface with the rest of the scene. What is each comparison for?

options.text: Comparing receptors recovers wavelength, and comparing with the scene is a proposed way to keep a surface’s color constant as lighting changes.
options.why: Correct. Comparing receptors is needed for any color at all. It is not enough for constancy, which is where the proposed comparison with the scene comes in.

options.text: Comparing receptors keeps a surface’s color constant as lighting changes, and comparing with the scene recovers wavelength from the light.
options.why: That swaps the two. Comparing receptors gives wavelength, but the light from one surface still changes with the lighting, so it cannot by itself give constancy.

options.text: Both comparisons recover wavelength from light, the first from one surface’s light and the second from the light of the whole scene taken at once.
options.why: Only the comparison across receptors is about wavelength. Comparing a surface with its surroundings is a proposal for constancy, for judging the surface rather than the light.

options.text: Comparing receptors is enough for constancy as well, and comparing with the scene is needed only for surfaces that are dimly lit.
options.why: Comparing receptors is not enough for constancy. A surface’s color is judged from more than the light coming from that surface, however brightly it is lit.

items.stem: Under white light, a blue card sends the eye a particular mix of light. A gray card is then lit by a bluish lamp so that it sends the eye exactly that same mix, and a person still sees it as gray. A camera that sets each card’s color only from its three filters’ responses to that card’s light would record the gray card as blue. What can be concluded from the person’s seeing it as gray?

options.text: The person judges the card’s color from more than the light that comes from the card itself, unlike the camera.
options.why: Correct. The card’s own light matches the blue card’s exactly, so anything that used only that light would call it blue. Seeing it as gray requires information from beyond the card.

options.text: The person compares more kinds of receptor than the camera has filters, which gives a finer reading of the light.
options.why: Human beings compare three kinds of receptor, just as the camera compares three kinds of filter. More kinds would still read the same light from the card the same way.

options.text: The person’s receptors respond to the card’s light differently than they would to the blue card’s light.
options.why: The two cards send the eye exactly the same light, so the receptors respond to them the same way. The difference has to come from elsewhere in the scene.

options.text: The camera must have misread the card’s color, since a gray card cannot send the same light as a blue one.
options.why: It can, once the lighting changes. The light from a surface mixes the surface with the light falling on it, which is why constancy is a problem at all.

items.stem: At sunset, the light falling on a whole room turns reddish, and a white wall now sends the eye more red light than before. According to the proposal that a surface’s color is read from how it differs from the rest of the scene, why does the wall still look white?

options.text: Every other surface in the room is now redder as well, so the wall’s difference from its surroundings is unchanged.
options.why: Correct. A reddish light raises the red from every surface together. The wall’s difference from its surroundings is what stays the same, and on this proposal the wall’s color is read from that difference.

options.text: Light like the wall’s, in surroundings like these, has usually signified a white surface in past experience.
options.why: That is the other proposed procedure, the learned one. On the proposal in the question, the wall’s color is read from its difference from the rest of the scene, not from past experience.

options.text: The three kinds of receptor are compared, and that comparison by itself removes the red the sunset adds.
options.why: Comparing receptors recovers wavelength, but the wall’s own light really is redder now. Comparing receptors alone cannot tell red light on a white wall from a red wall.

options.text: The wall’s light now is compared with the light it sent at noon, and the color seen follows the earlier light.
options.why: Nothing in either proposed procedure compares a surface with its own past light. The comparison here is with the rest of the scene at the same moment.

items.stem: On the learned account of color constancy, why does a banana under a lamp still look yellow?

options.text: Light like the banana’s, in surroundings like these, has usually signified yellow in past experience.
options.why: Correct. On the learned account, a surface’s apparent color reflects what similar light, in similar surroundings, has usually meant before.

options.text: The banana differs from the rest of the lamp-lit scene in just the way that a yellow surface would differ.
