options.why: That is the scene-comparison procedure, which reads a surface against its surroundings at the moment. The learned account appeals to past experience instead.

options.text: The banana sends the eye the same light under the lamp as it does outdoors in daylight at noon.
options.why: The banana’s light changes a great deal between noon and a lamp. If it did not, constancy would be no problem at all.

options.text: The three kinds of receptor give the same comparison for the banana under the lamp as in daylight.
options.why: The light from the banana changes with the lighting, so the comparison across receptors changes too. That is why comparing receptors is not enough for constancy.

items.stem: Two procedures have been proposed for color constancy: reading each surface against the rest of the scene, and reading a surface’s light by what similar light has usually signified in past experience. Where do the two stand?

options.text: Both remain proposals about how constancy is achieved, and neither of the accounts is settled.
options.why: Correct. The comparison with the scene and the learned account are both live proposals. Neither has been shown to be how color constancy works.

options.text: Scene comparison is settled, since a camera’s automatic white balance carries out the same procedure.
options.why: White balance is a cruder version of scene comparison, and a camera’s doing it is no evidence about how people do. An early ratio version of the idea also did not work in all circumstances.

options.text: The learned account is settled, since the early ratio version of scene comparison was shown to fail.
options.why: One early version of scene comparison did not work in all circumstances, but that does not settle the question for the learned account. Neither account is settled.

options.text: Both have been set aside, since comparing receptors turned out to be enough for constancy.
options.why: Comparing receptors is not enough for constancy, because a surface’s color is judged from more than its own light. That is why the two procedures were proposed.

items.stem: A white shirt looks white both outdoors at noon and indoors under a yellowish lamp, although the light reaching the eye from the shirt differs between the two. In a short paragraph, explain why comparing the responses of the three kinds of receptor cannot by itself explain the shirt’s constant color, describe the two procedures that have been proposed to explain it, and say where those proposals stand.
items.answer: A comparison of the three kinds of receptor depends only on the light arriving from the shirt, and that light is yellower under the lamp than at noon. If color were judged from that light alone, the shirt would look yellowish indoors, so its color must be judged from more than the light coming from the shirt. One proposed procedure compares each surface with the rest of the scene. Under the lamp every surface sends back more yellow, so the shirt still differs from its surroundings the way a white surface does. The other proposed procedure is learned. The shirt looks white because light like its light, in surroundings like these, has usually signified a white surface in past experience. Neither account is settled.
rubric: Says the light from the shirt differs between the two settings, so comparing receptors on the shirt’s light alone gives different results in each.
States that a surface’s color is judged from more than the light coming from that surface.
Describes the scene-comparison procedure: under the lamp every surface sends more yellow, so the shirt is read from how it differs from its surroundings.
Describes the learned procedure: the color reflects what similar light in similar surroundings has usually signified in past experience.
Says neither proposal is settled, and does not name either one as correct.

items.stem: Recognizing an object from any angle is the invariance problem at its hardest, and what brains achieve is called tolerance rather than perfect invariance. What is the difference between the two?

options.text: Tolerant recognition survives a great deal of change in the image but not all of it, while perfect invariance would survive every change.
options.why: Correct. Recognition from a new angle usually succeeds, but some changes, such as a view at right angles to every view seen before, make errors far more likely. That limit is what separates tolerance from perfect invariance.

options.text: Tolerant recognition works for an object seen before from the angle now in view, while perfect invariance works for an object from any angle.
options.why: That would be almost no tolerance at all. Tolerant recognition survives a great deal of change in the image, including many angles never seen, though not every change.

options.text: Tolerant recognition survives changes of lighting and distance but not changes of viewing angle, while perfect invariance survives changes of angle too.
options.why: In object recognition, tolerance is applied above all to changes of viewing angle. Recognition survives many changes of angle, just not all of them.

options.text: Tolerant recognition rests on stored views of an object, while perfect invariance rests on the simple volumes the object is built from.
options.why: This pairs the two terms with the two accounts of recognition, by views and by parts. Both accounts are attempts to explain tolerance.

items.stem: What is a geon?

options.text: In the theory of recognition by parts, one of a small set of simple volumes, such as bricks, cylinders, and cones, from which object shapes are built.
options.why: Correct. On the parts account there are about three dozen geons. A cup, for instance, is a curved cylinder with a smaller curved cylinder attached to its side.

options.text: In the theory of recognition by views, one of a small set of stored images of an object, each from a different angle, against which new images are matched.
options.why: That describes the stored views of the views account, which keeps images of a whole object. Geons belong to the parts account, on which objects are built from simple volumes.

options.text: A feature of the sensory signal, such as texture growing finer with distance, that indicates how far away something is, given an assumption usually true of the world.
options.why: That is a depth cue. A geon is a simple volume, such as a brick or a cone, that serves as a building block of object shapes on the parts account.

options.text: A unit in an artificial neural network that responds to one edge feature, such as a straight or a curved edge, wherever that feature appears in an image.
options.why: Networks trained on photographs are sensitive to the edge features that tell geons apart, but a geon is not a unit. It is a simple volume from which, on the parts account, object shapes are composed.

items.stem: Picture a brick turned slowly in front of an observer. Its outline in the image changes at every angle, yet its straight edges stay straight in the image and its parallel edges stay nearly parallel. Why are edge features like these central to the parts account?

options.text: Such features rarely arise by accident of viewpoint, so they come from the object and survive most changes of viewpoint.
options.why: Correct. A straight edge in an image almost always comes from a straight edge in the world. Because the features that identify a geon survive most changes of viewpoint, they are what an account of tolerance needs.

options.text: Such features are what a stored view records most exactly, so a new view is matched to the stored views by comparing them.
options.why: Matching a new view against stored ones is the views account. Edge features matter to the parts account because they rarely arise by accident of viewpoint.

options.text: Such features are what networks trained on photographs are given in advance, so people and networks end up relying on the same cues.
options.why: Networks trained only to name photographs pick up these features without being given them. Edge features matter to the parts account because they rarely arise by accident of viewpoint.

options.text: Such features change least when the light changes, so they keep the brick’s apparent color the same from noon to dusk.
options.why: Keeping a surface’s color steady as the light changes is color constancy, a separate case of invariance. Edge features matter to the parts account because they survive most changes of viewpoint.

items.stem: Two line drawings of a watering can have the same amount of contour removed. In one drawing, the gaps fall in the middle of edges. In the other, the gaps fall where the spout and the handle join the body, and the remaining lines run smoothly across those joins. On the parts account, what should happen when people try to name the two drawings?

options.text: People will name the drawing with mid-edge gaps but fail on the one with hidden joins, since only the mid-edge drawing leaves each part recoverable.
options.why: Correct. With the amount of contour held equal, what matters is whether the parts can still be found. When the joins were hidden in the original test, people failed almost completely, even with five seconds to look.

options.text: People will name both drawings about equally well, since the same amount of contour is missing from each, and the amount is all that matters.
options.why: The amount was held equal on purpose, so that it could not explain a difference. On the parts account, a difference is expected, because only one drawing hides where the parts join.

options.text: People will fail on the drawing with mid-edge gaps but name the one with hidden joins, since smooth lines across the joins keep the outline whole.
options.why: That reverses the result. Smoothing the lines across the joins is what hides the parts, and on the parts account hidden parts are what defeat recognition.

options.text: People will name the drawing with hidden joins if given several seconds, since the joins can be worked out by studying the lines that remain.
options.why: When joins were hidden, people failed almost completely even with five seconds to look. More time does not restore parts that cannot be recovered from the lines.

items.stem: People learn a novel object, a shape of bent tubing, from two views 60 degrees apart, both taken around its vertical axis. They are then shown three new views: one halfway between the learned views, one 30 degrees beyond them, and one from directly above, at right angles to both. On the views account, how should errors on the three new views compare?

options.text: Fewest errors on the view between the learned views, more on the view beyond them, and the most on the view from directly above.
options.why: Correct. On the views account a new view is recognized by how close it is to the stored views. People who learned novel wire shapes showed exactly this order: between best, beyond worse, right angles worst.

options.text: Fewest errors on the view from directly above, more on the view between the learned views, and the most on the view 30 degrees beyond them.
options.why: The view from above lies at right angles to both learned views, so it is the farthest from what was stored. On the views account it should produce the most errors, not the fewest.

options.text: Fewest errors on the view beyond the learned views, more on the view between them, and the most on the view from directly above.
options.why: A view beyond the learned ones lies farther from the stored views than a view between them does. On the views account, views beyond are recognized less well than views between.

options.text: About the same number of errors on all three views, since none of the three new views is one of the views that was learned.
options.why: Being new does not settle it. On the views account a new view is recognized by how close it is to the stored views, so errors grow with distance from them.

items.stem: How are the parts account and the views account of object recognition now usually seen in relation to each other?

options.text: As ends of a continuum of tasks, with viewpoint mattering most for telling similar objects apart, and much less for kinds that differ in parts.
options.why: Correct. Telling which of several similar objects is in view depends heavily on viewpoint. Telling a mug from a bucket, which differ in their parts, depends on it much less.

options.text: As accounts of two different senses, with the views account covering recognition by sight, and the parts account covering recognition by touch.
options.why: Both accounts are about vision. Parts and views are two ways of explaining how an object is recognized by sight from a new angle.

options.text: As two stages of one process, with the parts recovered first from the image, and the views stored afterward once the parts are known.
options.why: No such ordering is proposed. The two accounts are placed at two ends of a range of tasks, from telling similar objects apart to telling kinds apart.

options.text: As accounts of two different species, with the views account covering recognition in monkeys, and the parts account covering recognition in people.
options.why: People and monkeys showed the same pattern for views between, beyond, and at right angles to learned ones. The two accounts divide tasks, not species.

items.stem: A museum worker has two tasks. One is telling which of four nearly identical bronze bells is on display. The other is telling a bell from a spoon. If the parts and views accounts are ends of a continuum of tasks, how should a change of viewing angle affect each task?

options.text: It should hurt telling the four bells apart far more, since viewpoint matters most for similar objects and much less for different kinds.
options.why: Correct. The four bronze bells are similar objects, and telling similar objects apart depends heavily on viewpoint. A bell and a spoon are kinds that differ in their parts, and telling such kinds apart depends on viewpoint much less.

options.text: It should hurt telling a bell from a spoon far more, since that task rests on matching each new view against stored views of whole objects.
options.why: This reverses the two ends of the continuum. Viewpoint matters most for telling similar objects apart. Kinds that differ in their parts, like a bell and a spoon, are recognized with much less dependence on viewpoint.

options.text: It should hurt both tasks about equally, since every object is stored as a set of views, whatever the task it is recognized for.
options.why: That treats the views account as the whole story. On the continuum, viewpoint matters heavily for telling similar objects apart and much less for telling kinds apart.

options.text: It should hurt neither task at all, since bells and spoons are both built from geons whose edge features survive every change of viewpoint.
options.why: Edge features survive most changes of viewpoint, not every one. Also, the four bells are similar objects, and telling similar objects apart depends heavily on viewpoint.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain how an object is recognized from a new angle on the parts account and on the views account, give one finding that supports each account, and say how the two accounts are now usually reconciled.
items.answer: On the parts account, objects are recognized as arrangements of simple volumes called geons. Geons are told apart by features of their edges that rarely arise by accident of viewpoint, so those features survive most changes of angle. Supporting the parts account, people named line drawings with contour removed when the parts stayed recoverable. They failed almost completely when the same amount was removed where the parts join. On the views account, an object is stored as a set of views, and a new view is recognized by how close it is to the stored ones. Supporting the views account, people who learned novel wire shapes from a few views recognized new views between the learned ones well, views beyond them less well, and views at right angles worst. The two accounts are now usually seen as ends of a continuum of tasks. Telling similar objects apart depends heavily on viewpoint, while recognizing kinds that differ in their parts, like a mug and a bucket, depends on it much less.
rubric: Describes the parts account: objects as arrangements of simple volumes (geons), identified by edge features that survive most changes of viewpoint.
Describes the views account: an object stored as a set of views, with a new view recognized by how close it is to the stored ones.
Gives a supporting finding for each account, such as the contour-removal result for parts and the between, beyond, and right-angle pattern for views.
States that the accounts are now seen as ends of a continuum of tasks, with viewpoint mattering more for telling similar objects apart than for telling kinds apart.

items.stem: Networks trained only to name objects in photographs have been compared with the parts account of recognition. What do these networks share with that account, and where do they fall short of it?

options.text: They are sensitive to edge features that rarely arise by accident of viewpoint, but confuse objects with one part moved, which people rarely do.
options.why: Correct. The networks pick up the accident-proof edge features without being given them. But they fail where the parts account makes its prediction, confusing objects whose parts are arranged differently, which people rarely do.

options.text: They represent objects as arrangements of geons, as the parts account does, but need far more photographs than people do before they can represent them.
options.why: Networks trained on photographs show little sign of representing three-dimensional shape or the arrangement of parts, so they do not represent objects as arrangements of geons. What they share is sensitivity to edge features.

options.text: They are sensitive to the same edge features as the parts account, but only after those features have been built into them before any training.
options.why: The networks picked up the features unaided, from training only to name objects in photographs. Nothing about the features was given to them in advance.

options.text: They store each object as a set of views, as the parts account does, but fail on views at right angles to the photographs they were trained on.
options.why: Storing views is the views account, not the parts account. The shortfall that was found concerns parts: networks confuse objects with one part moved.

items.stem: A test object is a cylinder with a cone set on top of it. A second version is identical except that the cone has been moved below the cylinder, so each part keeps all its edge features and only where one part sits has changed. Why does a pair like this make a sharp test of whether networks trained on photographs classify objects the way people recognize them on the parts account?

options.text: On the parts account the versions differ only in the arrangement of parts, so a system sensitive to edge features but not to arrangement would confuse them.
options.why: Correct. The geons and their edge features are unchanged, so only arrangement separates the versions. People rarely confuse such versions and networks confuse them easily, which fits the networks’ showing little sign of representing how parts are arranged.

options.text: On the parts account edge features alone are enough to separate the versions, so any system sensitive to those features should keep the two versions distinct.
options.why: Edge features identify each geon, but here every geon is unchanged. On the parts account, the versions differ only in how the geons are arranged.

options.text: The change alters many features of the image at once, so whichever system tells the versions apart must be using the larger set of features.
options.why: Only one thing changes, the place of one part. That is what makes the test sharp: a system that fails it is failing on the arrangement of parts and nothing else.

options.text: The change produces a version the network was never trained on, so any confusion would mean only that its set of training photographs was too small.
options.why: People have not seen the moved version before either, yet they rarely confuse it with the original. The networks’ failure falls exactly where the parts account makes its prediction, on the arrangement of parts.

items.stem: A network is trained to name objects in photographs overlaid with fine diagonal scratches, and it comes to name scratched photographs well. It is then tested on photographs overlaid with fine crosshatching, which looks much like the scratches to a person. Given what training on altered copies has been found to do, what is the most likely result?

options.text: The network does far worse on the crosshatching while people cope with it untrained, since training gave little tolerance beyond what was trained.
options.why: Correct. Training on altered copies gave a network tolerance to the trained alteration and very little beyond. People, by contrast, handle distortions they have never encountered.

options.text: The network does about as well on the crosshatching, since the two overlays look alike and training on one covers others that look similar.
options.why: Looking alike to a person did not help in the noise test. A network trained on one noise scored near chance on a second noise that looks similar to people.

options.text: The network does better than people on the crosshatching, since a network trained on one overlay has been found to beat people on overlays.
options.why: The network did beat people, but only on the noise it was trained on. On a similar-looking noise it fell to near chance, so its advantage did not carry over.

options.text: The network and people both do far worse on the crosshatching, since no system copes with a kind of distortion it has never been trained on.
options.why: People handle distortions they have never encountered. In the noise test, that difference between people and the network was the central result.

items.stem: A network trained on images sprinkled with one kind of visual noise scored 80% correct on that noise, against 46% for people. On a second noise that looks similar to a person, the same network scored about 10%, with chance at 6%. What do these results say about whether training on altered copies of images is enough to explain tolerance?

options.text: Training on altered copies gave tolerance to the noise that was trained and very little beyond it, so it falls short of what people show.
options.why: Correct. Near-chance performance on a similar-looking noise means the trained tolerance did not reach beyond the trained alteration. People handle distortions they have never encountered.

options.text: Training on altered copies gave tolerance beyond what people show, since the trained network outscored people by a wide margin on the first noise.
options.why: The wide margin held only on the noise that was trained. On the second noise the network fell to near chance, so its tolerance was narrow, not broad.

options.text: Training on altered copies gave real tolerance to both noises, since a score of about 10% on the second noise is still above the 6% chance level.
options.why: A score of 10% against a 6% chance level is close to guessing. The network had very little tolerance beyond the trained noise, not tolerance to both.

options.text: Training on altered copies is enough to explain people’s tolerance too, since people scored only 46% on a noise that they had never been trained on.
options.why: People’s 46% means the trained noise was hard for them. But people handle distortions they have never encountered, while the network’s skill collapsed on a noise it had not been trained on.

items.stem: What is the fovea?

options.text: A small pit at the center of the retina, densely packed with cones, that provides sharp vision at the center of gaze.
options.why: Correct. Fine detail comes only from this small region. Just six degrees from the line of sight, the human ability to see detail has already fallen by about three quarters.

options.text: A visual pathway from the primary visual cortex into the parietal lobe, concerned with motion, location, and guiding action.
options.why: That is the dorsal stream. The fovea is in the eye itself: a small pit at the center of the retina that provides sharp vision at the center of gaze.

options.text: The part of the thalamus that relays signals from the retina on to the primary visual cortex at the back of the brain.
options.why: That is the lateral geniculate nucleus. The fovea is a small pit at the center of the retina, densely packed with cones.

options.text: A photoreceptor sensitive enough to respond to very dim light, which supports vision at night but not detail or color.
options.why: That is a rod. The fovea is a region of the retina packed with cones, and its very center has no rods at all.

items.stem: A network for naming objects is usually trained on sharp photographs. How does that input differ from what a primate eye supplies at any one moment?

options.text: The eye gets fine detail only in a small region at the center of gaze, so most of what it sees at once is blurry, with a sharp window that jumps.
options.why: Correct. Fine detail comes only from the fovea, so the eyes keep moving to bring each part of a scene onto it in turn. A network’s photographs are sharp all over.

options.text: The eye gets fine detail evenly across the whole view, so at any moment it takes in a whole scene more sharply than a photograph can show it.
options.why: Detail is far from even. Just six degrees from the line of sight, the ability to see detail has fallen by about three quarters.

options.text: The eye gets its finest detail just to one side of the center of gaze, where there are rods, so it looks slightly beside whatever it examines.
options.why: Looking to one side helps with a faint star, because the very center of the fovea has no rods. But fine detail comes from the cones packed into the fovea, at the center of gaze.

options.text: The eye gets an image as sharp as a photograph, but only while it holds perfectly still, which is why it pauses for a time between its jumps.
options.why: An image held perfectly still on the retina fades from view within seconds. And even between jumps, only the small region at the center of gaze is sharp.

items.stem: Because a primate eye sees most of a scene blurry at any one moment, some networks were trained on a mixture of sharp and blurry images instead of on sharp photographs alone. How did these networks differ from networks trained on sharp photographs?

options.text: They relied on shape more often, resisted noise better, and matched the responses of early visual cortex better.
options.why: Correct. Networks given input more like what a primate eye supplies changed on all three counts, including a better match to early visual cortex. Part of the difference between networks and people may lie in what each learns from.

options.text: They relied on texture more often, resisted noise less well, and matched the responses of early visual cortex less well.
options.why: That reverses each finding. Training on a mix of sharp and blurry images made the networks rely more on shape and resist noise better.

options.text: They named sharp photographs worse and blurry ones no better, since the blur only removed detail they needed for naming.
options.why: The blurry images did not simply remove useful detail. Networks trained on the mixture relied more on shape and resisted noise better.

options.text: They came to label objects correctly from any angle around their axis, as the monkeys trained on many views had done.
options.why: Recognition from any angle came from monkeys trained on views spread around an object. The finding for blur training concerned shape, noise, and early visual cortex.

items.stem: Kittens and human infants come to avoid a visible drop only after moving around under their own power; being carried through the same scenes is not enough. A further idea is added to these studies: that a moving animal collects many views of each object, varied as the world varies them, and that experience of this kind may help build recognition from any angle. How should that further idea be described?

options.text: As an inference beyond the studies, which tested avoiding a drop rather than recognizing objects from many angles.
options.why: Correct. In these studies, self-produced movement mattered for learning to see. The idea about collecting many views is offered as an inference that goes beyond them, not as a finding.

options.text: As a finding of the studies, in which kittens moving under their own power recognized objects from more angles.
options.why: The studies measured whether kittens and infants avoided a visible drop. They did not test recognizing objects from different angles, so the idea about views is not their finding.

options.text: As a finding about monkeys, which came to recognize objects from any angle after moving freely around them for months.
options.why: The monkeys were trained on three to five views spread around an object; they did not move around it. In the reading, their training is described as the kind of experience a moving animal collects.

options.text: As the reason the carried kittens failed, since being carried gave them too few views of each object to learn to avoid the drop.
options.why: The carried kittens were taken through the same scenes, so they were not short of views. What they lacked was moving under their own power, and the idea about collecting views goes beyond the studies.

items.stem: A new network’s internal activity predicts the responses of neurons in a monkey’s visual cortex better than any earlier model, and its labels match people’s answers on a large set of photographs. A science writer concludes that the network sees the way primates do. According to the reading, how should that conclusion be judged?

options.text: A close match to answers and brain activity is not evidence that the network works like a primate brain, as a digital clock matches a mechanical one and works nothing like it.
options.why: Correct. A digital clock predicts the time on a mechanical clock perfectly by a completely different mechanism. A match, even to brain activity, is not by itself evidence of the same workings.

options.text: A close match to brain activity, unlike a match to answers alone, is evidence that the network works like a primate brain, since activity reflects the workings behind the answers.
options.why: Matching brain activity is a closer match, but still a match. A network that matches even human brain activity is not thereby shown to work the way a brain does.

options.text: A close match is evidence that the network works like a primate brain if the network was also trained on as many images as a primate sees in its lifetime.
options.why: The amount of training does not turn a match into evidence about workings. What helps is a test that changes one thing and checks whether the model fails where people fail.

options.text: A close match is no evidence at all about the network, since a network and a brain are made of different materials and can never be usefully compared.
options.why: Comparisons can be informative when they are designed well. The strongest tests change one thing at a time and check whether the model fails where people fail.

items.stem: Researchers want to find out whether a network that names objects as accurately as people do also works the way people do. Which of these tests would be strongest?

options.text: Change one thing about the images, such as moving one part of each object, and check whether the network fails where people fail.
options.why: Correct. A test of this kind asks whether the network’s errors fall where people’s do. Removing contour in two different ways was a test of the same kind for the parts account.

options.text: Train the network on many more photographs, and check whether its overall accuracy climbs even further above that of people.
options.why: Higher accuracy is still only a match, or a better score, on answers. It is not evidence that the network gets its answers the way people do.

options.text: Give the network a new set of ordinary photographs, and check whether its overall accuracy stays close to that of people.
options.why: Matching people’s answers is not evidence of matching workings, just as a digital clock matches a mechanical one and works nothing like it.

options.text: Record brain activity while people view the same photographs, and check whether the network’s internal activity predicts it closely.
options.why: A close match to brain activity is still a match, and is not by itself shown to reflect the same workings. The strongest tests check whether the model fails where people fail.

items.stem: A network trained on images sprinkled with one kind of visual noise outscores people on that noise, and someone concludes that it handles visual noise the way people do, only better. In a short paragraph, explain why outscoring or matching people is not evidence that a model works the way a human brain does, and describe the strongest kind of test. Then say what happened when the same network was tested on a second, similar-looking noise, and what that result means for training on altered copies of images.
items.answer: A model that matches or beats people’s answers, or even matches brain activity, is not thereby shown to work the way a brain does. A digital clock predicts a mechanical clock’s time perfectly while working nothing like it. The strongest tests change one thing at a time and check whether the model fails where people fail. When this network was tested on a second kind of noise, one that looks similar to a person, it scored only about 10%, close to the 6% expected by chance. So training on altered copies gave it tolerance to the alteration it was trained on and very little beyond. People, by contrast, handle distortions they have never encountered.
rubric: States that matching or outscoring people is not evidence that a model works the way a brain does, using the clock comparison or an equivalent example.
Describes the strongest kind of test: change one thing and check whether the model fails where people fail.
Reports that on a second, similar-looking noise the network scored near chance (about 10% against 6%; exact numbers not required).
Concludes that training on altered copies gave tolerance to the trained alteration and very little beyond, while people handle distortions they have never encountered.

pools.title: Locating and Separating Sounds, and Combining Senses

items.stem: What is an interaural time difference?

options.text: The difference in when a sound reaches the two ears, which helps indicate where the sound comes from.
options.why: Correct. The ear nearer the source hears the sound first, and the size of that head start depends on the direction the sound comes from.

options.text: The difference in how loud a sound is at the two ears, caused by the head shadowing the far ear.
options.why: That is the interaural level difference, the other comparison between the ears. It depends on loudness rather than on timing, and it matters mainly for high pitches.

options.text: The difference between where a point’s images fall in the two eyes, which depends on how near the point is.
options.why: That is binocular disparity, the comparison between the two eyes that vision uses to recover depth. An interaural time difference is a comparison between the two ears.

options.text: The delay of about a tenth of a second before news of an image slipping across the retina turns into a correction.
options.why: That is the delay a slow body faces in acting on old information. An interaural time difference is far smaller, a matter of millionths of a second between the ears.

items.stem: Which term names the difference in loudness of a sound at the two ears, caused by the head shadowing the far ear, which helps indicate where a high-pitched sound comes from?

options.text: interaural level difference
options.why: Correct. The head casts an acoustic shadow over the far ear, so the sound is a little quieter there. Low pitches bend around the head, which is why this cue serves mainly for high pitches.

options.text: interaural time difference
options.why: That is the difference in when a sound reaches the two ears, the near ear hearing it first. It is the main cue for low pitches, and it concerns timing rather than loudness.

options.text: binocular disparity
options.why: That is the difference between the positions of a point’s images in the two eyes, which carries information about depth. It compares the eyes, not the ears.

options.text: auditory scene analysis
options.why: That is grouping the components of one mixed sound wave into the sources that produced them. It sorts out which sounds belong together, not where a sound comes from.

items.stem: A high whistle and a low hum both come from the same spot, off to a listener’s left and slightly in front. In a few sentences, explain which difference between the two ears mainly locates each sound and why, and what cue tells the listener that the whistle is in front rather than behind.
items.answer: Both sounds reach the left ear first and are a little quieter at the right ear. But low pitches bend around the head, so the head casts almost no acoustic shadow for the hum, and the hum gives little difference in level. The hum is located mainly by the interaural time difference, the left ear hearing it first. The whistle is high-pitched, so the head shadows the right ear and the whistle is clearly quieter there. It is located mainly by the interaural level difference. Neither difference settles front from back, because a source at the mirror-image spot behind would give the same differences. The folds of the outer ear filter a sound differently depending on where it comes from, and that filtering tells the listener the whistle is in front. Those filtering cues have to be learned, since every person’s ears are shaped differently.
rubric: Says the low hum is located mainly by the interaural time difference, the near ear hearing it first.
Says low pitches bend around the head, so the hum produces little difference in level between the ears.
Says the high whistle is located mainly by the interaural level difference, because the head shadows the far ear for high pitches.
Says front and back are told apart by the folds of the outer ear filtering the sound by direction, since the differences between the ears leave front and back ambiguous.

items.stem: A sound comes from directly in front of a listener, and later the same sound comes from directly behind. In both cases it reaches the two ears at the same moment and at the same loudness. Which cue can tell the two positions apart?

options.text: The filtering by the folds of the outer ear, which changes a sound differently depending on the direction of its source.
options.why: Correct. With the source straight ahead or straight behind, the two ears receive the same timing and the same level. The folds of the outer ear are what mainly tell front from back, and up from down.

options.text: The interaural time difference, since a sound from behind reaches both ears a little later than a sound from in front does.
options.why: An interaural time difference is a difference between the two ears, and here there is none: both ears hear the sound together. Arriving later overall does not say which side the sound came from.

options.text: The interaural level difference, since the head casts its acoustic shadow over both ears for a sound from behind.
options.why: The head’s shadow makes one ear quieter than the other. A sound from directly behind reaches both ears equally, so it gives no difference in level to read.

options.text: The place where signals from the two ears meet along a row of detectors, which differs for a sound in front and behind.
options.why: That place stands for a time difference between the ears. Straight ahead and straight behind both give no time difference, so the signals meet at the same place for either.

items.stem: A volunteer wears soft molds that change the shape of the folds of both outer ears, leaving the head and the positions of the ears unchanged. If the outer-ear cues work as described in the reading, which pattern of results is most likely?

options.text: Telling up from down gets worse at first while telling left from right is unaffected, and up-down judgments improve with experience.
options.why: Correct. The folds mainly tell up from down and front from back, and the differences between the two ears, which locate left and right, are untouched. Because the filtering cues have to be learned, new folds can be learned too.

options.text: Telling left from right gets worse at first while telling up from down is unaffected, and left-right judgments improve with experience.
options.why: That reverses the roles of the cues. Left and right come from the differences between the ears, which the molds leave alone, while the folds serve mainly for up and down and front and back.

options.text: Telling up from down gets worse and stays worse, since the filtering cues an outer ear provides are fixed from birth and cannot be relearned.
options.why: The filtering cues are learned, because every person’s ears are shaped differently. A cue that has to be learned in the first place can be learned again for new folds.

options.text: Nothing changes, since every cue to the direction of a sound comes from the differences between the sound at the two ears.
options.why: The differences between the ears leave up and down, and front and back, ambiguous. The folds of the outer ear supply those, so changing the folds should matter.

items.stem: In a delay line, signals from the left ear enter a row of detectors at one end and signals from the right ear enter at the other, and each detector responds only when signals from both sides arrive together. A sound source moves from straight ahead to far off to the left. What happens in the row?

options.text: The point where the two signals meet moves from the middle of the row toward the end where the right ear’s signals enter.
options.why: Correct. A sound from the left gives the left ear’s signal a head start, so it travels farther along the row before it meets the right ear’s signal. Where the signals meet stands for one time difference, and so one direction.

options.text: The point where the two signals meet moves from the middle of the row toward the end where the left ear’s signals enter.
options.why: That reverses the geometry. The left ear’s signal starts first, so it covers more of the row before the right ear’s signal reaches it, and the meeting point moves away from the left ear’s end.

options.text: The detector in the middle of the row keeps responding, but more strongly, because the sound is now louder at the left ear.
options.why: A delay line measures timing, not loudness. The difference in loudness between the ears is a separate cue, the interaural level difference, and it does not move the meeting point.

options.text: Every detector along the row responds at once, because the left ear now hears the sound before the right ear does.
options.why: Each detector responds only when signals from both ears arrive at the same moment. A time difference therefore picks out one place along the row, not all of it.

items.stem: Two procedures have been proposed for measuring the tiny difference in when a sound reaches the two ears. How do they differ?

options.text: One turns a time difference into a place along a row of detectors, and the other reads direction from the balance of two broad channels.
options.why: Correct. A delay line maps a time difference onto the detector where the two ears’ signals coincide. The other procedure needs no map: each of two broad channels favors one side, and the balance of activity between them gives the direction.

options.text: One measures the difference in when a sound arrives at each ear, and the other measures the difference in how loud it is at each ear.
options.why: Those are the two differences between the ears, timing and level. Both proposed procedures are ways of measuring the timing difference alone.

options.text: One locates sounds to the left or to the right, and the other uses the folds of the outer ear to locate sounds above or below.
options.why: The outer ear’s folds are a separate cue, mainly for up and down and for front and back. Both proposed procedures measure the left-right timing difference.

options.text: One reads direction off the cochlea’s map, which is laid out by pitch, and the other reads direction with no map at all.
options.why: The cochlea’s map is laid out by frequency, and says which pitches are present, not where a sound came from. The map in a delay line is a row of detectors on which a place stands for a time difference.

items.stem: At night, a camper hears two equally faint sounds: a car horn of a familiar kind, and the call of an animal the camper has never heard before. For which sound can its loudness signal how far away it is?

options.text: The car horn, because its loudness at the source is already known, so a faint horn signals a distant one.
options.why: Correct. Loudness signals distance only for sounds whose loudness the listener already knows. The animal call could be a quiet call nearby or a loud one far away.

options.text: The animal call, because an unfamiliar sound is attended to more closely, so its loudness is judged more exactly.
options.why: Attention does not supply the missing fact. Without knowing how loud the call is at its source, a faint call could be quiet and near or loud and far.

options.text: Both sounds, because a sound that arrives faint has traveled farther than a sound that arrives loud.
options.why: That holds only for sounds that are equally loud at their source. A quiet sound nearby and a loud sound far away can arrive equally faint.

options.text: Neither sound, because hearing recovers the direction of a sound but gives no information about its distance.
options.why: Distance is partly available to hearing, not missing altogether. Loudness signals distance for sounds of known loudness, such as a familiar horn.

items.stem: Loudness can serve as a cue to how far away a sound is, much as image size can serve as a cue to how far away an object is. What do the two cues have in common?

options.text: Each indicates distance only when the true loudness of the sound, or the true size of the object, is already known.
options.why: Correct. A faint sound may be quiet and near or loud and far, just as a small image may come from a small object nearby or a large one far away. Knowing the true loudness or size settles it.

options.text: Each indicates distance by comparing what two sensors receive, the two ears for a sound and the two eyes for an object.
options.why: Comparing two sensors is how hearing recovers direction and how stereo vision recovers depth. Loudness and image size work as distance cues without any such comparison.

options.text: Each indicates exact distance in any setting, since loudness and image size both shrink at a fixed rate with distance.
options.why: Both do shrink with distance, but a quiet sound nearby gives the same loudness as a loud sound far away. Neither cue settles distance without knowing the source.

options.text: Each indicates distance only for a sound or an object that moves, since only a change over time reveals how far away something is.
options.why: Motion parallax needs movement, but loudness and image size do not. Each works for a still sound or object, provided its true loudness or size is known.

items.stem: What is auditory scene analysis?

options.text: Grouping the components of a mixed sound wave into the separate sources that produced them.
options.why: Correct. Each ear receives one wave, the sum of every sound reaching it. Auditory scene analysis recovers which parts of that wave belong to which source.

options.text: Comparing the sound that reaches the two ears in order to recover the direction it came from.
options.why: That describes the interaural cues, timing and level, which locate a sound. Auditory scene analysis groups the parts of a mixture into sources.

options.text: Combining estimates from hearing and another sense by weighting each according to how reliable it is.
options.why: That is cue combination, which merges signals that share a cause. Auditory scene analysis works within hearing, sorting one mixed wave into its sources.

options.text: Laying out the receptors of the cochlea so that neighboring frequencies vibrate neighboring places.
options.why: That is tonotopy, the cochlea’s map by frequency. The map says which frequencies are present, not which source produced each of them.

items.stem: Two singers hold notes at the same time. In which case is a listener most likely to hear them as two separate singers?

options.text: When they sing at different pitches, so each voice’s components are multiples of a different lowest frequency.
options.why: Correct. Components that are whole-number multiples of one lowest frequency are heard as one sound. Voices at different pitches form two such sets, so they separate more easily than voices at the same pitch.

options.text: When they sing at the same pitch, so the components of the two voices line up and reinforce one another.
options.why: Components that line up as multiples of one lowest frequency are heard as one sound. Two voices at the same pitch are therefore harder to separate, not easier.

options.text: When they start each note at exactly the same moment, so the shared start marks the two voices as two sources.
options.why: Parts of a sound that start together usually come from one source. A shared start pulls the voices together rather than apart.

options.text: When they stand far apart, so that location, the strongest cue for sounds heard at one moment, can group them.
options.why: Location is a weak cue for grouping sounds heard at the same moment. It becomes a strong cue for following one source over time.

items.stem: A synthesizer plays a note built from components at 200, 400, 600, and 800 hertz, all starting together, and a listener hears one note. On the next trial, the 600-hertz component is switched on slightly before the others. What is the listener likely to hear?

options.text: A separate tone at 600 hertz popping out of the note, heard alongside a note made of the remaining components.
options.why: Correct. Parts that start together are usually grouped as one source. A component that starts a little earlier than the rest tends to pop out and be heard as a separate tone.

options.text: One note just as before, since the 600-hertz component is still a whole-number multiple of 200 hertz.
options.why: Harmonic relations do group components, but timing matters as well. A component of such a note that starts early tends to pop out as a tone of its own.

options.text: A note with a lower pitch than before, since the early component pulls the pitch of the whole note downward.
options.why: Starting early changes how the components are grouped, not the pitch the others carry. The remaining components are still multiples of 200 hertz.

options.text: No 600-hertz tone at all, since a component that starts early is masked by the louder components that follow it.
options.why: Nothing in the grouping cues hides an early component. The usual result is the reverse: the component that starts early stands out as its own tone.

items.stem: An alarm alternates between a high beep and a low beep. Played slowly, it is heard as one pattern hopping up and down. The alarm is then sped up a great deal. What is a listener likely to hear?

options.text: Two separate streams of beeps, one high and one low, each forming a pattern with its own rhythm.
options.why: Correct. Grouping works across time. Slowly alternating tones are heard as one melody, and fast ones split into two streams by pitch.

options.text: One faster pattern hopping up and down, since speed changes the rhythm but not the grouping.
options.why: Speed is exactly what changes the grouping. Past some rate, the high and low beeps stop forming one pattern and split into two streams.

options.text: A single steady tone at a pitch between the two, since fast beeps blend into their average.
options.why: The beeps are not averaged into one pitch. They are sorted into two streams, a high one and a low one, each heard with its own rhythm.

options.text: Only the high beeps, since a higher pitch masks a lower one once the beeps come close together.
options.why: Neither pitch drops out. Both are still heard, but as two separate streams rather than one pattern hopping up and down.

items.stem: At a crowded party, a guest has one ear blocked by an earplug. Compared with listening with both ears, which task is likely to become much harder?

options.text: Following one friend’s conversation from moment to moment, amid all the other voices and noise filling the room.
options.why: Correct. Location is a strong cue for following one talker over time, and locating a talker to the left or right depends on comparing the two ears. Blocking one ear makes a conversation in a crowd much harder to follow.

options.text: Hearing that the parts of a single voice belong together, since harmonic relations are detected by comparing the ears.
options.why: Harmonic relations are relations among the frequencies in one sound, and one ear receives all of them. Grouping by those relations does not need a comparison between ears.

options.text: Hearing the pitch of a low note whose lowest frequency is missing, since that pitch comes from comparing the ears.
options.why: That pitch is inferred from the pattern of the components that remain, which one ear receives. It does not depend on comparing the ears.

options.text: Noticing that a new sound has begun, since the start of a sound is signaled by a difference between the ears.
options.why: Each ear on its own registers when a sound starts. Common onset groups the parts of a sound without any comparison between the ears.

items.stem: A sound’s location can help a listener group what they hear. How does location’s usefulness differ between grouping sounds heard at a single moment and following one source over time?

options.text: Location is a weak cue for grouping sounds heard at one moment, but a strong one for following one source over time.
options.why: Correct. At a single moment, location adds little to grouping. Over time it helps a listener stay with one talker, which is why two ears help so much in a noisy room.

options.text: Location is a strong cue for grouping sounds heard at one moment, but a weak one for following one source over time.
options.why: That reverses the finding. Location contributes little at a single moment, and helps a great deal in following one talker through a noisy room.

options.text: Location is a strong cue in both cases, since grouping sounds of any kind begins by working out where each one came from.
options.why: Grouping at one moment draws on regularities such as common onset and harmonic relations, and location turns out to add little there. It is a strong cue only for following one talker over time.

options.text: Location is a weak cue in both cases, since grouping has to be finished before the direction of any sound can be worked out.
options.why: Location is weak for sounds heard at the same moment. For following one talker over time it is strong, and blocking one ear makes a crowded conversation much harder.

items.stem: A small speaker cannot produce the lowest frequency of a cello note, but it does produce the note’s higher components, which are whole-number multiples of that lowest frequency. What pitch are listeners likely to hear?

options.text: The pitch of the missing lowest frequency, inferred from the pattern formed by the other components that remain.
options.why: Correct. With the lowest frequency removed, listeners still hear its pitch. The pitch is an inference about the source, drawn from how the remaining components are related.

options.text: The pitch of the lowest component the speaker does produce, since pitch is set by the lowest frequency present.
options.why: If pitch were simply the lowest frequency present, removing it would raise the pitch. Listeners instead still hear the pitch of the missing frequency.

options.text: No definite pitch, since a note that lacks its lowest frequency leaves a listener nothing to base a pitch on.
options.why: The remaining components carry the pattern of the missing frequency, and listeners use it. They hear a definite pitch, the pitch of the frequency that is not there.

options.text: The pitch of the loudest of the remaining components, since the strongest frequency in a sound determines its pitch.
options.why: No single component sets the pitch. The pitch heard is that of the missing lowest frequency, inferred from how the remaining components are related.

items.stem: When the lowest frequency is removed from a sound made of that frequency and its whole-number multiples, listeners still hear the pitch of the removed frequency. What can be concluded from this result?

options.text: Pitch is an inference about the source of a sound, not a property of any one of the components that reach the ear.
options.why: Correct. No component at that frequency reaches the ear, yet its pitch is heard. The pitch is constructed from the pattern of the components that remain.

options.text: Pitch is the frequency of the loudest component of a sound, which removing the lowest one leaves in place.
options.why: If pitch were the loudest component’s frequency, listeners would hear that component’s pitch. The pitch heard belongs to no component that is present.

options.text: Pitch is worked out by comparing a sound at the two ears, a comparison that removing one frequency leaves intact.
options.why: Comparing the two ears is how the direction of a sound is recovered. Pitch is an inference from the frequencies in the sound, here about one that is absent.

options.text: Pitch is a fixed physical property of the sound wave, which the ear reads off without needing any inference.
options.why: If pitch were read off the wave, a sound with nothing at the lowest frequency would lack that frequency’s pitch. Since listeners hear that pitch anyway, the pitch must be inferred.

items.stem: In a park, a flute and a tuba play different notes at the same time, and each of a listener’s ears receives one pressure wave, the sum of both instruments. In a short paragraph, explain why recovering the two instruments from this wave is an ill-posed problem, name two regularities of real sound sources that help group the components heard at one moment, and describe how grouping can also work across time.
items.answer: Each ear receives one wave, the sum of both instruments, and many different combinations of sources could have produced that same wave. So the wave alone does not settle what the sources were, which makes the problem ill-posed. Auditory scene analysis gets around this by relying on how real sources usually behave. Components that start at the same moment usually come from one source. And a source that vibrates regularly, like a flute or a tuba, produces frequencies that are all whole-number multiples of one lowest frequency, so the flute’s components are heard as one sound and the tuba’s as another. Because the two play at different pitches, they separate more easily than two instruments on the same note would. Grouping also works across time. If high and low notes alternate quickly, they split into two streams, one high and one low, so a run of quick flute and tuba notes can be heard as two separate lines rather than one zigzag.
rubric: Says the summed wave could have been produced by many different combinations of sources, so the wave alone does not settle what the sources were.
Says the problem is solved by relying on how real sound sources usually behave.
Names common onset: components that start at the same moment are grouped as one source (or the converse, that a component starting early pops out as a separate tone).
Names harmonic relations: components that are whole-number multiples of one lowest frequency are heard as one sound, which separates instruments playing at different pitches.
Describes streaming: quickly alternating high and low tones split into two streams, one high and one low.

items.stem: In a badly dubbed film, an actor’s lips move a full second before the matching words are heard, and viewers stop hearing the voice as coming from the actor’s mouth. Which problem of combining senses does this case turn on?

options.text: Deciding whether the sight and the sound share one cause, which so large a gap in timing makes unlikely.
options.why: Correct. Sight and sound that arrive together from one place probably share a cause. A full second apart, the lips and the voice no longer seem to, so the mouth does not capture the voice.

options.text: Weighting two signals that share a cause, with hearing weighted more because it is more precise about location.
options.why: Vision, not hearing, is usually the more precise sense about location. And weighting applies to signals that share a cause, which is exactly what the timing gap calls into question.

options.text: Resolving an ambiguity in one sense with another, as the canals settle a tilt from an acceleration.
options.why: That is a different use of a second sense, supplying information the first one lacks. Here the question is whether the lips and the voice belong to one event.

options.text: Grouping one sound wave into its sources, since the voice and the film’s music are spread through one mixture.
options.why: That is auditory scene analysis within hearing. The dubbing problem crosses the senses: whether what is seen and what is heard share a cause.

items.stem: Combining senses involves two problems: deciding whether two signals share a cause, and weighting signals that do share one by how reliable each is. Why does the shared-cause question have to be settled first?

options.text: A weighted average makes sense only for two estimates of one event; averaging estimates of two different events gives an estimate of neither.
options.why: Correct. Weighting by reliability combines two estimates of one thing. When a sight and a sound come from different events, there is no one thing to estimate, which is why capture stops once the signals seem to have separate causes.

options.text: Deciding on a shared cause switches off the less reliable sense, and the weighting can begin only after that sense is out of the way.
options.why: No sense is switched off in cue combination. Each keeps a weight in line with its reliability, and the shared-cause question settles whether to combine the signals at all.

options.text: Deciding on a shared cause is the faster of the two steps, so it finishes first, though either order would give the same result.
options.why: The order is not a matter of speed. Weighting assumes one cause, so weighting signals from two different events would give an estimate of nothing in the world.

options.text: Deciding on a shared cause is how the reliability of each sense gets measured, and the weighting then uses that measure as its input.
options.why: Reliability is a property of each sense’s estimate, such as how blurred an image is. The shared-cause question is separate: whether the two signals belong together at all.

items.stem: Which term names combining estimates from several sources of evidence, such as two senses, by weighting each according to how reliable it is?

options.text: cue combination
options.why: Correct. When a bar’s seen and felt heights disagreed, judgments fell between them, weighted toward the more reliable sense, and the combined judgment was more precise than either sense alone.

options.text: auditory scene analysis
options.why: That is grouping the components of one mixed sound wave into their sources. It sorts what belongs together within hearing rather than weighting estimates by reliability.

options.text: depth cue
options.why: That is a feature of a sensory signal that, given an assumption usually true of the world, indicates how far away something is. It is one source of evidence, not a way of weighting several.

options.text: efference copy
options.why: That is a copy of a movement command, kept so that the expected sensory results of a movement can be compared with what the senses report. It predicts rather than weighs.

items.stem: A person judges the size of a ball they can both see and hold. The ball is made to look slightly larger than it feels, and in good light the judgment falls close to the seen size. The room is then made very dim. How does the judgment change?

options.text: It moves toward the felt size, because dim light makes vision less reliable, so vision is given less weight.
options.why: Correct. Each sense is weighted by its reliability. When vision is made noisier it counts for less, so the combined judgment shifts toward touch.

options.text: It stays near the seen size, because vision is the more precise sense and keeps the same weight in any light.
options.why: Vision usually is the more precise sense, but its weight follows how reliable it is at the moment. Made noisier, vision counts for less, and the judgment moves toward touch.

options.text: It jumps all the way to the felt size, because a sense that turns noisy is switched off and given no weight.
options.why: Noisier vision is weighted less, not discarded. The judgment still falls between the two senses, now closer to touch.

options.text: It moves to a point beyond both senses, because two senses that disagree more push the judgment past either.
options.why: Judgments fall between the seen and the felt sizes, as a weighted average. Disagreement moves the judgment within the range between them, not beyond it.

items.stem: In a dark room, a flash of light is blurred until it is a faint, spread-out glow, and at the same moment a click sounds from a spot a little to one side of it. Where does the flash seem to be?

options.text: Close to where the click was, because blurring has made hearing the more precise sense about location here.
options.why: Correct. Capture follows reliability. Vision usually captures a sound’s location, but blur a flash enough and the relation reverses, so the click captures the flash.

options.text: Where the flash was, because vision is the sense that captures location from hearing, blurred or not.
options.why: Vision captures location when it is the more precise sense, as it usually is. Blurring the flash enough makes hearing the more precise sense, and the relation reverses.

options.text: At a point exactly halfway between them, because two senses that disagree about location get equal weight.
options.why: The weights follow reliability, not a fixed split. With the flash blurred, hearing is the more reliable sense about location and gets more of the weight.

options.text: Nowhere definite, because a blurred flash gives no location at all and a click cannot supply one.
options.why: A blurred flash still gives a location, only a less precise one. And a click can supply one: blurred enough, the flash is captured by the click.

items.stem: A puppeteer’s voice comes from a loudspeaker. With the loudspeaker just beside the puppet, the voice seems to come from the puppet’s moving mouth. The loudspeaker is then moved to the far side of a large hall. What is likely to happen, and why?

options.text: The voice is heard at the loudspeaker, since sight and sound so far apart no longer seem to share a cause.
options.why: Correct. Vision captures the voice only while the two signals seem to come from one event. Far enough apart, capture stops, and each signal is heard or seen where it really is.

options.text: The voice is still heard at the puppet, since vision is more precise about location at any distance.
options.why: Vision is more precise, but its precision only matters for signals that share a cause. Far enough apart, sight and sound are taken as separate events, and capture stops.

options.text: The voice is heard midway between the loudspeaker and the puppet, since a large conflict is averaged like a small one.
options.why: Averaging applies to signals taken to share a cause. A conflict this large breaks that link, so the voice is no longer pulled toward the puppet at all.

options.text: The voice seems to come from everywhere at once, since echoes in a large hall confuse a listener about direction.
options.why: Echoes arrive from every direction yet rarely mislead, because the first sound to arrive dominates the judgment. The listener can still tell where the loudspeaker is.

items.stem: To the balance sensors that respond to gravity and acceleration, tilting the head back and speeding up forward produce the same signal. What settles which of the two happened?

options.text: The canals of the inner ear sense rotation, which tilting the head produces and speeding up does not.
options.why: Correct. Tilting the head rotates it, and the canals respond to rotation. Speeding up forward involves no rotation, so the canals resolve the ambiguity the other sensors leave.

options.text: The two ears receive sound at slightly different times, a difference that changes when the head tilts back.
options.why: That is the interaural time difference, a cue to where a sound comes from. It says nothing about whether the head tilted or the body sped up.

options.text: The folds of the outer ear filter sound differently once the head has tilted, which reveals the new angle.
options.why: The outer ear’s folds help locate a sound source, mainly up from down and front from back. They are not a sense of the head’s own motion.

options.text: A copy of the movement command is present for tilting and absent for speeding up, which tells the two apart.
options.why: A copy of the command exists for any movement the animal makes itself, a tilt of the head or a lunge forward alike. When either motion is imposed from outside, as in a vehicle, there is no command at all.

items.stem: In cue combination, two senses that share a cause are weighted by reliability and averaged. The canals of the inner ear help with the tilt-or-acceleration ambiguity in a different way. What is the difference?

options.text: The canals settle which of two readings of the acceleration signal is right, instead of being averaged in with it.
options.why: Correct. The acceleration signal fits both a tilt and a forward acceleration. The canals report rotation, which only the tilt produces, so they settle which reading is right.

options.text: The canals are more reliable than the acceleration sensors, so their estimate is averaged in with the larger of the two weights.
options.why: That describes cue combination, two estimates of one quantity weighted and averaged. The canals do something else: they settle which of two readings of an ambiguous signal is right.

options.text: The canals switch the acceleration sensors off whenever the head turns, so only one of the two signals is left to use.
options.why: Switching a sense off is dimming, one way of handling self-caused signals. The canals leave the acceleration sensors working and add rotation, which settles the ambiguity.

options.text: The canals settle whether the two signals share a cause, which is the problem of scene analysis across the senses.
options.why: Deciding on a shared cause is the first problem of combining senses. The canals help with a different one: telling which of two causes produced one ambiguous signal.

items.stem: At dusk, a hiker hears a branch snap and at the same moment glimpses a deer moving among the trees, a little to the left of where the snap seemed to be. In a short paragraph, explain the two problems involved in combining what the hiker saw and heard, and how the deer’s location would be judged at dusk compared with at noon.
items.answer: The first problem is deciding whether the snap and the movement share a cause. They came from about the same place at the same moment, so they probably do, and only then does it make sense to combine them. The second problem is that the two signals, though they share a cause, disagree slightly about where the deer is. Cue combination weights each signal by its reliability, so the judged location falls between where the deer was seen and where the snap was heard. At noon, vision is much more precise about location than hearing, so the judgment would fall close to where the deer was seen, the way a ventriloquist’s voice is captured by the puppet. At dusk, vision is noisier, so it counts for less, and the judgment moves toward where the snap was heard. Either way, the combined judgment is more precise than either sense alone.
rubric: Identifies the first problem as deciding whether the sight and the sound share a cause, judged from their coming from about the same place at the same moment.
Identifies the second problem as combining signals that share a cause but disagree, by weighting each according to its reliability.
Says that at noon vision is the more precise sense about location, so the judgment falls close to where the deer was seen.
Says that at dusk vision is less reliable, so it gets less weight and the judgment moves toward where the snap was heard.

pools.title: From Eye to Arm, and Predicting One’s Own Sensations
pools.covers: reading §8.2.8, §8.2.9, §8.2.10, §8.2.11 · lecture 8.2 slides from_eye_to_arm, a_copy_of_the_command, predicting_ones_own_sensations, learning_from_mismatch

items.stem: The mapping from eye angles to arm angles can be pictured as a rubber sheet, stretched and bent until each point in the space of eye angles lands on the arm angles that reach it. A table that stored the answer for every point would do the same job. What does a network that learns the mapping gain over such a table?

options.text: It holds the mapping in far fewer stored values, set by adjusting its weights, and it can relearn the mapping as the body changes.
options.why: Correct. A table needs an entry for every point. A network captures the same stretched sheet in its weights, and because the weights can be adjusted again, the mapping can be relearned as the body grows or changes.

options.text: It gives an exact answer at each point, where a table gives rough answers for points that fall between its stored entries.
options.why: A table that stored the answer for every point would already be exact. What the network gains is far fewer stored values and the ability to relearn.

options.text: It copies the eye angles straight across to the arm angles, so it needs no stored values and the mapping never has to be relearned.
options.why: Copying the numbers across is exactly what fails: a target at eye angles of 55 and 85 calls for arm angles of 62 and 12. The sheet has to be stretched and bent, not copied.

options.text: It fixes the mapping once for every body of its kind, so its stored values never have to change as one animal’s body grows and ages.
options.why: That reverses the point. Bodies grow, tire, and change, so a mapping that could never change would soon be wrong. Being able to relearn is one of the network’s advantages.

items.stem: Just before a saccade, the image of a lamp falls on one particular spot on the retina. Just after the saccade, the image of a doorway falls on that same spot. What follows about the directions of the lamp and the doorway in the world?

options.text: They lie in different directions, and working out how far apart needs a record of how far the eyes moved.
options.why: Correct. A spot on the retina gives direction relative to the eye. Once the eye has jumped, the same spot stands for a new direction in the world, so turning a retinal position into a direction needs a running record of where the eyes point.

options.text: They lie in the same direction, since a given spot on the retina always stands for one direction in the world.
options.why: A spot on the retina gives direction relative to the eye, not relative to the world. Every movement of the eye changes which direction in the world that spot stands for.

options.text: They lie in the same direction, since the image motion of each saccade is predicted and subtracted from what arrives.
options.why: Predicting and subtracting the image motion of a saccade keeps the world from seeming to jump. It does not stop a retinal spot from standing for a new direction after the eye has moved.

options.text: They lie in different directions, and how far apart can be read off the retina alone, with no record of the eyes.
options.why: The directions do differ, but the retina alone cannot say by how much. The same spot stands for a new direction after every eye movement, so the size of the movement has to be known as well.

items.stem: A target flashed briefly in front of a monkey, and just afterward the monkey’s eyes were pushed off course. Its next saccade still landed on the place where the flash had been. What can be concluded from that result?

options.text: The monkey’s brain combined where the flash had fallen on the retina with where the eyes had gone since, keeping a record of eye position.
options.why: Correct. Once the eyes had been pushed, retinal position alone would have aimed the saccade wrongly. Landing on the flash means the brain kept a running record of where the eyes pointed and combined it with the retinal position.

options.text: The monkey’s brain aimed the saccade by where the flash had fallen on the retina alone, since that spot gives the flash’s direction in the world.
options.why: Aiming by the retinal spot alone would have sent the saccade off by however far the eyes had been pushed. A retinal spot gives direction relative to the eye, not the world.

options.text: The monkey kept its eyes on the flash while they were pushed, so the flash’s image never left the center of its retina.
options.why: The flash was brief and the eyes were pushed off course afterward, so the image could not be kept centered. The saccade found the flash by combining its retinal position with a record of where the eyes had gone.

options.text: The monkey’s brain learned the flash’s location over many trials, adjusting its aim in proportion to each miss.
options.why: Learning in proportion to each miss describes how a mapping is relearned, as in prism throwing. Here the saccade landed on target on the trial itself, from the retinal position plus a record of eye position.

items.stem: In a dark room, a person sees a small glowing light whose image falls to the left of the center of the retina. The light then goes out, and the person turns the eyes to the right before reaching toward it in the dark. Besides where the light fell on the retina, what is needed to work out where the light was?

options.text: A record of how far the eyes have turned since the light went out, to combine with where its image fell on the retina.
options.why: Correct. After the eyes turn, the spot where the light fell stands for a different direction. Combining the old retinal position with a running record of eye position recovers where the light was, as monkeys do when their eyes are pushed off course.

options.text: A new image of the light on the retina, since a target can be located only while its image is still falling on the retina.
