options.why: A remembered target can still be located: monkeys whose eyes were pushed after a flash still looked to where it had been. What is needed is a record of how the eyes have moved since.

options.text: The size of the light’s image on the retina, since its distance alone is enough to say where the light was.
options.why: Distance matters for a reach, but it does not give direction. Once the eyes have turned, direction needs the old retinal position combined with a record of the eye movement.

options.text: The current angles of the person’s shoulder, elbow, and wrist, since the arm’s own position says where the light was.
options.why: The arm’s angles are needed to plan the movement, but they carry nothing about where the light was. That comes from the retinal position plus the eye movement since.

items.stem: A fly inside a drum painted with vertical stripes turns to follow the drum when the drum rotates. When the fly turns on its own inside a still drum, its eyes receive the same sweep of stripes, yet it does not turn back to follow them. Which two possible answers were proposed for why it does not turn back?

options.text: Its response to visual motion is switched off while it moves, or it expects the motion of its own turn and subtracts that from its eyes’ report.
options.why: Correct. These are the two answers, and they make different predictions once an eye is reversed: switching off predicts normal behavior, and subtraction predicts spinning.

options.text: Its eyes report the stripes too late to drive a response during its own turn, or the sweep blurs so much during the turn that no motion is seen.
options.why: The fly’s eyes do receive the same sweep in both cases, and they do drive a response when the drum turns. The puzzle is why the same input brings no response when the fly’s own turn produced it.

options.text: It weights its leg sensors above its eyes during a turn, or it treats the sweep of stripes and its own turn as having separate causes.
options.why: Weighting senses by reliability, and deciding whether two signals share a cause, are the problems of combining senses. Neither was one of the two answers to the fly’s puzzle.

options.text: Its eyes and legs describe the turn in different coordinates, or it relearns the link between its eyes and legs after every turn it makes.
options.why: Different coordinates are a problem for turning a seen target into a movement, and relearning keeps a mapping up to date as the body changes. Neither explains why the fly’s own turn brings no response.

items.stem: An animal’s eye is rotated so that it sees left and right reversed. Suppose the animal normally expects the image motion its own turn will cause and subtracts that from what its eyes report. Why should it then spin when it turns inside a still, striped drum?

options.text: Expected and actual motion now add instead of canceling, so each turn leaves an error that calls for more turning.
options.why: Correct. With the eye reversed, the image moves the opposite way from what the turn predicts. Subtracting the expectation doubles the motion instead of removing it, and the error drives more turning, which makes more error.

options.text: Its response to visual motion is switched off while it turns, so nothing stops a turn once the turn has started.
options.why: Switching off is the other answer, and it predicts normal behavior, since a switched-off response does not care which way the eye faces. It cannot explain the spinning.

options.text: The expected motion and the actual motion still cancel exactly, so it cannot tell that it is turning and never stops.
options.why: If the two still canceled, there would be no error and nothing to drive more turning. Reversing the eye is what stops them from canceling.

options.text: The reversed eye now sends its signals late, so each correction responds to a turn that has already ended and overshoots it.
options.why: Late feedback does tend to overshoot, but rotating the eye does not delay its signals. The spinning comes from the direction of the image motion, not its timing.

items.stem: A student objects that the eye-reversal experiments on the fly and the fish could not establish that animals compare expected input with sensed input, since no one recorded from a single neuron. What is the best reply?

options.text: The two possible answers predict different behavior, and the animals did what only a comparison predicts, so behavior alone is enough.
options.why: Correct. Switching off predicts normal behavior with a reversed eye, and subtraction predicts spinning. The animals spun, so a comparison between expected and sensed input exists, established without recording a single neuron.

options.text: The experiments did record from neurons, in the part of the fish’s brain receiving the rotated eye, and that is where the comparison was found.
options.why: No neuron was recorded in these experiments. The case rests on behavior: the animals spun, which only subtraction predicts.

options.text: The objection is right, and the comparison remained a guess until cells that subtract a prediction were recorded in later work.
options.why: Later work did find such cells, but they were not needed to establish the comparison. Reversing an eye made animals spin, which only subtraction predicts, and that was already enough to settle the question.

options.text: Behavior carries information only about whether animals move, so the comparison was instead inferred from their anatomy.
options.why: Anatomy played no part. The argument runs from behavior: one answer predicts normal behavior, the other predicts spinning, and the animals spun.

items.stem: A fly turning on its own inside a still, striped drum does not turn back to follow the stripes. In a short paragraph, give the two possible explanations, say what each one predicts for an animal whose eye has been rotated so that it sees left and right reversed, and explain what the animals’ actual behavior established.
items.answer: One explanation is that the response to visual motion is switched off whenever the animal moves. The other is that the animal expects the image motion its own turn will cause and subtracts that expectation from what its eyes report. Switching off predicts normal behavior with a reversed eye, because a switched-off response does not care which way the eye faces. Subtraction predicts spinning. With the eye reversed, the expected and actual motion add instead of canceling, so each turn leaves an error that calls for more turning. The animals spun, as subtraction predicts. So a comparison between expected and sensed input exists, and it was established from behavior alone, without recording a single neuron.
rubric: Names switching off the response to visual motion during movement as one explanation.
Names expecting the motion of one’s own turn and subtracting it as the other explanation.
Says switching off predicts normal behavior with a reversed eye, since the eye’s direction would not matter.
Says subtraction predicts spinning, because expected and actual motion add, so each turn calls for more turning.
Says the animals spun, so a comparison of expected with sensed input was established from behavior, without recording neurons.

items.stem: What is an efference copy?

options.text: A copy of a movement command, kept so that the expected sensory consequences of the movement can be compared with what the senses report.
options.why: Correct. The copy lets the nervous system anticipate what the movement will do to the senses, so the self-caused part of the input can be told apart from the rest.

options.text: Sensation caused by the animal’s own movement, such as the sweep of the image across the retina each time the eyes jump to a new target.
options.why: That is reafference, the input the comparison has to deal with. An efference copy is the copy of the command used to anticipate it.

options.text: A learned signal, opposite in shape to an expected self-caused input, that cancels that input when the two are added together.
options.why: That is a negative image, learned in electric fish from the pairing of command and input. An efference copy is the copy of the command itself.

options.text: A signal from receptors in the muscles, tendons, and joints that reports the body’s own position and movement as the movement happens.
options.why: That is proprioception, which measures movement directly. An efference copy is a copy of the command, available without waiting for the movement to be sensed.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “A signal derived from a movement command and sent to sensory areas, so that the sensory effects of the movement can be anticipated”.

options.text: corollary discharge
options.why: Correct. The term was coined for the signal behind the pufferfish experiment, and it is now used almost interchangeably with efference copy.

options.text: forward model
options.why: A forward model is a process that predicts what a command will do to the body and the senses. The defined thing is a signal derived from the command, which such a prediction can draw on.

options.text: reafference
options.why: Reafference is the sensory input caused by one’s own movement. It is what gets anticipated, not the signal that anticipates it.

options.text: proprioception
options.why: Proprioception is the sense of the body’s own position and movement, from receptors in the muscles, tendons, and joints. It reports a movement as it happens, rather than being derived from the command that caused it.

items.stem: How does an efference copy relate to a corollary discharge?

options.text: The two terms, coined independently in work on a fly and a fish, name the same kind of signal and are now used almost interchangeably.
options.why: Correct. Both name a signal taken from a movement command and used to anticipate its sensory effects. The two names arose separately and have converged.

options.text: An efference copy is a copy of a movement command, while a corollary discharge is a measurement of that movement made by the balance organs.
options.why: Measuring movement is the job of the vestibular system and proprioception. A corollary discharge is derived from the command, just as an efference copy is.

options.text: An efference copy dims a sense during movement, while a corollary discharge predicts a specific sensation and subtracts it.
options.why: Dimming and predicting are two uses of a copy of the command, not two different signals. Either term can name the copy, whichever use it is put to.

options.text: An efference copy is found only in insects such as flies, while a corollary discharge is found only in fish and in other vertebrates.
options.why: The terms came from experiments on a fly and on a fish, but they do not divide the animal kingdom between them. They name the same kind of signal wherever it occurs.

items.stem: A pufferfish with one eye rotated and the other covered swam in tight circles. It kept circling even after both of its balance organs had been removed. Why did that result matter?

options.text: Its expectation of image motion could not come from sensing the movement, which led to the proposal of a copy of the command.
options.why: Correct. With the balance organs gone, the expectation the circling depends on had to come from something other than measuring the movement. That is what led to the proposal of a copy of the movement command.

options.text: Its circling was a balance disorder caused by the surgery that removed the organs, rather than an effect of the rotated eye.
options.why: Turning the rotated eye back to its normal position stopped the circling, so the eye, not a balance problem, caused it. The balance organs mattered because removing them left the circling in place.

options.text: Its response to visual motion had been switched off whenever it swam, since nothing else could have kept it circling in that way.
options.why: Switching off would leave a fish with a rotated eye behaving normally, since a switched-off response does not care which way the eye faces. Circling is what subtraction predicts.

options.text: Its covered eye had taken over the work of the balance organs once they were gone, sensing each of its turns in their place.
options.why: The covered eye received no image to sense a turn with. The point was that the expectation survived without any sensing of the movement, which led to the proposal of a copy of the command.

items.stem: Suppose instead that removing both balance organs had stopped the circling of a fish with one eye rotated. What would that result have suggested about where the fish’s expectation of image motion came from?

options.text: It depended on sensing the movement with the balance organs, rather than on a copy of the movement command.
options.why: Correct. If the circling needed the balance organs, the expectation being subtracted would have depended on measuring the turn. In the actual experiment the circling survived their removal, so that possibility was ruled out.

options.text: It came from a copy of the movement command, since only a command could tell the fish which way it was turning.
options.why: That is the conclusion the real result, continued circling, led to. Had removing the balance organs stopped the circling, the expectation would have depended on them instead.

options.text: It came from nowhere, since circling that stops without balance organs means the fish was subtracting nothing at all.
options.why: The circling with the eye rotated is itself the evidence that something is subtracted. Removing the balance organs could only change where the expectation came from.

options.text: It came from the covered eye, since that eye would then be the one source of information left about the turn.
options.why: A covered eye receives no image of the surroundings, so it carries nothing about the turn. The question is whether the expectation comes from measuring the movement or from the command.

items.stem: A copy of a movement command can be used to dim a sense while an animal moves, or to predict a specific sensory consequence and subtract it. Which kind of self-caused signal does each use suit?

options.text: Dimming suits brief, simple self-caused signals, and predicting and subtracting suits complex, long-lasting ones.
options.why: Correct. A fish’s lateral line is turned down while it swims, and a person’s hearing while they speak. For complex, long-lasting signals, prediction removes the self-caused part and leaves the rest.

options.text: Dimming suits complex, long-lasting self-caused signals, and predicting and subtracting suits brief, simple ones.
options.why: That reverses the pairing. Dimming a sense through a long, complex signal would turn down the world’s signals for all that time, while a prediction removes only the self-caused part.

options.text: Dimming suits the self-caused signals of fish, and predicting and subtracting suits those of mammals and people.
options.why: Both uses appear across animals: a fish dims its lateral line while swimming, and a person dims hearing while speaking. The division is by the kind of signal, not the kind of animal.

options.text: Dimming suits signals measured by the balance organs, and predicting suits signals that cannot be measured at all.
options.why: Measuring one’s own movement with the vestibular system and proprioception goes on alongside either use, and real nervous systems do both at once. Measurement is not what separates dimming from predicting.

items.stem: A small animal listens for insects in leaf litter. Two of its own movements make sound: a single sharp click of its jaws, lasting a few milliseconds, and the long, irregular rustle of its own footsteps as it walks for minutes at a time. Which use of a copy of the movement command suits the rustle, and why?

options.text: Predicting and subtracting it, since the rustle is complex and long-lasting, the kind of self-caused signal prediction suits.
options.why: Correct. Prediction suits complex, long-lasting self-caused signals: it removes the expected part and leaves anything else, such as an insect’s faint sound. Dimming suits the brief, simple jaw click.

options.text: Dimming hearing while it walks, since dimming works for any self-caused sound, brief or long-lasting, that the animal can anticipate.
options.why: Dimming works well for brief, simple signals such as the jaw click. Held through minutes of walking, it would turn hearing down for the insects as well.

options.text: Measuring its footsteps with proprioception alone, since a movement that is sensed directly needs no copy of the command at all.
options.why: Measuring movement goes on alongside a copy of the command, and real nervous systems use both. Knowing that a step happened does not by itself remove the complex sound it makes.

options.text: Predicting the rustle and subtracting it, since the rustle is brief and simple, which is the kind of self-caused signal prediction suits.
options.why: Prediction is the right use, for the opposite reason. It suits complex, long-lasting signals; brief, simple ones such as the jaw click suit dimming.

items.stem: What is a forward model?

options.text: A process that predicts the effects a movement command will have on the body and the senses, before the senses report them.
options.why: Correct. The prediction arrives ahead of the senses, and the difference between it and what actually arrives is information about the world.

options.text: A process that works out the movement command needed to produce a desired outcome, such as a hand closing on a cup.
options.why: That is an inverse model, which runs the other way, from a wanted outcome to the command that will produce it.

options.text: A copy of a movement command, kept so that the expected consequences of the movement can be compared with what the senses report.
options.why: That is an efference copy, the signal a prediction can be built from. A forward model is the process that predicts what the command will do.

options.text: A process that weights the estimates from two senses by how reliable each one is, and combines them into a single judgment.
options.why: That is cue combination, which merges evidence from several senses. A forward model predicts the sensory effects of one’s own commands.

items.stem: What is the term for the following? “A process that works out the movement command needed to produce a desired outcome”.

options.text: inverse model
options.why: Correct. An inverse model runs from a wanted outcome to the command that will produce it, the opposite direction from a forward model.

options.text: forward model
options.why: A forward model runs the other way, from a command to its predicted effects on the body and the senses.

options.text: efference copy
options.why: An efference copy is a copy of a command already issued, kept for comparison. It does not work out which command to send.

options.text: affordance
options.why: An affordance is an opportunity for action that a place or object offers to a particular body. It is not a process that computes a command.

items.stem: A person reaches for a cup. One process works out which commands to the shoulder, elbow, and wrist will bring the hand to the cup. Another predicts, from those commands, how the arm will move and what the fingers will feel when they touch the cup. What are these two processes?

options.text: Working out the commands is an inverse model, and predicting the movement and the touch is a forward model.
options.why: Correct. An inverse model runs from a wanted outcome, the hand at the cup, to the command. A forward model runs from the command to its effects on body and senses.

options.text: Working out the commands is a forward model, and predicting the movement and the touch is an inverse model.
options.why: That reverses the two models. A forward model runs from a command to its effects; an inverse model runs from a wanted outcome back to the command.

options.text: Working out the commands is an efference copy, and predicting the movement and the touch is a corollary discharge.
options.why: Both of those terms name a copy of a command, a signal rather than a process, and they are used almost interchangeably. They cannot divide these two processes between them.

options.text: Working out the commands and predicting the movement and the touch are each a forward model, since each looks ahead.
options.why: Only the prediction takes a command and forecasts its effects. Working out the commands starts from the outcome and produces the command, which is what an inverse model does.

items.stem: A person lifts a suitcase believed to be full, but it is empty, and the arm jerks upward. In terms of a forward model, what does the mismatch between the predicted and the actual feel of the lift carry?

options.text: Information about the world, since the part the prediction missed, here a suitcase lighter than expected, came from outside the body.
options.why: Correct. A forward model predicts what a command will do to body and senses. The part of the sensation it did not predict is information about the world, here that the suitcase is lighter than expected.

options.text: Nothing useful, since a forward model serves only to cancel self-caused sensation, and whatever is left over is just noise.
options.why: Canceling self-caused input is one use, but the leftover is the point. The difference between prediction and arrival is information about the world.

options.text: Information about the arm alone, since a forward model predicts the body, so any mismatch means the arm is weaker than it was.
options.why: A forward model predicts both body and senses, and here the arm is unchanged. The mismatch comes from the world, a suitcase lighter than predicted.

options.text: A new command, since a forward model runs from the wanted outcome, a suitcase held steady, to the command that will produce it.
options.why: That is an inverse model. A forward model runs from the command to its predicted effects, and the mismatch with what arrives carries information about the world.

items.stem: People moved a handle with one hand while a robot arm, following the handle, stroked the palm of the other hand. Self-produced strokes felt much less tickly than the same strokes from the robot alone. Adding a delay between handle and stroke made them ticklier, until at a fifth of a second they felt as tickly as strokes from outside. Why does the delay matter?

options.text: The prediction of the stroke is precise in time, so a stroke that arrives late no longer matches it and is not subtracted.
options.why: Correct. The sensation a person’s own movement will cause is predicted and subtracted. The prediction is tied to a moment, so a late stroke falls outside it and is felt more fully, until at a fifth of a second it feels external.

options.text: The delay gives the senses time to report the stroke fully, so the stroke is felt at its true strength rather than cut short.
options.why: The stroke is the same at every delay, and the senses report it either way. What changes is whether it still matches the prediction in time.

options.text: The delay makes the stroke seem to come from the robot, so people consciously choose to let themselves feel it as tickly.
options.why: No choice is involved. The change follows from the timing of the prediction, which a late stroke no longer matches.

options.text: The delay slows the robot’s stroke, and slower strokes feel ticklier than faster ones whatever the delay happens to be.
options.why: The stroke keeps the same speed and shape at every delay. Only its timing relative to the person’s own movement changes.

items.stem: Two children take turns pushing on each other’s shoulder, each trying to push exactly as hard as they were just pushed. The pushes keep getting harder, though each child insists on only matching the last one. What best explains the escalation?

options.text: Each child’s own push is partly predicted and subtracted, so it feels weaker, and each pushes back harder than the push received.
options.why: Correct. This is the finger-pressing result in a new setting. The sensation of one’s own push is partly canceled, so matching what was felt means pushing harder, and the force grows each turn.

options.text: Each child’s nervous system dims touch for the whole game, so every push, given or received, feels weaker than it really is.
options.why: Dimming everything alike would leave the comparison fair, and the pushes would not grow. The escalation needs one’s own push, and only that one, to feel weaker.

options.text: Each child predicts the other’s next push and subtracts it, so the push received feels weaker, and each one pushes back harder.
options.why: A forward model predicts the effects of one’s own commands, not someone else’s push. And if received pushes felt weaker, matching them would mean pushing more softly.

options.text: Each child’s push arrives later than the other expects, so the push received feels ticklier and therefore stronger than it is.
options.why: Delay matters for whether a self-produced touch matches its own prediction. A push from someone else was never predicted in the first place.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain why people cannot tickle themselves, and why adding a delay of about a fifth of a second between a person’s own movement and the stroke it produces makes the stroke feel as tickly as one from outside.
items.answer: When a person moves, a forward model predicts the sensation the movement will cause, and the predicted part is subtracted from what arrives. A self-produced stroke matches its prediction, so much of it is canceled, and it feels much less tickly than the same stroke from outside. The prediction is precise in time. A stroke that arrives late no longer matches it, so less of it is subtracted, and the longer the delay, the ticklier it feels. By about a fifth of a second, the stroke feels as tickly as one produced from outside.
rubric: Says a forward model, or a prediction from the movement command, anticipates the sensory consequences of the person’s own movement.
Says the predicted sensation is subtracted, so a self-produced stroke feels less tickly than the same stroke from outside.
Says the prediction is precise in time, so a delayed stroke no longer matches it.
Says a longer delay leaves more of the stroke unsubtracted, until at about a fifth of a second it feels as tickly as an external one.

items.stem: Every saccade sweeps the image across the retina, yet the world does not seem to jump. When a person instead presses gently on the outer corner of one eyelid, with the other eye closed, the world does seem to jump. Why the difference?

options.text: Pressing the eyelid moves the eye with no command, so no image motion was predicted and subtracted, and the sweep is seen as motion.
options.why: Correct. In a saccade, the image motion the command will cause is predicted and subtracted. A finger moving the eye issues no command, so nothing is subtracted and the sweep is taken for the world moving.

options.text: Pressing the eyelid moves the eye more slowly than a saccade does, so the sweep lasts long enough for the world to be seen moving.
options.why: Speed is not the difference. An eye moved without a command makes the world seem to jump because no image motion was predicted, so none of the sweep is subtracted.

options.text: Pressing the eyelid moves the eye in a direction that saccades never take, so no prediction has been learned for that motion.
options.why: An eye pushed in any direction without a command makes the world jump. What is missing is a command, and with it the prediction.

options.text: Pressing the eyelid blurs the image in that eye, so points cannot be matched between the two eyes’ views and the scene seems to shift.
options.why: Matching points between two views is the correspondence problem of stereo vision, and with the other eye closed there is only one view. The jump comes from a movement with no command behind it.

items.stem: A person whose eye muscles are temporarily paralyzed tries to look to the left, and the eye does not move. According to the account of a stable visual world given in the reading, which way should the world seem to jump, and why?

options.text: To the left, since a movement to the left was predicted from the command, and the image motion it predicted never arrived.
options.why: Correct. In the usual explanation, a command produces a predicted image motion that is subtracted from what arrives. Here the prediction is subtracted from nothing, and the world seems to jump in the direction of the attempted look.

options.text: To the right, since the eye stays put while the person expects to be looking left, so the world seems to slide the other way.
options.why: That reverses the direction of the jump. A predicted motion that never comes makes the world seem to jump in the direction of the attempted look, not away from it.

options.text: Not at all, since with no movement of the eye, the image on the retina stays where it was and nothing in the scene has changed.
options.why: The image is unchanged, but the prediction is not. A movement was expected and none occurred, and that mismatch is seen as the world jumping.

options.text: To the right, since an eye that moves with no command at all makes the world seem to jump the opposite way from the eye.
options.why: That is the pushed-eye case, with movement and no command. Here there is a command and no movement, the reverse arrangement, so the jump goes the other way.

items.stem: Many machine-learning researchers call a learned model that predicts the consequences of an agent’s own actions a world model. According to the reading, how does a forward model relate to that idea?

options.text: A forward model is one precise version of such an internal model, and whether current AI systems build genuine ones is debated.
options.why: Correct. The parallel is direct, since both predict the consequences of one’s own actions. Whether current AI systems build genuine internal models of the world is left as an open question.

options.text: A forward model is what current AI systems have been shown to build, which settles that they hold genuine internal models of the world.
options.why: That goes beyond the reading. Whether current AI systems build genuine internal models of the world is debated, and a forward model is one precise version of what such a model would be.

options.text: A forward model is the opposite of a world model, since it predicts the body’s own sensations and a world model predicts only outside events.
options.why: A world model in this sense predicts the consequences of the agent’s own actions, which is what a forward model does for an animal. The two are parallel, not opposites.

options.text: A forward model is a world model run in reverse, working back from a wanted outcome to the action that would produce it.
options.why: Working back from an outcome to an action is an inverse model. A forward model runs from command to consequences, the same direction as the world model described.

items.stem: Feedback from the senses arrives too late to steer some movements. Two answers to that delay are a forward model and a faster sense. Which answer does the reflex that keeps the eyes steady while the head turns use, and how?

options.text: A faster sense: the balance organs drive the reflex, which starts within about 10 to 15 milliseconds of the head movement.
options.why: Correct. Vision would report an image slip about a tenth of a second late. The balance organs sense the head’s rotation directly, and the reflex runs on them in place of vision.

options.text: A forward model: a copy of the command to turn the head predicts the coming image slip, and the eyes are steered by that prediction.
options.why: Steering by a prediction from the command is the forward-model answer to delay. The steadying reflex uses the other answer, a faster sense, the balance organs.

options.text: A faster sense: vision itself speeds up while the head turns, so an image slip is corrected within about 10 to 15 milliseconds.
options.why: The speed comes from the balance organs, not from vision. News of an image slip takes about a tenth of a second to become a correction.

options.text: A forward model: the reflex predicts where the eyes will land after each saccade and steers them there before vision reports.
options.why: Saccades are quick jumps to a new target, a different movement from holding the eyes steady during a head turn. The steadying reflex runs on the balance organs, a faster sense.

items.stem: A person reading a sign while jogging keeps the letters steady, even though the head bobs with every step. News that an image has slipped on the retina takes about a tenth of a second to become a correction. What keeps the eyes steady fast enough?

options.text: A reflex driven by the balance organs, which turns the eyes against each head movement within about 10 to 15 milliseconds.
options.why: Correct. The balance organs sense the head’s movement directly, so the reflex can start long before any visual report of a slip. It is a faster sense standing in for vision.

options.text: Visual feedback about the slip, which turns the eyes back onto the sign within about a tenth of a second of each step.
options.why: Feedback a tenth of a second late would always be correcting a slip that had already changed. Keeping the eyes steady while the head moves cannot wait for vision.

options.text: A quick saccade back to the sign after each bob, each jump lasting only tens of milliseconds and landing back on the letters.
options.why: Saccades are quick jumps to a new target, and each would come only after a slip had been seen. Steady gaze through head movement comes from the reflex driven by the balance organs.

options.text: A learned negative image of the slip caused by each step, which is added to the visual input so that the slip cancels out.
options.why: A negative image cancels a self-caused input within a sense, as in electric fish. It does not move the eyes, and the eyes have to move to keep the letters steady.

items.stem: A pilot flies a drone by watching its video feed, which reaches the screen a third of a second late. Steering by the video alone, the pilot keeps overshooting turns and weaving back and forth. Engineers add a display that uses the pilot’s own recent commands to estimate where the drone is now. Why should that steady the flight?

options.text: A prediction from the commands of where the drone is now is more current than the video, so corrections stop chasing a past position.
options.why: Correct. This is the forward model’s answer to delay. Predicting what the commands will do gives an estimate more current than the last report, and steering by it avoids the overshoot that late feedback causes.

options.text: The display speeds up the video feed until it is current, so the pilot now sees where the drone really is at each moment.
options.why: The feed is no faster than before. The display adds a prediction from the commands, which is more current than any video report.

options.text: The display dims the video while the drone turns, so self-caused changes in the picture no longer distract the pilot from steering it.
options.why: Dimming a sense suits brief, simple self-caused signals, and turning the picture down would leave the pilot with less to go on. The display predicts rather than dims.

options.text: The display averages the old video with the commands, weighting each by its reliability, which cancels out the delay in the feed.
options.why: Weighting sources by reliability is cue combination, which makes a judgment more precise. It does not by itself make old information current.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain why steering a movement by the senses’ latest report is a problem, and describe the two answers to that problem, using the reflex that keeps the eyes steady during a head turn as the example of one of them.
items.answer: The senses report on a delay. News that an image has slipped on the retina takes about a tenth of a second to become a correction, so a nervous system steering by that report is always correcting a situation that has already changed. One answer is a forward model. By predicting what a command will do, the nervous system can estimate where the body is now, more current than the senses’ last report, and steer by that estimate. The other answer is a faster sense. The reflex that keeps the eyes steady while the head turns is driven by the balance organs instead of vision, and it starts within about 10 to 15 milliseconds of the head movement, far sooner than a visual correction could.
rubric: Says the senses’ report is old by the time it arrives, so steering by it corrects a situation that has already changed.
Names a forward model, which predicts a command’s consequences to estimate where the body is now.
Says that estimate is more current than the senses’ last report and can be steered by.
Names a faster sense as the second answer, with the eye-steadying reflex driven by the balance organs rather than vision.
Says the reflex starts far sooner than a visual correction could, within roughly 10 to 15 milliseconds.

items.stem: A forward model has to keep being relearned as the body changes. What drives that learning, and how large is each change?

options.text: The difference between the predicted and the actual sensation, with each adjustment in proportion to how far the prediction was off.
options.why: Correct. This is the prediction error described in Module 5, used as the delta rule uses it: large errors bring large adjustments and small errors small ones.

options.text: The difference between the predicted and the actual sensation, with each adjustment the same size however far the prediction was off.
options.why: The signal is right, but the size is not. Adjusting in proportion to the error, as the delta rule does, makes large errors produce large corrections and small ones small corrections.

options.text: Repetition of the same command, with each adjustment strengthening the command’s link to whatever sensation came with it.
options.why: Strengthening whatever occurs together is closer to Hebb’s rule. A forward model learns from the mismatch between what was predicted and what arrived.

options.text: The strength of the sensation alone, with each adjustment larger the stronger the sensation, whether or not it was predicted.
options.why: A strong sensation that was correctly predicted calls for no change at all. What drives the learning is the mismatch, not the strength.

items.stem: People throwing at a target through prisms that shift their view to one side miss widely at first. The misses shrink quickly over the first few throws and then more slowly as they near the target. Which learning rule fits that pattern?

options.text: Each correction is in proportion to its miss, so large early misses bring large corrections and small later misses small ones.
options.why: Correct. Adjusting in proportion to the error, the delta rule’s logic, shrinks a large miss quickly and a small one slowly. On average the miss was cut in half roughly every six throws.

options.text: Each correction is the same fixed size, so the misses shrink by an equal amount on every throw until they reach zero.
options.why: Fixed steps would shrink the miss by equal amounts, at a steady rate, rather than quickly at first and then slowly.

options.text: Each correction is made only when a miss passes some threshold, so the misses shrink and then stop short at that threshold.
options.why: A threshold rule would leave a steady leftover miss. Here the misses keep shrinking toward zero, more slowly as they get smaller.

options.text: Each throw strengthens whatever arm movement was just made, so the latest miss tends to be repeated and changes slowly.
options.why: Strengthening whatever was just done is closer to Hebb’s rule, and it would preserve a miss rather than shrink it. The correction depends on the size of the miss.

items.stem: People throw balls at a target while wearing goggles with prisms that shift their view of the world to one side. What happens to their throws while the prisms stay on?

options.text: The first throws miss widely to one side, and the misses then shrink throw by throw toward the target.
options.why: Correct. The first throws at a target two meters away missed by about half a meter, and the miss shrank with each throw, though people differed widely in how fast.

options.text: The first throws land on target, and the misses grow throw by throw as the shift takes hold.
options.why: The shift acts the moment the goggles go on, so the first throws are the worst. The misses then shrink as the mapping is relearned.

options.text: The first throws miss widely to one side, and the misses stay the same size while the prisms are on.
options.why: The misses do not stay put. The mapping from seeing to throwing is relearned from each miss, so the misses shrink throw by throw.

options.text: The first throws miss widely to one side, and the miss vanishes at once after one corrected throw.
options.why: Adaptation is gradual, not a one-step fix. On average the miss was cut in half roughly every six throws.

items.stem: What is an aftereffect?

options.text: An error in the opposite direction after removal of a distortion the nervous system had adapted to, evidence that a stored mapping changed.
options.why: Correct. Throwers who adapted to prisms miss the other way once the prisms come off. The error runs opposite to the original distortion because the adapted mapping is still in place.

options.text: An error in the same direction as a distortion, made when the distortion is first put on and before the nervous system has adapted to it at all.
options.why: That is the initial miss, which shrinks as adaptation proceeds. An aftereffect comes after the distortion is removed, and it runs the other way.

options.text: A deliberate shift of aim to one side, made while a distortion is in place, that stops as soon as the distortion is removed.
options.why: Deliberately aiming off is the account the aftereffect rules out. The opposite miss after removal is evidence that a stored mapping changed and stayed changed.

options.text: A sensation caused by the animal’s own movement, such as the sweep of the image across the retina that each saccade produces.
options.why: That is reafference, sensation caused by one’s own movement. An aftereffect is an opposite error that follows the removal of an adapted distortion.

items.stem: Two accounts could explain how prism throwers stop missing. In one account, they simply learn to aim off to one side while the prisms are on. In a second account, the stored mapping from what they see to how they throw changes. Which observation is evidence for the changed mapping, and why?

options.text: With the prisms off, the first throws miss the other way by most of the original amount, since the changed mapping stays in place.
options.why: Correct. That opposite miss is the aftereffect. Throwers who had only been aiming off on purpose could stop once the prisms came off; a changed mapping persists and sends the throws the other way.

options.text: With the prisms on, the misses shrink throw by throw, since only a changed mapping could cut the miss gradually rather than all at once.
options.why: Shrinking misses are evidence that something was learned, but they fit either account. The two accounts come apart only once the prisms come off.

options.text: With the prisms off, the first throws land on target at once, since a changed mapping switches back as soon as the view is normal again.
options.why: Landing on target at once would fit a strategy dropped when the prisms come off. A changed mapping is stored, so it persists and produces a miss the other way.

options.text: With the prisms off, the misses shrink again over the next throws, since the mapping has to be learned anew rather than recalled.
options.why: The misses do shrink again after the prisms come off, but that recovery alone does not separate the accounts. The telling observation is the first opposite miss.

items.stem: A computer mouse is set so that the pointer moves twice as far as usual for each movement of the hand. Over an hour, a person overshoots less and less and adapts. The setting is then switched back to normal. What should the person’s first few pointer movements do, and what would that be evidence of?

options.text: Fall short of their targets, an aftereffect, which is evidence that the stored mapping from seeing to reaching had changed.
options.why: Correct. The adapted mapping makes small hand movements for each distance, which suited the doubled setting. With the setting back to normal, the error runs the opposite way to the original overshoot.

options.text: Overshoot their targets as they did at first, which is evidence that the person never really adapted to the doubled setting.
options.why: Overshooting is what the doubled setting caused before adaptation. Once the person has adapted and the setting is switched back, the error runs the other way.

options.text: Land on their targets at once, which is evidence that the person had been deliberately moving the hand less while the setting was doubled.
options.why: That would fit a deliberate adjustment dropped when the setting changed. An opposite error, falling short, is what a changed and persisting mapping produces.

options.text: Fall short of their targets, which is evidence that the hand has grown tired from an hour of making small, careful movements.
options.why: Falling short is the expected result, but fatigue is not the reason. The error runs opposite to the distortion the person adapted to, which is the mark of an aftereffect.

items.stem: When a person first puts on strong magnifying glasses, the image slips across the retina with each turn of the head. Why, and what happens over the following hours to days?

options.text: The steadying reflex was set for unmagnified vision, so it turns the eyes too little; it then strengthens until the slip disappears.
options.why: Correct. Magnification makes the image move farther for each turn of the head, so the old setting falls short. The reflex is recalibrated from the slip and grows stronger.

options.text: The steadying reflex was set for unmagnified vision, so it turns the eyes too far; it then weakens until the slip disappears.
options.why: The direction is reversed. A magnified image moves farther with each head turn, so the eyes must turn farther, and the reflex grows stronger.

options.text: The glasses slow the signals from the balance organs, so the reflex arrives late; the signals then speed up until the slip disappears.
options.why: Nothing about the glasses slows the balance organs. The reflex is on time but set for the wrong optics, and its strength is what changes.

options.text: Vision has to take over from the reflex while the glasses are worn, so the slip lasts until the person learns to keep the head still.
options.why: Vision is too slow to steady the eyes during a head turn, a tenth of a second behind. The reflex itself is recalibrated, over hours to days.

items.stem: A person has worn magnifying glasses for several days, and the image no longer slips when the head turns. What happens just after the glasses come off, and what kind of effect is it?

options.text: For a while the strengthened reflex moves the eyes too far, so the image slips the other way, an aftereffect of the changed setting.
options.why: Correct. The new setting persists for a while after the glasses come off. The error runs opposite to the original slip, the same kind of aftereffect as the opposite miss in prism throwing.

options.text: The reflex returns at once to its old setting, since only vision had adapted to the glasses and the reflex itself never changed at all.
options.why: The reflex itself changed, growing stronger over hours to days. That new setting persists for a while after the glasses come off.

options.text: The image slips the same way as when the glasses first went on, since the reflex has to be learned again from the very start.
options.why: Slipping the same way would mean the reflex was too weak. After adapting it is too strong for unmagnified vision, so the slip runs the other way.

options.text: The image stays steady, since the strengthened reflex now suits unmagnified vision as well as it suits magnified vision.
options.why: One setting cannot suit both, because magnification changes how far the image moves with each head turn. The strengthened setting overshoots for a while.

pools.title: Receptor Sheets, the Retina, and Cone Classes
pools.covers: reading §8.3.1, §8.3.2, §8.3.3 · lecture 8.3 slides from_receptor_sheet_to_cortex, the_retina_computes, cone_classes

items.stem: What is retinotopy?

options.text: The arrangement of a visual area so that neighboring points in the visual field are represented by neighboring neurons.
options.why: Correct. Light from neighboring directions falls on neighboring places on the retina, and a retinotopic area keeps that neighbor-to-neighbor layout in its neurons. It is vision’s topographic map, laid out by direction.

options.text: The arrangement of an area of the brain so that neighboring frequencies of sound are represented by neighboring neurons.
options.why: That is tonotopy, the layout of the cochlea and of the areas it feeds. It is hearing’s map, laid out by pitch rather than by direction.

options.text: The arrangement of a brain area so that neighboring points on the surface of the body are represented by neighboring neurons.
options.why: That is somatotopy, the layout of touch’s map. Retinotopy is the same kind of arrangement for points in the visual field.

options.text: The sorting of incoming axons so that all the axons from receptors of one type converge on the same small cluster of neurons.
options.why: That describes the glomeruli of the olfactory bulb, which sort smell’s inputs by receptor type. Nothing about that arrangement carries location, whereas retinotopy keeps the layout of the visual field.

items.stem: Which term names the following? “The arrangement of the cochlea, and of the areas it feeds, so that neighboring frequencies are represented by neighboring receptors or neurons”.

options.text: tonotopy
options.why: Correct. Tonotopy is hearing’s map. Different frequencies vibrate different places along the cochlea, and the areas the cochlea feeds keep that order by frequency.

options.text: cochlea
options.why: The cochlea is the organ that has this arrangement, the fluid-filled organ of hearing in the inner ear. The arrangement itself, by frequency, is tonotopy.

options.text: retinotopy
options.why: Retinotopy is the same kind of arrangement for vision, with neighboring points in the visual field represented by neighboring neurons. It maps direction, not frequency.

options.text: somatotopy
options.why: Somatotopy is the same kind of arrangement for touch, with neighboring points on the body represented by neighboring neurons. It maps location on the body, not frequency.

items.stem: What is somatotopy?

options.text: The arrangement of a brain area so that neighboring points on the body are represented by neighboring neurons.
options.why: Correct. Touch’s receptors are laid out across the skin, and a somatotopic area keeps that layout, so neighboring places on the body are represented by neighboring neurons.

options.text: A distorted drawing of the body whose parts are sized by how much of the cortex each of them occupies.
options.why: That describes the homunculus, the map of the body across the somatosensory or motor cortex, as it is often drawn. Somatotopy is the neighbor-to-neighbor arrangement that such a map has.

options.text: The arrangement of a visual area so that neighboring points in the visual field are represented by neighboring neurons.
options.why: That is retinotopy, vision’s map, laid out by direction. Somatotopy is the same kind of arrangement for locations on the body.

options.text: The sense of the body’s own position and movement, carried by receptors in the muscles, tendons, and joints.
options.why: That is proprioception, which is a sense rather than a layout. Somatotopy is how a brain area is arranged, with neighboring points on the body represented by neighboring neurons.

items.stem: Light from each direction falls on a different place on the retina, while smell’s receptor neurons are scattered across the lining of the nose. What does each of these layouts give an animal before any neuron has computed anything?

options.text: The retina’s layout gives the direction of the light relative to the eye, and smell’s layout gives nothing about where an odor came from.
options.why: Correct. In most senses the layout of the receptor sheet carries information by itself. Where light falls on the retina already says which direction it came from. Smell’s scattered receptors carry nothing about location.

options.text: The retina’s layout gives the distance of each object from the eye, and smell’s layout gives the direction that an odor drifted in from.
options.why: Distance is not laid out anywhere on the retina; it has to be computed from differences between views. And nothing in smell’s layout carries location.

options.text: The two layouts each give location for free, the retina’s by the direction of light and smell’s by the sorting of receptor types in the bulb.
options.why: The olfactory bulb sorts smell’s inputs by receptor type, which is a sorting by what molecule was caught, not by where it came from. Only the retina’s layout carries location.

options.text: Neither layout gives anything for free, since every fact about the world has to be computed by neurons after the receptors respond.
options.why: A receptor sheet’s layout carries information before any computation. Where light falls on the retina says which direction it came from, with no further step.

items.stem: Imagine a burrowing animal that finds its food by touching it with a fleshy snout. The snout is packed far more densely with touch receptors than any other part of its skin, and the animal uses the snout for nearly everything it does. What share of the animal’s body map in the cortex would the snout be expected to take?

options.text: A share much larger than the snout’s physical size, since a map’s proportions follow receptor density and how much each part is used.
options.why: Correct. Maps are not drawn to scale. The hands and lips take large shares of the human body map for the same reason that a densely supplied, heavily used snout would.

options.text: A share in proportion to the snout’s physical size, because a topographic map keeps the layout of its receptor sheet exactly.
options.why: A map keeps the neighbor-to-neighbor layout of the sheet, not its proportions. Proportions follow the density of receptors and how much the part is used.

options.text: A share smaller than the snout’s physical size, because a heavily used part sends so many signals that fewer neurons are needed.
options.why: Dense receptors and heavy use go with a larger share of the map, not a smaller one, as with the hands and lips in the human body map.

options.text: No share of the body map, because a snout used to find food would be mapped along with smell rather than with touch.
options.why: A snout pressed against things is sensed by touch receptors in its skin, and those feed the body map. What a part is used for changes the size of its share, not which map it belongs to.

items.stem: The center of gaze is a small part of the visual field, yet it takes up a large share of the visual map in the brain. What accounts for this?

options.text: A map’s proportions follow the density of receptors and how much that part of the sheet is used, and both are high at the center of gaze.
options.why: Correct. Cones crowd into the fovea, and the center of gaze is the part of the visual field put to the heaviest use. So it takes a large share of the visual map, just as the hands and lips do in the map of the body.

options.text: The visual map is drawn to scale, and the center of gaze takes a large share because more of the world lies straight ahead than off to the sides.
options.why: Maps are not drawn to scale, and the center of gaze is a small part of the field. Its large share comes from dense receptors and heavy use.

options.text: The center of gaze is where signals from the two eyes first converge, and extra neurons are needed there to compare the images.
options.why: The two eyes’ signals do first converge on single neurons in the visual cortex, which makes it the first place disparity can be computed. That convergence is not why the center of gaze takes a large share; dense receptors and heavy use are.

options.text: The center of gaze is served by rods, which pool many signals onto each cell, and that pooling takes a larger area of the map.
options.why: The very center of the fovea has no rods at all. It is packed with cones, and that density is part of why the center of gaze takes a large share.

items.stem: What is the lateral geniculate nucleus?

options.text: The part of the thalamus that relays signals from the retina onward to the primary visual cortex.
options.why: Correct. Vision passes through the thalamus on its way to the cortex, as hearing, touch, and taste do, and the lateral geniculate nucleus is the visual relay there.

options.text: The place where the two optic nerves meet and the fibers from the inner half of each retina cross over.
options.why: That is the crossing of the optic nerves, which comes before the lateral geniculate nucleus. After the crossing, signals pass through the lateral geniculate nucleus to the primary visual cortex.

options.text: The midbrain structure that holds aligned maps of visual and auditory space and turns the eyes toward things.
options.why: That is the superior colliculus, the mammalian tectum. The lateral geniculate nucleus is in the thalamus, and it relays retinal signals to the cortex.

options.text: The first place in the visual pathway where signals from the two eyes converge on single neurons.
options.why: That is the primary visual cortex, the first place disparity can be computed. The two eyes’ signals reach it after passing through the lateral geniculate nucleus.

items.stem: Suppose an injury blocked every relay through the thalamus while leaving the receptors and the cortex intact. Which sense could still send its signals to its own area of cortex by its usual route?

options.text: Smell, because the olfactory bulb projects straight to the olfactory cortex, with no first stop in the thalamus.
options.why: Correct. Smell is the exception among the senses that reach the cortex. Its signals go from the olfactory bulb straight to olfactory cortex.

options.text: Hearing, because its signals pass through several stations in the brainstem, which carry them on to auditory cortex.
options.why: Hearing does pass through several brainstem stations, but then through the thalamus before it reaches the auditory cortex.

options.text: Balance, because it has no single primary cortical area, so its signals reach the cortex without a relay in the thalamus.
options.why: Balance is irregular in having no single primary area, but its signals still pass through the thalamus to the several cortical areas they reach.

options.text: Taste, because its receptors sit in taste buds on the tongue, close enough to the brain that their signals need no relay.
options.why: Taste’s signals pass through the brainstem and then the thalamus on their way to taste cortex. Being near the brain does not exempt a sense from the relay.

items.stem: Smell and balance each depart from the usual route that a sense takes from its receptors to the cortex. How do the two departures differ?

options.text: Smell skips the thalamus, going from the bulb straight to olfactory cortex; balance has no single primary area, and vision joins it in the brainstem.
options.why: Correct. Smell is the one sense that reaches the cortex without a relay in the thalamus. Balance does pass through the thalamus, but it reaches several cortical areas rather than one, and visual signals join it at its very first stop in the brainstem.

options.text: Smell has no single primary area and spreads across several; balance skips the thalamus, going from the inner ear straight to a cortical area of its own.
options.why: That swaps the two. Smell has its own olfactory cortex, reached without the thalamus. Balance passes through the thalamus to several areas, with no single primary one.

options.text: Smell reaches the thalamus only after its inputs are sorted by receptor type; balance reaches it only after vision joins it in the cortex.
options.why: Smell never passes through the thalamus. And visual signals join balance at its very first stop in the brainstem, long before the cortex.

options.text: Smell and balance each skip the thalamus entirely, smell because its bulb lies near the cortex and balance because it feeds the cerebellum.
options.why: Only smell skips the thalamus. Balance’s signals go to the brainstem and the cerebellum, and also through the thalamus to several cortical areas.

items.stem: The retina gives an animal the direction of a light almost for free, but the cochlea does not give it the direction of a sound. In a few sentences, explain this difference in terms of how each sense’s receptors are laid out, and say what hearing is left to do as a result.
items.answer: In most senses the receptors form a sheet whose layout carries information before any neuron computes anything. The retina’s receptors are laid out by direction: light from each direction falls on a different place, so which receptors respond already says where the light came from. The cochlea’s receptors are laid out by frequency instead, so which of them respond says what pitches are in a sound, not where it came from. Hearing therefore has to compute direction by a further step, from the differences between what reaches the two ears.
rubric: States that a receptor sheet’s layout carries information before any computation is done.
Says the retina’s receptors are laid out by direction, so where light falls gives the direction it came from.
Says the cochlea’s receptors are laid out by frequency, so which of them respond gives pitch rather than direction.
Concludes that hearing has to compute direction by a further step rather than read it off the layout.

items.stem: The retina is sometimes compared to the film in a camera. In what way does the comparison fail?

options.text: The retina grows out of the developing brain and processes the image before any signal leaves the eye; film only records it.
options.why: Correct. Film records the light that falls on it. The retina is brain tissue, and by the time its output leaves along the optic nerve it has already pooled, filtered, and adjusted the image.

options.text: The retina passes each receptor’s signal along its own line to the brain unchanged, while film blends neighboring points together.
options.why: Little leaves the eye unchanged. Many rods pool onto one cell, ganglion cells respond to contrast, and each slides its working range with the light.

options.text: The retina can respond to light only within a tenfold range, while film can record anything from starlight to bright daylight.
options.why: Each ganglion cell covers only about a tenfold range at a time, but it slides that range to match the scene, so the retina works across the billionfold range from starlight to daylight.

options.text: The retina holds a single kind of receptor spread evenly across its surface, while film has grains of several different kinds.
options.why: The retina has two kinds of photoreceptor, rods and cones, and they are not spread evenly: the cones crowd into the fovea, whose very center has no rods.

items.stem: What is a photoreceptor?

options.text: A receptor cell in the retina that transduces light, of which rods and cones are the two main kinds.
options.why: Correct. The photoreceptor is the retina’s receptor cell. A pigment inside it changes shape when it absorbs light, and that is where the conversion of light into a neural signal begins.

options.text: A cell that carries the retina’s output to the brain and responds most to a spot unlike its surroundings.
options.why: That describes a ganglion cell. Ganglion cells receive signals that began in the photoreceptors, and their axons form the optic nerve.

options.text: A receptor cell topped with a bundle of stiff projections whose bending opens channels directly.
options.why: That is a hair cell, the receptor of hearing, balance, and the lateral line. A photoreceptor transduces light through a pigment and a chain of chemical reactions instead.

options.text: A part of the thalamus that relays signals from the eye onward to the primary visual cortex.
options.why: That is the lateral geniculate nucleus, a relay that sits well beyond the retina. The photoreceptor is the receptor cell in the retina itself.

items.stem: Touch and smell receptors respond to their stimuli by releasing more transmitter, but a photoreceptor responds to light by releasing less. A classmate concludes that a photoreceptor cannot signal light reliably, since its response runs the wrong way. What is the best reply?

options.text: The direction of the change does not matter for the code; what matters is that the same change follows light consistently.
options.why: Correct. A cell downstream can respond to a drop in transmitter as reliably as to a rise, provided the drop always follows light. What carries the information is the consistency of the change, not its direction.

options.text: A photoreceptor releases less transmitter only in dim light, and it switches to releasing more once the light is bright.
options.why: A photoreceptor responds to light by releasing less transmitter, whatever the light level. The classmate’s mistake is to assume that the direction of the change matters at all.

options.text: The drop in transmitter is reversed by lateral inhibition in the retina, which turns it into a rise before it leaves the eye.
options.why: Lateral inhibition gives ganglion cells their center–surround receptive fields. No reversal is needed, since the consistency of the change, not its direction, carries the code.

options.text: The chain of reactions inside the cell turns the drop into a rise, so the cell does release more transmitter in light.
options.why: The chain of reactions amplifies the effect of a single absorption; it does not reverse the response. And a response that runs the other way is no obstacle to a reliable code.

items.stem: Which term names the following? “A photoreceptor sensitive enough to respond to very dim light, which supports vision at night but not detail or color”.

options.text: rod
options.why: Correct. A rod responds reliably to a single particle of light, which suits it to dim light. Many rods pool their signals onto one cell, which is part of why rod vision gives up detail.

options.text: cone
options.why: A cone is the other kind of photoreceptor. It needs more than a hundred particles of light to respond, and it supports daylight vision, detail, and color.

options.text: hair cell
options.why: A hair cell is the receptor of hearing, balance, and the lateral line, opened by the bending of its bundle. It does not respond to light.

options.text: fovea
options.why: The fovea is a small pit at the center of the retina, packed with cones and with no rods at its very center. It supports sharp vision, not vision in dim light.

items.stem: What is a cone?

options.text: A photoreceptor that works in bright light and supports detail and color, and comes in kinds that are compared.
options.why: Correct. A cone needs more than a hundred particles of light to respond, so it works in daylight. Cones crowd into the fovea, and comparing the responses of different kinds of cone is what gives color.

options.text: A photoreceptor sensitive enough to respond to very dim light, which supports vision at night but not detail or color.
options.why: That is a rod. Rods respond to a single particle of light and handle dim light, while cones handle daylight, detail, and color.

options.text: A small pit at the center of the retina, densely packed with receptors, that gives sharp vision at the center of gaze.
options.why: That is the fovea, the place where cones crowd together. The cone is the receptor cell, not the pit that holds so many of them.

options.text: A cell carrying the retina’s output that responds strongly to a spot unlike its surroundings and weakly to even light.
options.why: That is a ganglion cell, with a center–surround receptive field. Cones are photoreceptors, where light is first transduced.

items.stem: On a dark night, an observer finds that a faint star vanishes when looked at directly but reappears when the gaze shifts slightly to one side of it. What explains this?

options.text: The center of the fovea holds only cones, which need over a hundred particles of light, while rods lie off center and respond to one.
options.why: Correct. Looking straight at the star puts its image on the very center of the fovea, which has no rods. Looking slightly aside puts the image where rods, sensitive enough to respond to a single particle, can catch it.

options.text: The center of the fovea holds only rods, which pool their signals so heavily that a single faint point of light is lost among them.
options.why: That reverses the layout. The very center of the fovea has no rods at all; it is crowded with cones, which need far more light than rods do.

options.text: Ganglion cells at the center of gaze respond weakly to a spot of light, so a star that is looked at directly is muted by lateral inhibition.
options.why: Ganglion cells respond strongly to a spot that differs from its surroundings, and a star against a dark sky is just such a spot. What changes with the gaze is which photoreceptors catch the light.

options.text: The star’s light reaches only one eye when it is looked at directly, and its image fades until the eyes are turned slightly away.
options.why: Light from a distant star reaches both eyes wherever the gaze is pointed. What changes with the shift of gaze is which photoreceptors catch the light.

items.stem: Many rods feed their signals onto a single outgoing cell, while in the fovea one cone feeds one outgoing cell. What does each arrangement gain, and what does it give up?

options.text: Pooled rods gain sensitivity by adding faint signals but lose which rod caught the light; one cone per cell keeps location but gives up sensitivity.
options.why: Correct. Wiring trades sensitivity for location. Pooled rods add faint signals together, so dim light is detected, but the outgoing cell no longer says which rod caught it. One cone per cell keeps exact location and gives up that sensitivity.

options.text: Pooled rods gain exact location by averaging out the noise in many rods’ signals; one cone per cell gains sensitivity but loses where the light fell.
options.why: That swaps the two. Pooling adds signals for sensitivity and loses location, while one cone per cell keeps location and gives up sensitivity.

options.text: Pooled rods gain color by comparing rods tuned to different wavelengths; one cone per cell keeps brightness but gives up color.
options.why: Rods do not support color, and color comes from comparing kinds of cone. The trade in the wiring is between sensitivity and location.

options.text: Pooled rods gain speed by sending one signal in place of many; one cone per cell keeps accuracy but responds more slowly to change.
options.why: Pooling is a trade of location for sensitivity, not of accuracy for speed. Adding many rods’ faint signals together is what lets dim light be detected.

items.stem: In the networks described in Module 7, pooling combines the detections of a feature over a small neighborhood into one output. The convergence of many rods onto one cell in the retina is described as the same kind of trade. What do the two share?

options.text: Each combines many inputs into one output, gaining something useful but giving up which input was active.
options.why: Correct. Pooling in a network gained tolerance by giving up position. Rod convergence gains sensitivity, by adding faint signals together, and gives up which rod caught the light.

options.text: Each combines many inputs to sharpen the location of a signal, averaging away the noise in any one of them.
options.why: Combining inputs gives up location rather than sharpening it. After pooling, the output no longer says which input was active.

options.text: Each responds strongly to a spot that differs from its surroundings and only weakly to even input across its field.
options.why: That describes the center–surround receptive fields of ganglion cells, produced by lateral inhibition. What rod convergence shares with pooling is the combining of inputs and the loss of which one was active.

options.text: Each keeps every input on a line of its own to the output, so that nothing about the pattern of inputs is lost.
options.why: That describes the one-to-one wiring of cones in the fovea, which keeps location. Pooling and rod convergence do the opposite, combining many inputs into one.

items.stem: A ganglion cell of the kind that responds to spots brighter than their surroundings is lit in two ways. First, a small bright spot falls on the center of its receptive field, with the rest of the field dark. Then light of the same brightness is spread evenly across the whole field. How does the cell respond?

options.text: Strongly to the spot and weakly to the even light, because light falling on the surround inhibits the response.
options.why: Correct. A center–surround cell responds to a spot that differs from its surroundings. Even light falls on the surround as well, and inhibition from the surround weakens the response. That is lateral inhibition at work.

options.text: Strongly to the even light and weakly to the spot, because the even light delivers more light to the cell in total.
options.why: Total light is not what the cell reports. A center–surround cell responds weakly to even light across its whole field.

options.text: Equally to the spot and to the even light, because the center of the field receives the same light in each case.
options.why: The center does receive the same light in each case, but the surround does not. Light on the surround inhibits the response, so even light gives a weak one.

options.text: Not at all to either one, because ganglion cells respond to changes over time and not to any pattern across space.
options.why: Ganglion cells do report change over time, but they also report contrast across space, which is just what a spot unlike its surroundings provides.

items.stem: Light varies over a billionfold range from starlight to daylight, but each ganglion cell responds over only about a tenfold range at any one time. How does the retina handle the difference?

options.text: Each cell slides its tenfold range up or down to match the overall light in the scene, much as a camera adjusts its exposure.
options.why: Correct. By shifting its working range with the light level, a ganglion cell stays responsive in starlight and in daylight. The result is that the retina reports mostly contrast and change.

options.text: Each cell covers a different tenfold slice of the full range, so that some cells handle starlight and others handle daylight.
options.why: That would split the range among cells. Instead, each cell moves its own range to match the scene, the way a camera adjusts its exposure.

options.text: Each cell reports the overall light level directly, compressing the billionfold range so that it fits into a tenfold one.
options.why: Reporting the overall light level is just what the retina mostly does not do. It sends a report of contrast and change, with each cell sliding its range to the scene.

options.text: Rods cover the billionfold range by themselves, so the ganglion cells handle only the light that reaches the cones.
options.why: Rods handle dim light and cones handle daylight, and every ganglion cell faces the same limit. Each one slides its own tenfold range to match the scene.

items.stem: Suppose all the light in a scene doubles, on every surface at once. In a few sentences, explain why this changes little of what the retina reports to the brain, using what ganglion cells respond to and how they adjust to the level of light.
items.answer: Ganglion cells, which carry the retina’s output, have center–surround receptive fields. Each responds strongly to a spot that differs from its surroundings and weakly to even light, which is lateral inhibition at work. So what a ganglion cell signals is contrast, how one spot differs from its neighbors. Each cell also responds over only about a tenfold range of light at a time. It slides that range to match the overall level of the scene, much as a camera adjusts its exposure. When all the light doubles, each spot and its surroundings double together, so how they differ stays much the same. And the cells’ ranges shift to the new level. The retina reports mostly contrast and change, and an overall doubling changes little of that report.
rubric: Says ganglion cells respond strongly to a spot that differs from its surroundings and weakly to even light (center–surround receptive fields, or lateral inhibition).
Says each ganglion cell covers only a limited range of light at a time and shifts that range to match the overall level of the scene.
Explains that doubling everything leaves how each spot differs from its neighbors largely unchanged.
Concludes that the retina reports mostly contrast and change rather than the overall level of light.

items.stem: A stroke destroys the primary visual cortex in the left half of a person’s brain. Given how the fibers of the optic nerves cross, which part of what the person sees is affected?

options.text: The right half of the visual world, as it is seen by each of the two eyes.
options.why: Correct. Fibers from the inner half of each retina cross, so each half of the brain receives the opposite half of the visual world, from both eyes. Losing the left visual cortex affects the right half of the world in each eye.

options.text: Everything that is seen by the left eye, across the whole visual world.
options.why: That would follow if each eye fed only one half of the brain. Because the inner fibers cross, each half of the brain receives signals from both eyes.

options.text: The left half of the visual world, as it is seen by each of the two eyes.
options.why: Each half of the brain receives the opposite half of the visual world, not the same half. Damage on the left affects the right half of the world.

options.text: Everything that is seen by the right eye, across the whole visual world.
options.why: That would follow if every fiber crossed. Only the fibers from the inner half of each retina cross, so each half of the brain receives signals from both eyes.

items.stem: Measuring binocular disparity means comparing the two eyes’ images of the same point. Signals from the eyes pass through the lateral geniculate nucleus on their way to the cortex. Why is the primary visual cortex, and not the lateral geniculate nucleus, the first place disparity can be computed?
