options.text: The two eyes’ signals first converge on single neurons in the visual cortex, and a comparison needs neurons receiving from both eyes.
options.why: Correct. Passing through the same structure is not the same as converging on the same neurons. The two eyes’ signals first meet on single neurons in the visual cortex, so that is the first place disparity can be computed.

options.text: The optic fibers cross only after the lateral geniculate nucleus, so until the cortex each half of the brain has just one eye’s signals.
options.why: The fibers cross where the two optic nerves meet, before the lateral geniculate nucleus, so each half of the brain already receives signals from both eyes. What waits for the cortex is their convergence on single neurons.

options.text: Disparity is a difference in color between the two eyes’ images, and color is first computed in the visual cortex from the cones.
options.why: Disparity is a difference in the positions of a point’s images in the two eyes, not in their color. A random-dot stereogram, made only of black and white dots, still produces depth.

options.text: Disparity can be measured only after an object has been identified, and objects are first identified in the primary visual cortex.
options.why: Stereo does not require identifying any object first. In a random-dot stereogram, neither eye’s image contains the square, yet the square appears once the two images are compared.

items.stem: A young animal has normal eyes with overlapping fields, but one eye is kept covered throughout early development and then uncovered, so that both eyes now work. What does the account of how stereo circuits develop predict for this animal?

options.text: Its stereo vision is likely to be impaired, because stereo circuits need both eyes working together during a critical period.
options.why: Correct. The circuits for stereo are probably largely built in, but they still need both eyes working together during development. Missing that critical period can leave stereo impaired even after both eyes work.

options.text: Its stereo vision should be normal, because stereo circuits are built in and need only two working eyes with overlapping fields.
options.why: The circuits are probably largely built in, but built in does not mean independent of experience. They need both eyes working together during a critical period.

options.text: Its stereo vision should develop normally a little later, because stereo circuits can be learned from experience at any age.
options.why: Stereo circuits are probably largely built in, not learned at any age. What they need from experience is both eyes working together during a critical period in development, not at some later time.

options.text: Its stereo vision should be sharper than usual, because the uncovered eye was used more and gained extra disparity cells of its own.
options.why: Disparity is computed by neurons that receive from both eyes. One eye used alone gives those neurons nothing to compare.

items.stem: How do the kinds of cone in a zebrafish compare with those in a dog?

options.text: The zebrafish still uses all four kinds the earliest vertebrates had, an ultraviolet one among them, while the dog has two, as most mammals do.
options.why: Correct. The earliest vertebrates already had genes for four kinds of cone, and many shallow-water bony fish still use them all. Mammals lost two of the four, so most have only two kinds today.

options.text: The zebrafish has two kinds, as the earliest vertebrates did, while the dog has four, after mammals gained two more kinds along the way.
options.why: That reverses the history. Four kinds came first, and mammals lost two of them rather than gaining any.

options.text: The zebrafish has three kinds, as human beings do, while the dog has only one kind, which is why a dog has no color vision at all.
options.why: A single kind of cone cannot signal color, but the dog has two kinds, as most mammals do. The zebrafish has four.

options.text: The zebrafish and the dog each have four kinds, since the cone genes of the earliest vertebrates passed unchanged to all their descendants.
options.why: The genes for four kinds did not pass down unchanged. Mammals lost two of the four, so a dog has two kinds of cone.

items.stem: Most mammals today have only two kinds of cone, after the loss of two of the four kinds the earliest vertebrates had. Many researchers link that loss to how early mammals lived, a well-supported hypothesis rather than a settled fact. What way of life is the loss linked to?

options.text: A long period of activity mainly at night, when sensitivity to dim light mattered far more than color.
options.why: Correct. Early mammals were probably small animals active mostly at night. Many researchers link the loss of two kinds of cone to that long nocturnal period, though the link is a well-supported hypothesis rather than a settled fact.

options.text: A shift to activity in bright daylight, when sharp detail at the center of gaze mattered more than color.
options.why: Sharp detail at the center of gaze is what a primate picking fruit in daylight needs, and the fovea that supplies it came much later, in the ancestors of tarsiers and monkeys. Early mammals were probably active mostly at night.

options.text: A life spent mostly underground, in burrows where almost no light of any kind ever reached the eye.
options.why: Early mammals were probably small, but the way of life linked to the loss is activity mainly at night. In dim light, sensitivity matters far more than color.

options.text: A shift to finding food mainly by smell and hearing, when vision of any kind mattered very little.
options.why: The link many researchers draw is to a long nocturnal period, when sensitivity to dim light mattered far more than color. That is a claim about which kind of vision mattered, not a claim that vision stopped mattering.

items.stem: In the line leading to monkeys and human beings, how did forward-facing eyes and a fovea arrive?

options.text: Forward-facing eyes came first, in primates still active at night, and a fovea came later, in the ancestors of tarsiers and monkeys.
options.why: Correct. The features of the primate eye appeared in steps. Forward-facing eyes came while primates were still nocturnal, and a fovea arose later, in the ancestors of tarsiers and monkeys.

options.text: A fovea came first, in primates that were still active at night, and forward-facing eyes came later, in the ancestors of tarsiers and monkeys.
options.why: That reverses the order. Forward-facing eyes came first; the fovea came later.

options.text: The two arrived together, in the ancestors of tarsiers and monkeys, since a fovea is of little use without a pair of eyes that face forward.
options.why: The two features came in separate steps, not together. Forward-facing eyes came first, in primates still active at night.

options.text: Forward-facing eyes came first, once primates became active in daylight, and a fovea came later, in the ancestors of apes alone.
options.why: The order is right, but the details are not. Forward-facing eyes came while primates were still active at night, and the fovea appeared in the ancestors of tarsiers and monkeys, not of apes alone.

items.stem: A hawk and a macaque monkey each have a fovea, a pit in the retina packed with cones that gives sharp vision at the center of gaze. Does this shared feature show that the two inherited the fovea from a common ancestor that had one?

options.text: No; foveas evolved separately in several lineages, including many birds, so two animals with foveas need not share an ancestor with one.
options.why: Correct. In primates, the fovea appeared late, in the ancestors of tarsiers and monkeys, long after the lines leading to birds and to primates had split. Foveas also evolved separately in other lineages, including many birds, so the shared feature alone does not show common descent.

options.text: Yes; a structure as specific as a fovea could arise only once, so every animal that has one inherited it from a single common ancestor.
options.why: Foveas evolved separately in several lineages, including many birds. A specific structure can arise more than once.

options.text: Yes; the earliest vertebrates already had a fovea, along with genes for four kinds of cone, and both of these lines kept it.
options.why: The earliest vertebrates had genes for four kinds of cone, but the fovea is not traced back to them. In primates it came late, in the ancestors of tarsiers and monkeys.

options.text: No; the macaque’s fovea came from a duplicated gene, while the hawk’s came from a pigment retuned to longer wavelengths.
options.why: Gene duplication and a retuned pigment belong to the history of the cone classes, not of the fovea. The fovea is a feature of the retina’s layout, and it arose separately in several lineages.

items.stem: How did a third kind of cone arise in the ancestors of Old World monkeys, apes, and human beings?

options.text: The gene for a long-wavelength pigment was duplicated, and the two copies drifted apart in the wavelengths they absorb.
options.why: Correct. One long-wavelength gene became two, and as the copies diverged in the wavelengths they absorb, the result was a third kind of cone.

options.text: One of the two kinds of cone lost in early mammals came back, restoring a pigment that fish had kept all along.
options.why: Primate color vision did not recover the fish’s. The third kind came from duplicating an existing long-wavelength gene, not from the return of a lost kind.

options.text: A rod pigment came to be used in some of the cones, giving them a sensitivity between the two existing kinds.
options.why: Rods and cones remain distinct kinds of photoreceptor. The third cone came from a duplicated long-wavelength cone gene whose copies drifted apart.

options.text: An existing short-wavelength pigment shifted to absorb a new wavelength, with no new copy of any gene being made.
options.why: A retuned old pigment is the history of the human blue cone, which carries the ultraviolet pigment shifted to longer wavelengths. Shifting one pigment without copying its gene changes a kind rather than adding one; the third kind came from a duplicated long-wavelength gene.

items.stem: Old World monkeys, apes, and people have three kinds of cone, and so do howler monkeys, which are New World monkeys. How are the two cases related?

options.text: In each case a long-wavelength pigment gene was duplicated, but the two duplications happened independently, not in a shared ancestor.
options.why: Correct. The third cone of Old World monkeys, apes, and people came from a duplicated long-wavelength gene, and in howler monkeys the same gene was duplicated independently.

options.text: Howler monkeys inherited their third cone from the ancestor they share with Old World monkeys, apes, and human beings.
options.why: The duplication in howler monkeys happened independently, not in an ancestor shared with the Old World line. Most other New World monkeys have a different arrangement.

options.text: In each case the ultraviolet pigment of early vertebrates came back into use, restoring one of the kinds that mammals had lost.
options.why: Neither case is a restoration. The third cone came from a duplicated long-wavelength gene in each line, and the old ultraviolet pigment survives, retuned, in the blue cone.

options.text: Howler monkeys have three kinds only in some females, the arrangement found in most other New World monkeys and not in Old World primates.
options.why: That arrangement belongs to most other New World monkeys. In howler monkeys the long-wavelength gene was duplicated, independently of the Old World line.

items.stem: A biologist compares the pigment of the human blue cone with the four cone pigments of a zebrafish. By descent, which zebrafish pigment is the human blue-cone pigment most closely related to?

options.text: The ultraviolet pigment, which in the line leading to human beings was retuned to absorb longer wavelengths of light.
options.why: Correct. The human blue cone carries the early vertebrates’ ultraviolet pigment, retuned to longer wavelengths. Its sensitivity has shifted, but its descent runs back to the ultraviolet kind.

options.text: The blue pigment, which the line leading to human beings kept unchanged while other mammals lost it.
options.why: The names suggest this match, but the human blue cone descends from the ultraviolet pigment. Mammals lost two of the four kinds, and the human blue cone is the old ultraviolet one, retuned.

options.text: The red pigment, since the human blue cone arose when a long-wavelength gene was duplicated and one copy drifted far from the other.
options.why: Duplicating a long-wavelength gene produced the third cone of the Old World line, not the blue cone. The blue cone descends from the ultraviolet pigment.

options.text: No zebrafish pigment, since the human blue-cone pigment arose new in primates and has no counterpart in fish at all.
options.why: The human blue cone is old, not new. It carries the ultraviolet pigment the earliest vertebrates already had, retuned to longer wavelengths.

items.stem: A classmate says that the color vision of monkeys, apes, and people is a recovery of the four-cone color vision of fish, regained after early mammals lost it. How does this claim fare against the history of cone classes?

options.text: It fails, because primate color vision came from a copied long-wavelength gene and a retuned ultraviolet pigment, not a return of lost kinds.
options.why: Correct. The third cone came from duplicating a long-wavelength gene, and the blue cone carries the old ultraviolet pigment shifted to longer wavelengths. New structures came from old parts, the lesson drawn for the vertebrate brain in Module 6.

options.text: It holds, because people now have the same ultraviolet cone that zebrafish use, after the cone was switched back on in primates.
options.why: People have no ultraviolet cone. The old ultraviolet pigment survives in the human blue cone, retuned to longer wavelengths.

options.text: It holds, because the three kinds of cone in primates match three of the four kinds in fish, so that only one lost kind is still missing today.
options.why: Counting kinds of cone does not show where they came from. The primate third cone is a copy of a long-wavelength gene, not one of the two kinds that mammals lost.

options.text: It fails, because primates have fewer kinds of cone than fish do, so what they have cannot count as color vision at all.
options.why: Three kinds of cone, compared, do give color vision, since at least two are needed. The claim fails for another reason: primate color vision is not a recovery of the fish’s.

items.stem: About 8% of men in the United States have some form of red–green color deficiency. In a short paragraph, explain how people came to have their two long-wavelength cones, why that history makes red–green deficiency common, and why primate color vision is not a recovery of the color vision of fish.
items.answer: The earliest vertebrates had genes for four kinds of cone, and many fish still use all four, but mammals lost two, and most mammals have only two kinds. In the ancestors of Old World monkeys, apes, and people, the gene for one long-wavelength pigment was duplicated, and the two copies drifted apart in the wavelengths they absorb, which gave a third kind of cone. The two genes sit side by side on the X chromosome, which makes them easy to miscopy, and miscopying them is what produces red–green deficiency. Primate color vision did not bring back the kinds that mammals lost. It came from a copied gene, and from the old ultraviolet pigment retuned to longer wavelengths in the blue cone, which is the lesson of new structures from old parts.
rubric: Says the third cone arose when a long-wavelength pigment gene was duplicated and the copies drifted apart in the wavelengths they absorb.
Says the two long-wavelength genes sit side by side on the X chromosome and are easily miscopied, which produces red–green deficiency.
States that primate color vision is not a return of the kinds of cone that mammals lost.
Says primate color vision came from existing parts, a copied gene and (in the blue cone) a retuned ultraviolet pigment, as new structures from old parts.

pools.title: Two Streams and the Ear
pools.covers: reading §8.3.4, §8.3.5 · lecture 8.3 slides two_streams, the_ear_from_old_parts, cochlea_hair_cell_owl

items.stem: What is the dorsal stream?

options.text: The visual pathway that runs from primary visual cortex into the parietal lobe, concerned with motion, location, and guiding action.
options.why: Correct. Beyond primary visual cortex, dozens of visual areas are grouped into two broad streams. The dorsal stream is the one that runs up into the parietal lobe and handles motion, location, and the guidance of action.

options.text: The visual pathway that runs from primary visual cortex into the temporal lobe, concerned with the form of objects and with telling them apart.
options.why: That is the ventral stream, the other broad stream beyond primary visual cortex. The dorsal stream runs into the parietal lobe instead and is concerned with motion, location, and guiding action.

options.text: The relay in the thalamus that carries signals from the retina to primary visual cortex, before any of the further visual areas are reached.
options.why: That is the lateral geniculate nucleus, the visual relay in the thalamus. The dorsal stream lies beyond primary visual cortex, running into the parietal lobe.

options.text: The route on which fibers from the inner half of each retina cross, so that each half of the brain receives the opposite half of the visual world.
options.why: That is the crossing of the optic fibers on the way from the eyes. The dorsal stream begins much later, beyond primary visual cortex, and runs into the parietal lobe.

items.stem: Which term names the visual pathway that leaves primary visual cortex for the parietal lobe and is concerned with motion, location, and guiding action?

options.text: dorsal stream
options.why: Correct. The dorsal stream runs up from primary visual cortex into the parietal lobe. The ventral stream runs into the temporal lobe instead and is concerned with form and objects.

options.text: superior colliculus
options.why: The superior colliculus is the mammalian tectum, a midbrain structure with aligned maps of visual and auditory space that turns the eyes and head toward things. It is not a pathway leading out of primary visual cortex.

options.text: lateral geniculate nucleus
options.why: The lateral geniculate nucleus is the relay in the thalamus that carries signals from the retina to primary visual cortex, so it comes before that area rather than beyond it.

options.text: motor cortex
options.why: Motor cortex lies just in front of the somatosensory cortex and sends fibers to the spinal cord. Guiding action draws on the dorsal stream, but the dorsal stream itself is a visual pathway into the parietal lobe.

items.stem: After damage to one region of cortex, a monkey can still tell a cup from a key, but it now misjudges which of two places a reward was hidden in. A second monkey, with damage to a different region, finds the hidden reward easily but can no longer tell the cup from the key. Which description of the damage fits these two cases?

options.text: The monkey misjudging the hiding place has parietal damage, in the dorsal stream, and the monkey confusing cup and key has temporal damage, in the ventral stream.
options.why: Correct. Parietal damage in monkeys impairs judging where things are, and temporal-lobe damage impairs telling objects apart. That is the division between a dorsal stream for location and a ventral stream for form and objects.

options.text: The monkey misjudging the hiding place has temporal damage, in the ventral stream, and the monkey confusing cup and key has parietal damage, in the dorsal stream.
options.why: This reverses the two streams. The ventral stream, in the temporal lobe, handles form and objects, so its damage impairs telling a cup from a key. The dorsal stream, in the parietal lobe, handles location.

options.text: Both monkeys have damage in the parietal lobe, since judging where a reward lies and telling two objects apart both depend on the stream that guides action.
options.why: Guiding action is one job of the dorsal stream, but telling objects apart is the ventral stream’s. When damage spares one ability and impairs the other, two different streams are involved.

options.text: Neither monkey’s damage can be assigned to one stream or the other, since the two streams are not specialized and they exchange signals throughout.
options.why: The streams do exchange signals throughout, but they are still specialized. They are not independent, which is a different claim from not being specialized at all.

items.stem: After a stroke damages parts of her visual cortex, a woman sees the world in dirty shades of gray. Her cones respond to light normally when tested, and she still knows that a school bus is yellow, though she cannot see it as yellow. What can be concluded about color from her case?

options.text: Seeing color depends on processing beyond the cones, since damage to visual cortex abolished it while her cones kept on working.
options.why: Correct. Her cones still respond, yet she sees in gray. So color is not finished in the eye. It depends on what visual cortex does with the cones’ signals, although how it does so is still unclear.

options.text: Seeing color depends on the cones alone, so her stroke must have left her with only one working kind of cone instead of three.
options.why: That describes a color deficiency that starts in the eye, such as the red–green deficiency that comes from miscopied cone pigment genes. Her cones work normally, so her loss lies beyond them.

options.text: Seeing color depends on one area of visual cortex alone, since damage there abolishes it and damage to other areas leaves it untouched.
options.why: Color does depend on visual cortex, since her cones work and yet she sees in gray. But a large study of stroke patients found that color deficits did not map neatly onto one area, and how color arises beyond the cones is still unclear.

options.text: Seeing color depends on the dorsal stream, since the stroke that removed her color vision would also leave pouring liquid looking frozen.
options.why: A frozen-looking pour comes from losing a region of cortex specialized for motion, a different loss in a different patient. Losing color does not imply losing motion.

items.stem: In monkeys, one area of the ventral stream has many neurons that respond to the color of a stimulus regardless of how it moves. In people, damage to visual cortex can abolish color while the cones still work. A student concludes that the brain has a single color center. Does the evidence from stroke patients support that conclusion?

options.text: No: in a large study, color deficits after stroke did not map neatly onto one area, and how color arises beyond the cones remains unclear.
options.why: Correct. The monkey neurons and the cases of lost color are real, but the large stroke study did not find color deficits tied neatly to one area. How the cones and the neurons beyond them produce color, including its constancy, is still unclear.

options.text: Yes: in a large study, color deficits after stroke followed damage to the one area whose neurons respond to color, and to no other area of cortex.
options.why: That is the result the student expected, and it is not what the large stroke study found. Color deficits did not map neatly onto one area.

options.text: No: color is spread evenly across visual cortex, so damage to any one part of it abolishes color just as readily as damage to any other part.
options.why: Color is lost after damage to particular areas of visual cortex, not after damage anywhere. What the stroke study found is that those deficits did not map neatly onto a single area, which is a weaker claim than an even spread.

options.text: Yes: color constancy has been traced to that one area, which compares the responses of the different cones across the whole of a scene.
options.why: How color constancy arises beyond the cones is still unclear, and no single area has been shown to produce it. Neither proposed account of color constancy is settled.

items.stem: After carbon monoxide poisoning damaged her visual cortex, a patient could not say, or show with her hand, how a slot was tilted. Yet she could post a card through the same slot about as accurately as the people she was compared with. What account of the two visual streams was proposed from cases like hers?

options.text: The ventral stream serves vision for perception, such as reporting a slot’s tilt, and the dorsal stream serves vision for action, such as posting a card.
options.why: Correct. She had lost the ability to report the tilt but kept the ability to act on it. That pattern led to the proposal that the ventral stream serves perception and the dorsal stream serves action, an account later qualified.

options.text: The dorsal stream serves vision for perception, such as reporting a slot’s tilt, and the ventral stream serves vision for action, such as posting a card.
options.why: This reverses the account. The dorsal stream runs into the parietal lobe, which is concerned with location and guiding action, so it is the stream paired with action.

options.text: The ventral stream serves form and the dorsal stream serves motion, so she lost sight of the slot’s shape but could still follow the card as it moved along.
options.why: That is the account of the streams by what they process, form against motion and location. It does not explain her case, since posting the card needed the slot’s tilt, which she could not report.

options.text: Both streams serve perception, and action is guided by motor cortex alone, which her poisoning left intact while it damaged both of the streams equally.
options.why: Posting the card accurately needed the slot’s tilt, which only vision could supply. So something visual was still guiding her hand, and on the perception–action account that guidance came from the dorsal stream.

items.stem: A patient with damage to visual cortex cannot say whether a door handle is horizontal or vertical, and cannot match its angle by turning a card in her hand. Yet when she reaches to open the door, her hand rotates to fit the handle before it arrives. If the two visual streams are divided into vision for perception and vision for action, how is her case read?

options.text: Her ventral stream, which serves perception, is impaired, while her dorsal stream, which serves action, still uses the handle’s angle to guide her hand.
options.why: Correct. She cannot report the angle, yet her reach is shaped by it. On the perception–action account that means vision for perception is impaired and vision for action is spared, though the streams turned out to be specialized rather than independent.

options.text: Her dorsal stream, which serves perception, is impaired, while her ventral stream, which serves action, still uses the handle’s angle to guide her hand.
options.why: This reverses the account. The dorsal stream runs into the parietal lobe and is the one paired with guiding action, so a spared reach is attributed to it.

options.text: Her case is optic ataxia, since parietal damage leaves people able to reach accurately but unable to say how an object they see is oriented.
options.why: Optic ataxia is the opposite kind of loss: inaccurate reaching, especially for objects away from the center of gaze, with recognition largely spared. Her reaching is accurate.

options.text: She finds the handle’s angle by touch on each new attempt, so vision plays no part in shaping her grip, and the account does not apply to her case.
options.why: Her hand rotates to fit the handle before it arrives, so the angle is reaching her movement before any touch. Vision is guiding the reach even though she cannot report what she sees.

items.stem: What is optic ataxia?

options.text: Inaccurate reaching for objects, especially those away from the center of gaze, after damage to the parietal lobe, with recognition largely spared.
options.why: Correct. A person with optic ataxia reaches badly for objects off to the side. Reaching for objects looked at directly is nearly normal, and the objects can still be recognized.

options.text: Inability to recognize objects by sight after damage to the temporal lobe, with reaching for the objects and grasping them accurately largely spared.
options.why: That is closer to a loss in the ventral stream, the stream for form and objects. Optic ataxia follows parietal damage and impairs reaching, not recognizing.

options.text: Inability to see motion after damage to a region of cortex specialized for it, so that pouring tea looks frozen and approaching cars seem to jump closer.
options.why: That describes a patient who lost a region of cortex specialized for motion. Optic ataxia is a disorder of reaching, after parietal damage.

options.text: Loss of color vision after damage to particular areas of visual cortex, so that the world looks dirty gray although the cones still work normally.
options.why: That is the loss of color after cortical damage, with working cones. Optic ataxia leaves seeing intact and impairs reaching for objects away from the center of gaze.

items.stem: After a stroke in the parietal lobe, a man can name every object on a table. When he looks straight at a cup and reaches for it, his hand goes to it nearly normally. When he keeps his eyes on the cup and reaches for a pen off to one side, his hand misses by several centimeters. Which description fits his difficulty?

options.text: Optic ataxia, since his reaching fails for objects away from the center of gaze while his recognition of the objects is spared.
options.why: Correct. Reaching badly for objects off to the side, with nearly normal reaching for objects looked at directly and recognition intact, is the pattern of optic ataxia after parietal damage.

options.text: A failure of the ventral stream, since naming the objects in front of him and reaching for them both depend on recognizing what they are.
options.why: He names every object, so recognition is intact, and recognition is what the ventral stream serves. His trouble is reaching for objects off to the side.

options.text: An aftereffect, since reaching errors that run consistently one way are the sign that a stored mapping from eye to arm has changed.
options.why: An aftereffect is an error that follows the removal of a distortion the nervous system had adapted to, such as prisms. Nothing was adapted to here, and his errors depend on whether he is looking at the object.

options.text: A loss of the cortical region for motion, since misjudging where a nearby object lies is what that loss produces, as when cars seem suddenly close.
options.why: Losing the region for motion made pouring tea look frozen and moving cars seem far away and then suddenly close. The pen is still, and his errors depend on whether he is looking at it, which is the pattern of optic ataxia.

items.stem: A patient who could not report a slot’s tilt but could post a card through it was once paired with patients with optic ataxia as mirror images: she could act on what she failed to perceive, and they could perceive what they failed to reach for. Why is that pairing weaker than it first appeared?

options.text: She was tested on objects she looked at directly, while optic ataxia mostly affects objects off to the side, so the two patterns are not matched.
options.why: Correct. A mirror image would need the two losses tested on the same kind of target. Her tests used objects at the center of gaze, and optic ataxia mostly affects objects away from it. Later testing even found signs of optic ataxia in her.

options.text: She was tested on objects off to the side, while optic ataxia mostly affects reaching for objects looked at directly, so the two patterns are not matched.
options.why: This reverses both halves. She was tested on objects she looked at directly, and optic ataxia mostly affects objects away from the center of gaze.

options.text: Optic ataxia turned out to follow damage to the temporal lobe, the same region damaged in her case, so both patterns come from a single stream.
options.why: Optic ataxia follows damage to the parietal lobe. The pairing is weak because the patterns were tested on different kinds of target, not because of where the damage lay.

options.text: Her accurate posting turned out to rely on touch rather than on vision, so her case has no bearing on the visual streams at all.
options.why: Nothing about her case was explained away by touch. The pairing is weak because she was tested on objects at the center of gaze, while optic ataxia mostly affects objects off to the side.

items.stem: Some illusions make one of two equal disks look larger than the other. If vision for action ran independently of vision for perception, a person’s grip would open to the true size of each disk even while they judged one disk larger. When four laboratories tested 144 people with the same procedure, what did they find, and what follows from it?

options.text: Grasping was fooled by the illusion about as much as judgments of size were, so the two streams are best seen as specialized rather than independent.
options.why: Correct. The famous claim that grasping escapes a size illusion did not hold up. Grasping and judgment were fooled about equally, which fits two specialized streams that exchange signals throughout.

options.text: Grasping escaped the illusion while judgments of size were fooled by it, so the dorsal stream works independently of the ventral stream after all.
options.why: That was the famous claim, and it is the one that failed. Across four laboratories, grasping was fooled about as much as judgment was.

options.text: Judgments of size escaped the illusion while grasping was fooled by it, so the ventral stream guides action and the dorsal stream guides perception.
options.why: Judgment was fooled too, so this pattern was not found. And it would reverse the pairing in the perception–action account, in which action goes with the dorsal stream.

options.text: Neither grasping nor judgments of size were fooled once the procedure was the same, so the illusion must have come only from careless testing in earlier work.
options.why: The illusion was real, and it fooled both. What the shared procedure removed was the earlier claim that grasping escapes it.

items.stem: A patient with damage to her visual cortex could not report how a slot was tilted, yet could post a card through it. She could not tell flat shapes of different widths apart by sight, yet her grip opened wider as she reached for the wider ones. In a short paragraph, explain what account of the two visual streams cases like hers led to, give two reasons the evidence for that account is weaker than it first appeared, and state what the evidence supports instead.
items.answer: Her case led to the proposal that the ventral stream serves vision for perception, which she had lost, and the dorsal stream serves vision for action, which she kept. Optic ataxia, which follows parietal damage, seemed to be the mirror image. But she was tested on objects she looked at directly, while optic ataxia mostly affects reaching for objects off to the side, so the two patterns are not a clean mirror image. Later testing found signs of optic ataxia in her as well. And when four laboratories tested 144 people with the same procedure, grasping was fooled by a size illusion about as much as judgments of size were. So the two streams are specialized rather than independent, and they exchange signals throughout.
rubric: States the account: the ventral stream serves vision for perception and the dorsal stream serves vision for action.

Gives one valid reason the evidence is weaker: she was tested on objects at the center of gaze while optic ataxia mostly affects objects off to the side; she herself showed signs of optic ataxia; or grasping was fooled by a size illusion about as much as judgment was.
Gives a second, different reason from that same list.
Concludes that the streams are specialized rather than independent.

items.stem: Monkeys were trained for months to recognize novel objects. Researchers then recorded from cells in inferior temporal cortex, at the far end of the ventral stream, and found that far more of the cells responded to particular views of the trained objects than to the objects across views. Which account of object recognition does this result fit?

options.text: Recognition by views, since view-tuned cells fit an account on which an object is stored as several views and new views are matched to them.
options.why: Correct. On the views account an object is stored as a set of views, and a new view is matched against the stored ones. Cells that respond to particular views of trained objects are what we would expect on that account.

options.text: Recognition by parts, since view-tuned cells fit an account on which an object is identified by edge features that survive changes between views.
options.why: Edge features that survive changes of view are the heart of the parts account, and a cell keyed to them would respond across views. Cells tied to particular views fit the views account instead.

options.text: Both accounts equally, since the two are now seen as ends of a continuum of tasks, so a recording of view-tuned cells fits either one.
options.why: The two accounts are often seen as ends of a continuum of tasks, but that does not make every result fit both. Cells tuned to particular views are what we would expect on the views account, while a cell keyed to parts would respond across views.

options.text: Neither account, since cells along the ventral stream respond to the motion and location of objects rather than to their form or their parts.
options.why: Motion and location are the dorsal stream’s concern. The ventral stream, which runs into the temporal lobe, is concerned with form and objects.

items.stem: The inner ear and the lateral line grow from a shared patch of tissue in the embryo’s head, and in sharks and salmon from a single thickening. They also use the same kind of receptor cell. According to the reading, how is the relation between the two best described?

options.text: As sisters with a shared origin, since shared tissue and a shared cell leave open whether one evolved from the other.
options.why: Correct. A shared patch of tissue and a shared receptor cell fit a common origin. They are not evidence that one organ descended from the other, and whether the inner ear evolved from the lateral line remains open.

options.text: As ancestor and descendant, since their shared tissue and shared cell mean that the inner ear evolved from the lateral line.
options.why: This is the claim often made, and it is unresolved. Shared tissue fits two organs with a common origin just as well as one organ descending from the other.

options.text: As ancestor and descendant, since their shared tissue and shared cell mean that the lateral line evolved from the inner ear.
options.why: From shared tissue alone, there is no telling which way any descent ran, or whether there was descent at all. The two are best seen as sisters.

options.text: As unrelated organs that came to look alike, each evolving separately in a different group of early fishes.
options.why: Organs that evolved separately would not be expected to grow from the same embryonic tissue, let alone a single thickening. The shared origin is what makes them sisters.

items.stem: The mammalian middle ear holds three small bones: the stapes, the malleus, and the incus. How do the histories of the stapes and of the malleus and incus differ?

options.text: The stapes began in fishes as a bone that braced the jaw, while the malleus and incus once formed the joint of the jaw itself.
options.why: Correct. The stapes began as the hyomandibula, a jaw-bracing bone in fishes. In mammals two more bones joined it, the malleus and incus, which once formed the jaw joint, and fossils preserve the stages in between.

options.text: The stapes once formed the joint of the jaw itself, while the malleus and incus both began in fishes as bones that braced the jaw.
options.why: This swaps the two histories. The stapes is the old jaw brace, and the malleus and incus are the old jaw joint.

options.text: All three began in fishes as bones that braced the jaw, and all three carried sound in the earliest land vertebrates.
options.why: Early land vertebrates had no eardrum, and the malleus and incus joined the stapes later, in mammals, from the old jaw joint.

options.text: All three began as the wall of the pouch behind an opening near each eye, which hardened into bone on land.
options.why: The pouch behind that opening became the air-filled middle ear and its tube to the throat, not the bones inside it.

items.stem: Early fishes had an opening behind each eye, which some air-breathing fishes still breathe through. In land vertebrates, what became of the pouch behind that opening?

options.text: It became the air-filled middle ear and the tube to the throat, and where thin skin sealed it off, the result was an eardrum.
options.why: Correct. The middle ear and the eardrum began as something else: the pouch behind an old breathing opening, sealed by a thin layer of skin.

options.text: It became the fluid-filled inner ear, which folded inward from the surface of the head and pinched off into a closed sphere there.
options.why: That is the history of the inner ear, which is as old as the vertebrates and starts in the embryo as a patch of the head’s surface folding inward.

options.text: It became the cochlea, which lengthened and coiled in most mammals so that a long tube could fit inside a small skull.
options.why: The cochlea is the hearing organ of the inner ear, which lengthened from a short strip. The pouch became the air-filled middle ear.

options.text: It closed over completely, and the bone beside it, which had braced the jaw, became the stapes that now carries sound.
options.why: The jaw brace did become the stapes, but the pouch did not close over. It became the air-filled middle ear, sealed by skin as an eardrum.

items.stem: A thumbtack concentrates the broad push of a thumb onto its small point, so the same force produces far more pressure there. In the ear, what corresponds to the thumb’s broad push, and what to the point?

options.text: The large eardrum collects the force of sound, and the small bones carry it to the much smaller opening into the inner ear.
options.why: Correct. Force collected over the large eardrum is concentrated by the bones onto a much smaller opening, which raises the pressure about two hundredfold. That is how sound in air gets into a fluid-filled inner ear.

options.text: The small opening into the inner ear collects the force of sound, and the bones spread it across the much larger eardrum.
options.why: This runs the thumbtack backward. Spreading force over a larger area lowers the pressure, and the problem is getting enough pressure into the fluid.

options.text: The folds of the outer ear collect the force of sound, and the eardrum spreads it evenly over the whole surface of the cochlea.
options.why: The folds of the outer ear filter sound by direction, which helps tell up from down and front from back. The concentration happens between the eardrum and the small opening.

options.text: The floppy far end of the cochlea collects the force of sound, and its stiff base concentrates it onto the hair cells there.
options.why: Stiffness along the cochlea’s membrane sorts sound by frequency, high near the base and low near the end. It does not concentrate force the way the eardrum and bones do.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain why sound traveling in air has trouble getting into the inner ear, how the eardrum and the small bones behind it overcome that problem, and what one of those bones began as.
items.answer: The inner ear is filled with fluid, and sound traveling in air mostly bounces off water, so little of it would get in. The eardrum is large, and the opening into the inner ear is much smaller. The eardrum and the bones behind it collect force over the eardrum and concentrate it onto that small opening, the way a thumbtack concentrates the push of a thumb onto its point. That raises the pressure about two hundredfold. The bones began as something else: the stapes began in fishes as the hyomandibula, a bone that braced the jaw.
rubric: Says that the inner ear is filled with fluid and that sound in air mostly bounces off water.
Says that force collected over the large eardrum is carried by the bones to a much smaller opening into the inner ear.
Says that concentrating the force onto a smaller area raises the pressure (about two hundredfold), as a thumbtack does.
Gives a correct origin: the stapes from a jaw-bracing bone in fishes, or the malleus and incus from the old joint of the jaw.

items.stem: Frogs, lizards, birds, and mammals all have eardrums that catch airborne sound. According to the reading, how did those eardrums arise?

options.text: They evolved late and separately, at least five times, in different groups of land vertebrates during the Triassic period.
options.why: Correct. Eardrums that catch airborne sound arose separately in at least five groups, more than 100 million years after vertebrates first came onto land. Before then, land vertebrates heard airborne sound poorly.

options.text: They evolved once and late, in a single group of land vertebrates during the Triassic period, and later groups inherited them.
options.why: The timing is right, but eardrums did not arise once. They evolved separately at least five times in different groups.

options.text: They were inherited from the first land vertebrates, which could hear airborne sound well from the time they came onto land.
options.why: Early land vertebrates had no eardrum and heard airborne sound poorly. Eardrums came more than 100 million years after the move onto land.

options.text: They were inherited from fishes, whose eardrums sealed the opening behind each eye and caught sound traveling through water.
options.why: Fishes hear with the balance organs of the inner ear and have no eardrum. The sealed pouch became an eardrum only in land vertebrates, and late.

items.stem: In a lizard the two eardrums are connected through the mouth, while in a mammal the two ears are acoustically isolated from each other. How does that difference change what each ear can tell about direction?

options.text: Each of the lizard’s ears is directional by itself, while the mammal’s ears give direction only by comparison of one ear with the other.
options.why: Correct. The connection between a lizard’s eardrums makes each ear directional on its own. Mammals lost that connection, so for them direction exists only in the difference between the two ears.

options.text: Each of the mammal’s ears is directional by itself, while the lizard’s ears give direction only by comparison of one ear with the other.
options.why: This reverses the two animals. The connection through the mouth is what makes each of the lizard’s ears directional, and mammals lack it.

options.text: Neither animal’s ears give direction, since hearing receptors are laid out by pitch, so direction has to come from the eyes instead.
options.why: The cochlea’s layout gives pitch rather than direction, but direction can still be computed from differences between the two ears. It does not have to come from vision.

options.text: Both animals’ ears are directional by themselves, since each hearing receptor responds best to motion in one direction, as in a fish’s ear.
options.why: A fish’s inner-ear receptors do give it direction directly. In land vertebrates, whether a single ear is directional depends on whether the two eardrums are connected.

items.stem: One proposal links mammals’ loss of coupled eardrums to their high-frequency hearing. Suppose a small mammal could hear low frequencies but no high ones. According to that proposal, which direction cues would it lack?

options.text: Level differences between the ears and outer-ear filtering, since only high frequencies are shadowed by the head and usefully filtered by the outer ear.
options.why: Correct. Only high frequencies are shadowed enough by a small head to differ in level between the ears, and only they are filtered usefully by the outer ear’s folds. On that proposal, those are the cues that high-frequency hearing gave mammals.

options.text: Timing differences between the ears, since a low-frequency sound reaches both of the ears at the same moment and so carries no difference in arrival time.
options.why: A low sound still reaches the near ear first, and low pitches are located mainly by timing. It is the level and filtering cues that need high frequencies.

options.text: Every direction cue, since without coupled eardrums a low-frequency sound produces no difference at all between what reaches its two ears in time or level.
options.why: Uncoupled ears still differ in when a low sound arrives, so timing remains. The cues that would be missing are level differences and outer-ear filtering.

options.text: No direction cue, since low frequencies bend around the head and so supply the level and filtering cues just as well as high frequencies do.
options.why: Low frequencies bending around the head is exactly why they produce little level difference. Shadowing and useful filtering both depend on high frequencies.

items.stem: The cochlea is said to work like a bank of overlapping filters. What feature of the cochlea fits that description?

options.text: Each place along its membrane vibrates most for a band of frequencies, with neighboring bands overlapping, so a sound is sorted by frequency.
options.why: Correct. The membrane is stiff at the base and floppy at the far end, so high frequencies vibrate it most near the base and low ones near the end. Each place acts as a filter for its band, which gives hearing its tonotopic map.

options.text: Each place along its membrane vibrates most for sound from one direction, with neighboring directions overlapping, so a sound is sorted by origin.
options.why: The cochlea’s layout gives pitch, not direction. Direction has to be computed from differences between the two ears.

options.text: Each hair cell along it responds to every frequency equally, and the brainstem later filters the combined signal into bands by comparing the two ears.
options.why: The sorting by frequency happens in the cochlea itself, because the membrane’s stiffness varies along its length. The brainstem compares the ears for direction.

options.text: Small muscles inside it contract while the animal vocalizes, so that the sound of the animal’s own voice is filtered out before reaching the brain.
options.why: The muscles that contract during vocalizing sit in the middle ear, and they dim the animal’s own voice. That is not what makes the cochlea a bank of filters.

items.stem: Suppose a person loses most of the hair cells near the base of the cochlea, while those toward the far end survive. What change in hearing would be expected?

options.text: Trouble hearing high-pitched sounds, since the stiff base of the membrane is where high frequencies vibrate it most.
options.why: Correct. The membrane is stiff at the base and floppy at the far end, so high frequencies peak near the base. Losing receptors there leaves high pitches with little to respond to them.

options.text: Trouble hearing low-pitched sounds, since the stiff base of the membrane is where low frequencies vibrate it most.
options.why: This reverses the map. Low frequencies vibrate the membrane most near the floppy far end, which is where the surviving hair cells lie.

options.text: Trouble hearing quiet sounds of every pitch equally, since each place along the membrane responds to all frequencies alike.
options.why: Each place along the membrane responds most to its own band of frequencies, so a loss at one place affects some pitches more than others.

options.text: Trouble telling where sounds come from, with pitch unaffected, since the base of the cochlea holds a map of sound direction.
options.why: The cochlea’s map is by frequency, not direction. A map of auditory space is computed later in the brain.

items.stem: What is a hair cell?

options.text: A receptor cell topped with a bundle of stiff projections whose bending opens channels directly, serving hearing, balance, and the lateral line.
options.why: Correct. Bending the bundle pulls channels open with no chemical steps in between. The same kind of cell serves hearing, balance, and a fish’s lateral line.

options.text: A receptor cell in the retina whose pigment changes shape on absorbing light, setting off an amplifying chain of chemical reactions inside the cell.
options.why: That is a photoreceptor, the receptor of vision. A hair cell responds to bending, and it opens its channels directly rather than through a chain of reactions.

options.text: A receptor neuron in the lining of the nose that makes one kind of smell receptor and sends its axon to a glomerulus in the olfactory bulb.
options.why: That is a smell receptor neuron. A hair cell responds to the bending of its bundle of stiff projections.

options.text: A receptor cell in the skin of some fishes that senses weak electric fields, laid out in rows along the surface of the fish’s body and head.
options.why: That is an electroreceptor, the receptor of the electric sense. A hair cell responds to mechanical bending.

items.stem: How does the way a hair cell responds to its stimulus differ from the way a photoreceptor responds to light?

options.text: Bending a hair cell’s bundle pulls channels open directly, while a photoreceptor’s pigment sets off a chain of chemical reactions first.
options.why: Correct. With no chemical steps in between, a hair cell can open its channels in as little as ten millionths of a second, the speed that timing-based localization needs.

options.text: A photoreceptor’s pigment pulls channels open directly, while bending a hair cell’s bundle sets off a chain of chemical reactions first.
options.why: This reverses the two. The photoreceptor is the one that works through an amplifying chain of reactions, and the hair cell opens its channels directly.

options.text: Both pull channels open directly, with no chemical steps in between, and they differ in stimulus, moving fluid for one and light for the other.
options.why: A hair cell does open its channels directly, but a photoreceptor does not. Its pigment changes shape on absorbing light and sets off a chain of chemical reactions that amplifies the effect.

options.text: Both work through a chain of chemical reactions that amplifies the signal, and they differ in stimulus, moving fluid for one and light for the other.
options.why: A photoreceptor does work through an amplifying chain of reactions, but a hair cell does not. It skips chemical steps entirely, which is what makes it fast.

items.stem: A sound slightly off to one side reaches the near ear a tiny fraction of a millisecond before the far one. In a short paragraph, explain why hair cells are fast enough for differences that small, why measuring them is still hard for neurons, how the barn owl’s brain solves the problem, and why that solution cannot simply be assumed for mammals.
items.answer: Bending a hair cell’s bundle pulls channels open directly, with no chemical steps in between, in as little as ten millionths of a second, which is the speed timing-based localization needs. But a single nerve impulse lasts about a thousandth of a second, a hundred times longer than the timing differences that matter. The barn owl’s brain has a delay line. Axons carrying signals from the two ears run in opposite directions along a row of neurons, and each neuron fires only when impulses from both ears arrive at the same moment, so the place along the row where they coincide stands for the time difference. Whether mammals do the same is debated. Many of their timing neurons prefer differences larger than their heads can produce, and timed inhibition reshapes their responses, so they may compare two broad channels instead. A model that fits one species need not hold in another.
rubric: Says that hair cells open their channels directly, without chemical steps, fast enough for timing (as little as ten millionths of a second).
Says that a nerve impulse lasts far longer than the timing differences that matter (about a hundred times, or about a thousandth of a second).
Describes the owl’s delay line: signals from the two ears run in opposite directions along a row of neurons that fire only when both arrive together, so a difference in time becomes a place.

Says that whether mammals use a delay line is debated, and gives a reason: timing neurons that prefer differences larger than the head produces, timed inhibition, or the alternative of two broad channels.

items.stem: In the barn owl’s brain, axons carrying signals from the two ears run in opposite directions along a row of neurons, and each neuron fires only when impulses from both ears arrive at the same moment. What does this arrangement turn a difference in arrival time into?

options.text: A place along the row, since which neuron receives both impulses together depends on how much of a head start one ear’s signal had.
options.why: Correct. The signal from the nearer ear travels farther along the row before it meets the other, so the neuron where they coincide stands for one time difference, and so for one direction. A difference in time becomes a place on a map.

options.text: A firing rate in every neuron of the row, since each neuron fires faster the larger the difference in arrival time between the ears.
options.why: In this arrangement every neuron has the same job, firing only on coincidence. What varies with the time difference is which neuron fires, not how fast all of them fire.

options.text: A difference in loudness, since impulses from the nearer ear arrive in greater numbers and excite the whole row more strongly.
options.why: Comparing loudness between the ears is a separate cue, handled by other neurons that set excitation from one ear against inhibition from the other. The owl’s row measures timing.

options.text: A pitch on the cochlea’s map, since each neuron along the row receives signals from a different place along the cochlear membrane.
options.why: The cochlea’s map is by frequency. The owl’s row maps a difference in arrival time, and so direction, which the cochlea does not lay out.

items.stem: The barn owl’s brain measures timing differences between the ears with a delay line. A student argues that mammals must do the same, since they face the same problem of timing differences far shorter than a nerve impulse. What is the best reply?

options.text: The student goes too far: whether mammals use the owl’s method is debated, and many of their timing neurons prefer differences larger than their heads produce.
options.why: Correct. The owl has a delay line, and whether mammals do is an open question. Many mammalian timing neurons prefer differences larger than their heads produce, and timed inhibition reshapes their responses, so mammals may compare two broad channels instead.

options.text: The student is right: any animal that locates sounds by timing has to turn a difference in time into a place on a map, just as the barn owl’s brain does.
options.why: A map is one procedure for measuring timing. Comparing the overall activity of two broad channels needs no map, and mammals may use that instead.

options.text: The student is wrong: mammals have been shown to locate sounds by level differences alone and to make no use at all of differences in arrival time between the ears.
options.why: Mammals do use timing; low pitches are located mainly by it. What is debated is how their neurons measure it, not whether they do.

options.text: The student is right: mammals and owls share the same kind of hair cell, and the same receptors must feed the same kind of timing circuit in the brain.
options.why: Sharing a receptor does not fix what the brain does with its signals. A model that fits one species need not hold for another.

items.stem: What is the superior colliculus?

options.text: The mammalian tectum, a midbrain structure that holds aligned maps of visual and auditory space and turns the eyes and head toward things.
options.why: Correct. In the superior colliculus, as in the barn owl’s tectum, a map of auditory space sits in register with the map of visual space, in the structure that orients the eyes and head.

options.text: The part of the thalamus that relays signals from the retina to primary visual cortex, keeping the retina’s map of the visual field.
options.why: That is the lateral geniculate nucleus, the visual relay in the thalamus. The superior colliculus is in the midbrain and aligns maps of visual and auditory space.

options.text: The area of cortex where hearing signals arrive from the thalamus, laid out by frequency so that neighboring pitches excite neighboring neurons.
options.why: That is auditory cortex, which is tonotopic and has no map of space. The superior colliculus holds a map of auditory space aligned with vision’s.

options.text: The group of brainstem neurons where signals from the two ears first come together and have their timing and their levels compared.
options.why: Those brainstem neurons do the first comparisons between the ears. The superior colliculus is the midbrain structure where the resulting map of sound direction lines up with vision’s.

items.stem: In a mammal, both auditory cortex and the superior colliculus receive signals from hearing. How do the maps they hold differ?

options.text: Auditory cortex is laid out by pitch and has no map of space, while the superior colliculus holds a map of auditory space aligned with visual space.
options.why: Correct. Auditory cortex keeps the cochlea’s tonotopic layout. The superior colliculus, the structure that turns the eyes and head toward things, holds a map of sound direction in register with vision’s map.

options.text: Auditory cortex holds a map of auditory space aligned with visual space, while the superior colliculus is laid out by pitch and has no map of space.
options.why: This reverses the two. Auditory cortex is the tonotopic one, and the superior colliculus holds the map of auditory space.

options.text: Both are laid out by pitch, as the cochlea is, and neither holds a map of space, since sound direction is never laid out across a whole sheet of neurons.
options.why: Sound direction can be laid out across neurons, as in the barn owl’s delay line, and the superior colliculus holds such a map.

options.text: Both hold maps of auditory space, but only auditory cortex lines its map up with vision, since the superior colliculus receives no visual input.
options.why: The superior colliculus holds maps of both visual and auditory space, in register. Auditory cortex has no map of space at all.

items.stem: What is a glomerulus?

options.text: A small spherical cluster in the olfactory bulb where axons of smell neurons making the same kind of receptor converge.
options.why: Correct. Smell neurons that make one kind of receptor are scattered across the nose, but their axons all end in the same few glomeruli. So each glomerulus collects the signals of one receptor type.

options.text: A small cluster of smell receptor neurons in the lining of the nose, all of which make the very same kind of receptor.
options.why: Neurons that make the same receptor are not clustered in the nose. They are scattered across its lining, and the gathering by receptor type happens where their axons end, in the glomeruli of the olfactory bulb.

options.text: A small cluster in a rat’s somatosensory cortex that receives the touch signals from a single whisker on its snout.
options.why: That describes a barrel, one of the clusters that make the whiskers’ large territories visible in a rat’s map of the body. A glomerulus belongs to smell, in the olfactory bulb.

options.text: A small organ along the side of a fish’s body, holding hair cells that respond to movements of the surrounding water.
options.why: That describes one of the organs of the lateral line. A glomerulus is a cluster of connections in the olfactory bulb, where the axons of smell neurons of one receptor type converge.

items.stem: Suppose every smell neuron in a mouse that makes one particular kind of receptor could be labeled with a dye. Where would the labeled cell bodies lie, and where would their axons end?

options.text: Scattered across the lining of the nose, with their axons converging on the same few glomeruli in the olfactory bulb.
options.why: Correct. Neurons that make the same receptor are scattered across the nose, but their axons all reach the same few glomeruli. So the sorting by receptor type happens in the bulb, not in the nose.

options.text: Clustered in one patch of the nose, with their axons ending in a matching patch of the bulb that keeps the nose’s layout.
options.why: That would be a topographic map, the way vision keeps the layout of the retina. Smell neurons of one kind are scattered, and the bulb sorts them by receptor type rather than by place in the nose.

options.text: Scattered across the lining of the nose, with their axons spreading out to reach most of the glomeruli in the bulb.
options.why: The neurons are scattered, but their axons do not spread out. All the axons from one receptor type converge on the same few glomeruli.

options.text: Clustered in one patch of the nose, with their axons passing through the thalamus on their way to olfactory cortex.
options.why: Among the senses that reach a cortex, smell is the one that skips the thalamus, since the olfactory bulb projects straight to olfactory cortex. And neurons of one receptor type are scattered across the nose, not clustered.

items.stem: Smell and color vision both identify something from the responses of their receptors. How do the two senses differ in the receptors they are argued to need?

options.text: Smell needs many kinds of narrowly tuned receptor, while color vision compares the responses of only three kinds of cone.
options.why: Correct. Color vision works by comparing three kinds of cone. Smell was argued to need many narrowly tuned kinds of receptor, and the large family of smell receptor genes fits that argument.

options.text: Smell needs three kinds of receptor, as color vision does, and each odor is told apart by comparing their three responses.
options.why: Three is the number for color vision’s cones. Smell was argued to need many narrowly tuned kinds of receptor, not three.

options.text: Smell needs one kind of receptor whose firing rises and falls with the odor, while color vision compares three kinds of cone.
options.why: A single kind of receptor could report only how strongly it was driven, just as a single cone cannot signal color. Smell was argued to need many kinds, each narrowly tuned.

options.text: Smell and color vision both need many kinds of narrowly tuned receptor, one for each odor and one for each color.
options.why: Color vision does not need a receptor for each color. It compares the responses of three kinds of cone. Only smell was argued to need many narrowly tuned kinds.

items.stem: Smell was argued to need many narrowly tuned kinds of receptor, rather than the few kinds color vision uses. Which of these facts best supports that argument about smell?

options.text: A human has about 400 working smell receptor genes, a mouse about 1,000, and even a lamprey a few dozen.
options.why: Correct. Smell’s receptors were found as a large family of genes, and hundreds of working receptor genes fit the many-receptor arrangement the argument called for, against color vision’s three kinds of cone.

options.text: In the mouse, about 25,000 smell receptor neurons send their axons to a single glomerulus of the olfactory bulb.
options.why: That counts how many neurons of one kind converge, not how many kinds of receptor there are. The argument concerns the number of receptor kinds, and the size of the receptor gene family is what bears on that.

options.text: The human eye has three kinds of cone, each with its own pigment that absorbs a different range of wavelengths.
options.why: That is a fact about color vision, the sense the argument sets smell against. It says nothing about how many kinds of receptor smell has. The large family of smell receptor genes does.

options.text: Nothing in the arrangement of the glomeruli carries any information about where an odor came from.
options.why: That is true of smell, but it concerns location, not how many kinds of receptor smell uses. The size of the smell receptor gene family is what bears on the number of kinds.

items.stem: Researchers record from the glomeruli of a mouse’s olfactory bulb while it sniffs a natural odor. According to the reading, which pattern of activity should they expect?

options.text: Only a small fraction of the many glomeruli become active, which is what is meant by sparse coding.
options.why: Correct. A natural odor activates only a small fraction of the glomeruli. That is sparse coding, in the sense used for patterns of activity in Module 7.

options.text: Nearly all of the glomeruli become active, each to a different degree, so every glomerulus helps code the odor.
options.why: That would be a dense pattern, with nearly every glomerulus taking part. A natural odor activates only a small fraction of the glomeruli.

options.text: Exactly one glomerulus becomes active, since each natural odor has a single glomerulus reserved for it.
options.why: Each glomerulus collects one receptor type, not one odor. A natural odor activates a small fraction of the glomeruli, not exactly one.

options.text: A patch of glomeruli becomes active whose position in the bulb marks the direction the odor came from.
options.why: The arrangement of the glomeruli carries nothing about location. Which glomeruli respond depends on which receptor types the odor drives.

items.stem: A popular article includes a drawing of the olfactory bulb with fruity odors in one region and smoky odors in the region next to it. The article’s writer calls this the bulb’s established map of odors. How does that claim fit what is known, according to the reading?

options.text: It goes beyond the evidence, since whether the arrangement of glomeruli forms an orderly map of odors is not known.
options.why: Correct. The bulb sorts its input by receptor type, but whether the arrangement of the glomeruli amounts to an orderly map of odors is not known. Calling the map established settles an open question.

options.text: It fits, since the glomeruli are known to be arranged so that similar odors activate neighboring glomeruli.
options.why: That is the article’s claim restated, and it is not established. Whether the glomeruli form an orderly map of odors is not known.

options.text: It fits, since the glomeruli are arranged by where their neurons lie in the nose, as vision’s map is by direction.
options.why: Smell neurons of one kind are scattered across the nose, so the bulb keeps no layout of the nose. It sorts by receptor type, and nothing in its arrangement carries location.

options.text: It goes beyond the evidence, since a natural odor is known to activate every glomerulus, leaving no region to map.
options.why: A natural odor activates only a small fraction of the glomeruli, which is sparse coding. The open question is whether their arrangement forms an orderly map of odors.

items.stem: Smell and touch both begin with receptors spread over a surface of the body. How do the two senses differ in whether their receptors carry where something is?

options.text: Touch receptors carry location above all, laid out across the skin, while the arrangement of smell’s glomeruli carries none.
options.why: Correct. Which touch receptors respond says where on the body the touch fell. Smell neurons of one kind are scattered across the nose and sorted by receptor type, so nothing in the arrangement carries location.

options.text: Smell receptors carry location, since neurons of one kind sit together in a patch of the nose, while touch carries only kinds of contact.
options.why: This reverses the two senses. Smell neurons of one kind are scattered, not grouped, and touch is the sense whose receptors carry location above all.

options.text: Both carry location equally well, since in each sense the receptors form a sheet whose layout is kept into the brain.
options.why: Touch keeps its layout as a map of the body. Smell does not: its scattered neurons are sorted by receptor type in the bulb, and that arrangement carries nothing about location.

options.text: Neither carries location directly, since in both senses it is computed from differences between two receptors, as in hearing.
options.why: Computing direction from differences between the two ears is hearing’s problem. Touch gets location from which receptors are pressed, and smell’s arrangement carries none at all.

items.stem: A person is holding a phone when it starts to buzz, and a moment later it starts to slip. The same patch of skin touches the phone throughout, yet the receptors that respond most strongly change. Which feature of touch accounts for the change?

options.text: Touch has several kinds of receptor, each a different filter, responding best to slipping, vibration, edges, or stretch.
options.why: Correct. Several kinds of touch receptor each respond best to a different kind of event in the skin: edges, slipping, vibration, or stretching. Buzzing and slipping drive different kinds, even in one patch of skin.

options.text: Touch has one kind of receptor, whose firing rises with pressure, so slipping and buzzing differ only in how hard they press.
options.why: Touch has several kinds of receptor, not one. Each acts as a different filter, so slipping and vibration drive different kinds.

options.text: Touch has several kinds of receptor, each found on a different part of the body, so each part of the hand feels one kind of event.
options.why: The kinds of touch receptor differ in what they respond to, not in which part of the body they cover. Here one patch of skin felt both events, and location comes from where the responding receptors lie.

options.text: Touch has many kinds of narrowly tuned receptor, one for each object, so a phone and a cup would each drive their own kind.
options.why: Having many narrowly tuned kinds of receptor is smell’s arrangement, for telling chemicals apart. Touch receptors are filters for kinds of contact, such as slipping or vibration, not detectors for particular objects.

items.stem: Two points pressed on a fingertip feel separate when they are only about 2 millimeters apart. On the upper arm, they must be about 40 millimeters apart. What accounts for the difference?

options.text: Touch receptors are packed far more densely in the skin of the fingertip than they are in the skin of the upper arm.
options.why: Correct. How finely a part of the body can feel depends on how densely its touch receptors are packed. The fingertip’s receptors are packed far more densely, so it feels more finely.

options.text: The fingertip’s area in somatosensory cortex is small, so its neurons are crowded together and tell nearby points apart.
options.why: The fingertip’s area of the body map is large, not small. In body maps, densely packed and heavily used parts like the hands take up big shares, and fineness of feeling follows receptor density.

options.text: The upper arm’s receptors respond only to stretching of the skin, which carries nothing about where a point is pressed.
options.why: Touch receptors of several kinds respond to edges, slipping, vibration, and stretch, and touch receptors carry location above all. The difference lies in how densely the receptors are packed.

options.text: The fingertip’s signals reach cortex through the thalamus, while the upper arm’s signals go straight to cortex.
options.why: Touch from every part of the body passes through the thalamus on its way to somatosensory cortex. Among the senses that reach a cortex, smell is the one that skips it. The difference lies in receptor density.

items.stem: Which term names a map of the body across the somatosensory or motor cortex, often drawn as a distorted figure whose parts are sized by how much cortex they occupy?

options.text: homunculus
options.why: Correct. The homunculus is drawn with huge hands and lips, because those parts take up large shares of the map of the body in somatosensory cortex.

options.text: somatotopy
options.why: Somatotopy is the arrangement itself, in which neighboring points on the body are represented by neighboring neurons. The homunculus is the distorted figure drawn from that map, its parts sized by the cortex they occupy.

options.text: retinotopy
options.why: Retinotopy is the arrangement of a visual area so that neighboring points in the visual field are represented by neighboring neurons. It maps the visual field, not the body.

options.text: proprioception
options.why: Proprioception is the sense of the body’s own position and movement, from receptors in the muscles, tendons, and joints. It is a sense, not a map drawn across cortex.

items.stem: Imagine a nearly blind burrowing mammal that finds its food by touching the soil constantly with a ring of fleshy appendages around its nose, densely packed with touch receptors. What would its somatosensory map most likely look like?

options.text: The ring around its nose would take up a very large share of the map, far out of proportion to its size on the body.
options.why: Correct. Each species’ body map is distorted in its own way, as with rat whiskers, raccoon paws, and the platypus bill. A map’s proportions follow receptor density and how much the animal uses each part, so a densely packed, heavily used ring would take a large share.

options.text: Each body part would take up a share of the map in proportion to its area of skin, so the small ring would take little.
options.why: Maps are not drawn to scale. Their proportions follow receptor density and how much the animal uses each part, which is why the human map has huge hands and lips.

options.text: The map would match the human pattern, with huge hands and lips, since every mammal’s body map is distorted the same way.
options.why: Each species’ map is distorted in its own way: in rats the whiskers take large territories, in raccoons the paws, and in the platypus the bill.

options.text: The ring would have no place in the map, since touch receptors around the nose send their signals to the olfactory bulb.
options.why: Touch receptors anywhere on the body feed the map of the body in somatosensory cortex. The olfactory bulb receives the axons of smell neurons, not of touch receptors.

items.stem: A violinist practices for hours a day over many years, making heavy use of the fingers of the left hand. According to the reading, what can happen to the map of the body in somatosensory cortex?

options.text: The map can reorganize, since body maps change after heavy use of a body part as well as after the part is lost.
