options.why: Correct. Body maps in somatosensory cortex reorganize after the loss of a body part, or after heavy use of one. Years of heavy use of the fingers fit the second case.

options.text: The map stays as it was, since a body map is fixed by the layout of the receptors in the skin and does not change.
options.why: Body maps follow the layout of the skin’s receptors, but they are not fixed. They reorganize after the loss of a body part, and after heavy use of one.

options.text: The map can reorganize only after a body part is lost, since heavy use leaves each part’s territory as it was.
options.why: Loss of a body part is one case of reorganization. Heavy use of a part is the other, and years of practice are heavy use.

options.text: The map stays as it was, since practice trains movements, which changes motor cortex but not the map of the body.
options.why: Practice involves feeling as well as moving, and the somatosensory map is the one described as reorganizing after heavy use of a body part.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain how the olfactory bulb turns smell’s scattered receptor neurons into an organized array, what the activity for a natural odor looks like across that array, and whether the arrangement carries location.
items.answer: Each smell neuron makes one kind of receptor, and the neurons that make the same receptor are scattered across the lining of the nose. Their axons, though, converge on the same few glomeruli, small spherical clusters of connections in the olfactory bulb. So the bulb turns a scattered sheet of receptors into an array sorted by receptor type. A natural odor activates only a small fraction of the glomeruli, which is sparse coding. Nothing about the arrangement of the glomeruli carries location, and whether it forms an orderly map of odors is not known.
rubric: Says each smell neuron makes one kind of receptor, and that neurons making the same receptor are scattered across the nose.
Says the axons of neurons making the same receptor converge on the same few glomeruli in the olfactory bulb.
Describes the result as an array sorted by receptor type.
Says a natural odor activates only a small fraction of the glomeruli, and names this sparse coding.
Says the arrangement of the glomeruli carries nothing about location.

items.stem: What is the motor cortex?

options.text: The area of cortex just in front of somatosensory cortex whose output fibers run to the spinal cord and help control voluntary movement.
options.why: Correct. Its output fibers cross to the opposite side on the way down, and some of them contact the motor neurons of the hand directly.

options.text: The area of cerebral cortex that receives signals from the skin’s touch receptors and holds a map of the body laid out by location on the skin.
options.why: That is the somatosensory cortex, whose map is drawn as the homunculus. The motor cortex lies just in front of it and sends its fibers down to the spinal cord.

options.text: The structure in the midbrain that holds aligned maps of visual and auditory space and turns the eyes and head toward things.
options.why: That is the superior colliculus, the mammalian tectum. The motor cortex is an area of the cerebral cortex whose fibers run to the spinal cord.

options.text: The part of the brain that recalibrates fast reflexes, such as the eye’s steadying reflex, using an error signal from the retina.
options.why: That is the cerebellum, which keeps the vestibulo-ocular reflex matched to a changing body. The motor cortex sends commands for voluntary movement down to the spinal cord.

items.stem: Two mammals are compared. One handles food with forepaws whose digits can move one at a time. The other uses its forelimbs mainly for walking and running. In which would direct connections from motor cortex to the motor neurons of the digits be expected to be larger?

options.text: In the food-handling mammal, since direct connections let digits move independently and are largest with skilled paws.
options.why: Correct. Some motor cortex fibers contact the motor neurons of the hand directly, which allows the fingers to move independently. Those direct connections are largest in species with skilled hands or forepaws.

options.text: In the running mammal, since running needs fast, forceful commands to the digits, and direct connections carry the most force.
options.why: Direct connections are tied to skill, not force. They allow fingers or digits to move independently of one another, and they are largest in species with skilled hands or forepaws.

options.text: Equally in both, since in every mammal the fibers of motor cortex reach the spinal cord and the digits in just the same way.
options.why: All motor cortex fibers run to the spinal cord, but the share that contacts the hand’s motor neurons directly differs between species. It is largest in species with skilled hands or forepaws.

options.text: In neither, since in mammals, as in fish, the tectum and brainstem steer the limbs and digits without any motor cortex.
options.why: A fish has no motor cortex, and its tectum and brainstem steer it. Mammals do have a motor cortex, and some of its fibers contact the motor neurons of the hand directly.

items.stem: The motor cortex and the somatosensory cortex both hold maps of the body, and both maps enlarge the hands and face. How do the two maps differ?

options.text: The motor map is far coarser, one site activating several muscles and zones overlapping, while the sensory map keeps separate segments.
options.why: Correct. In the motor map, one muscle can be activated from a patch millimeters wide, one site activates several muscles, and the zones for body parts overlap a great deal. In the sensory map, each body part has its own segment.

options.text: The motor map is much finer, with one site for each muscle and separate zones, while the sensory map’s zones for body parts overlap a great deal.
options.why: This reverses the two maps. The sensory map gives each body part its own segment, and the motor map is the coarse one, with overlapping zones.

options.text: The motor map is about as fine as the sensory map, but it lies just behind the somatosensory cortex rather than in front of it.
options.why: The motor cortex lies just in front of the somatosensory cortex, not behind it. And its map is much coarser, with overlapping zones.

options.text: The motor map runs in the reverse order from the sensory map, so that the face lies where the sensory map places the legs and feet.
options.why: The two maps share the same broad layout. The motor map differs by being much coarser, with sites that activate several muscles and zones that overlap.

items.stem: A brief electrical pulse is delivered to one small site in a monkey’s motor cortex, and then to a second site a millimeter away. According to the reading, which result should be expected?

options.text: Each pulse makes several muscles contract, and some of the same muscles contract from either of the two sites.
options.why: Correct. The motor map is coarse. A single site activates several muscles, and a single muscle can be activated from a patch of cortex millimeters wide, so neighboring sites share muscles.

options.text: Each pulse makes a single muscle contract, and no muscle can be made to contract from more than one site.
options.why: That would be a fine-grained map, with one site for each muscle. The motor map is coarse, with overlapping zones.

options.text: Each pulse acts like a touch on one small patch of skin, with the two sites standing for two neighboring patches.
options.why: That describes the somatosensory map, which keeps the layout of the skin’s receptors. Stimulating the motor cortex makes muscles contract.

options.text: Neither pulse has any effect, since the motor cortex holds no map of the body and acts only through the cerebellum.
options.why: The motor cortex does hold a map of the body, and its output fibers run down to the spinal cord. Stimulating it makes muscles contract.

items.stem: When stimulation of a site in a monkey’s motor cortex is kept up for longer, the monkey brings its hand to its mouth, or raises an arm as if in defense. What can be concluded about how the motor map is organized?

options.text: Around what the body does, so a site can produce a whole action rather than stand for one patch of the body.
options.why: Correct. A sensory map keeps the layout of a sheet of receptors. The motor map is organized around what the body does, and longer stimulation brings out whole actions.

options.text: Around the layout of a sheet of receptors, so that each site stands for one patch of skin, as in the sensory map.
options.why: That is how a sensory map is organized. Since longer stimulation produces whole actions, the motor map is organized around what the body does.

options.text: Around single muscles, so that each site stands for one muscle and an action is assembled one muscle at a time.
options.why: One site activates several muscles, and longer stimulation yields whole actions. The map is organized around actions, not single muscles.

options.text: Around the visual field, so that each site stands for the direction in which the eyes point while the hand moves.
options.why: A map laid out by direction in the visual field is vision’s. The motor map is a map of the body, organized around actions.

items.stem: A researcher records a single neuron in a monkey’s motor cortex while the monkey reaches in eight directions. The neuron fires most for reaches up and to the right, less for neighboring directions, and little for reaches down and to the left. Could the direction of any one reach be read from this neuron alone?

options.text: Not reliably, since direction is coded by a vote across many neurons, each preferring a different direction.
options.why: Correct. The neuron fires most for one direction but also fires, less strongly, for the directions next to it, so a moderate rate could come from a reach on either side of its preferred direction. Direction is coded by a vote across many neurons, which is a distributed code.

options.text: Yes, since each neuron in motor cortex codes a single direction, so this neuron’s firing names the direction of the reach.
options.why: The neuron prefers one direction but fires for others too, so its firing alone is ambiguous. Direction is coded across many neurons, not by single ones.

options.text: Not at all, since neurons in motor cortex code which muscles contract and carry no information about direction.
options.why: This neuron’s firing does vary with direction, since it has a preferred direction. Direction is read from the vote across many such neurons.

options.text: Yes, if its place on the motor map is known, since direction is coded by where on the map the activity lies.
options.why: Coding by place is how the superior colliculus links a seen target to an eye movement. In motor cortex, the direction of a reach is coded by a vote across many neurons.

items.stem: Consider two codes. A natural odor activates only a small fraction of the glomeruli in the olfactory bulb. The direction of a reach is coded by a vote across many neurons in motor cortex, each preferring a different direction. Which statement describes the two codes correctly?

options.text: The odor code is sparse, with few of many glomeruli active, and the direction code is distributed, with many neurons voting.
options.why: Correct. Sparse coding means only a small fraction of the units are active, as with the glomeruli for one odor. In a distributed code, a value is carried across many units, as with the vote across motor cortex neurons.

options.text: The odor code is distributed, with all the glomeruli active, and the direction code is sparse, with one of the neurons active per direction.
options.why: This reverses the two codes. Only a small fraction of the glomeruli respond to an odor, and many neurons, not one, vote on a direction.

options.text: Both are place codes, in which the position of the active glomeruli or neurons says where the odor came from or where the target lies.
options.why: Nothing in the arrangement of the glomeruli carries location, and the direction of a reach is coded by a vote, not by position on a map.

options.text: Both use one cell for each item, so that a single glomerulus stands for one odor and a single neuron for one direction.
options.why: A glomerulus collects one receptor type, not one odor, and a natural odor activates a small fraction of the glomeruli rather than one. A single neuron prefers a direction but does not code it alone.

items.stem: A light flashes above and to the left of where a monkey is looking, and activity appears at one point in the visual map of its superior colliculus. How does the layout of the colliculus help turn that point into an eye movement?

options.text: A map of eye movements lies directly beneath the visual map, in register, so the point can drive the eyes toward that place.
options.why: Correct. In the superior colliculus, a map of visual space sits directly above a map of eye movements, and the two line up. Layout alone solves part of the problem of turning a place on the retina into a movement.

options.text: A stored list gives the eye movement needed for every point on the retina, and the active point looks up its own entry in that list.
options.why: A stored list of answers would do the job, but it is not how the colliculus does it. There, the map of eye movements lies directly beneath the visual map, in register.

options.text: A map of auditory space lies in register with the visual map, so the sound of the flash tells the eyes where they should turn.
options.why: The colliculus does hold a map of auditory space in register with the visual one, but a flash of light makes no sound. What links the seen point to a movement is the map of eye movements beneath the visual map.

options.text: A vote across many neurons in motor cortex, each preferring a different direction, works out where the eyes should turn.
options.why: A vote across many neurons is how motor cortex codes the direction of a reach. In the colliculus, layout does the work, with the map of eye movements in register beneath the visual map.

items.stem: In a cat’s superior colliculus, a map of auditory space lies in register with a map of visual space. A mouse rustles to the cat’s left, activity appears at the matching place in the auditory map, and the cat turns its head toward the sound. What has probably happened between the map and the neck muscles?

options.text: The place of the activity has been converted into firing rates, a step likely needed wherever a sensory map drives a movement.
options.why: Correct. For the eyes, the motor neurons are driven by firing rates, not by places, so the collicular place code has to become a rate code. That conversion is likely needed wherever a sensory map drives a movement, and turning the head toward a sound is such a case.

options.text: Nothing more was needed, since once two maps are in register, the place of the activity moves the muscles directly.
options.why: Maps in register solve only part of the problem. For the eyes, the motor neurons are driven by firing rates rather than places, and a conversion from place to rate is likely needed wherever a sensory map drives a movement.

options.text: The place of the activity has been relayed through the thalamus, since every map passes through the thalamus before any movement.
options.why: The thalamus relays sensory signals on their way to the cortex. The step needed here is converting a place on a map into the firing rates that drive motor neurons.

options.text: The place of the activity has been checked against an error signal in the cerebellum, which corrects each movement before it begins.
options.why: The cerebellum recalibrates movements from error over time. Driving a movement from a map most likely requires converting a place into firing rates.

items.stem: In the superior colliculus, layout solves part of the problem of turning a seen place into a movement. Beyond the colliculus, how are mappings like a simulated crab’s, from eye angles to arm angles, thought to be carried?

options.text: In the strengths of many synapses, which learning and development can change, not in maps stacked in register.
options.why: Correct. In the colliculus, one map lying directly above another does part of the work. Mappings like the crab’s are thought to be carried by the strengths of many synapses, which learning and development can change.

options.text: In further maps stacked in register, with a map of arm angles lying directly beneath each of the maps of eye angles.
options.why: Stacked maps in register are the colliculus’s solution, and they handle only part of the problem. Mappings like the crab’s are thought to lie in changeable synapse strengths.

options.text: In a stored list that gives the arm angles for every pair of eye angles, fixed once the body stops growing.
options.why: A stored list would do the job, but the body keeps changing, so the mapping has to keep being relearned. Such mappings are thought to lie in synapse strengths that learning and development can change.

options.text: In single neurons, each standing for one target, so that whichever neuron is active names the arm angles needed.
options.why: One neuron for each target is not how such mappings are thought to be carried. They are thought to lie in the strengths of many synapses, spread across many neurons.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, compare the map of the body in motor cortex with the map in somatosensory cortex. Say what the two maps share, how they differ in grain, and what each is organized around.
items.answer: Both maps share the same broad layout of the body, and both enlarge the hands and face. But the motor map is much coarser. A single muscle can be activated from a patch of cortex millimeters wide, a single site activates several muscles, and the zones for different body parts overlap a great deal, where the sensory map gives each part its own segment. Longer stimulation of motor cortex produces whole actions, such as bringing a hand to the mouth or reaching. So the sensory map keeps the layout of a sheet of receptors, while the motor map is organized around what the body does.
rubric: Says both maps share the same broad layout of the body, with enlarged hands and face.
Says the motor map is coarser, giving either one muscle activated from a wide patch or one site activating several muscles.
Says the motor map’s zones for body parts overlap, where the sensory map gives each part its own segment.
Gives longer stimulation producing whole actions as evidence about how the motor map is organized.
States that the sensory map keeps the layout of a receptor sheet, while the motor map is organized around what the body does.

items.stem: A target appears at one place on the retina, and the eyes must jump to it. In a short paragraph, explain how the layout of the superior colliculus solves part of this problem, and what must still happen before the eye muscles move.
items.answer: In the superior colliculus, a map of visual space sits directly above a map of eye movements, and the two maps are in register. So activity at the target’s point in the visual map can drive the point beneath it in the map of eye movements, which moves the eyes toward that same place. That is layout solving part of the problem of turning a place on the retina into a movement. But a place on a map is not yet something the muscles can use. The motor neurons that pull on the eye are driven by firing rates, not by places, so the collicular place code has to be converted into a rate code. That conversion is likely needed wherever a sensory map drives a movement.
rubric: Says a map of visual space sits directly above a map of eye movements in the superior colliculus.
Says the two maps are in register, so a target at one point can drive the eyes toward that same point.
Says the motor neurons that move the eye are driven by firing rates, not by places.
States that the place code must be converted into a rate code before the eyes move.

pools.title: Calibration, Cancellation, and What Every Sense Does
pools.covers: reading §8.3.8, §8.3.9, §8.C · (lecture 8.3 stopped at slide 10 on 2026-10-16, so this pool's slides, the_cerebellum_calibrates, the_negative_image and what_every_sense_does, were not delivered; every item is reading-only under rules 9.9 and 9.10)

items.stem: What is the vestibulo-ocular reflex?

options.text: A fast response that turns the eyes opposite to a turn of the head, so that the image stays steady on the retina.
options.why: Correct. The balance organs sense the head’s turn and drive the eye muscles the other way, over a path as short as three neurons. The image holds still on the retina without waiting for vision.

options.text: A quick jump of the eyes to a new target, lasting only tens of milliseconds and over before any correction can arrive.
options.why: That is a saccade. A saccade sweeps the image across the retina to a new target; the vestibulo-ocular reflex keeps the image from moving while the head turns.

options.text: A signal derived from a command to move the eyes and sent to sensory areas, so that the image’s sweep can be anticipated.
options.why: That is a corollary discharge, a signal used to anticipate a movement’s sensory effects. The vestibulo-ocular reflex is driven by the balance organs sensing the head’s turn, not by a copy of a command.

options.text: The organs of balance in the inner ear, which sense rotation of the head, gravity, and acceleration as the body moves.
options.why: That is the vestibular system, which supplies the signal the reflex runs on. The reflex itself is the eye movement those organs drive, opposite to the head’s turn.

items.stem: A person jogging down a street can read a sign clearly, although the head bobs with every step. Standing still and reading a phone held in a shaking hand, the same person sees the words blur. What best explains the difference?

options.text: Head movement is sensed by the balance organs, which turn the eyes against it within milliseconds, while a shaking phone can be followed only by vision, whose news comes too late.
options.why: Correct. This is the contrast between a hand waved before a still head and a head shaken before a still hand. The vestibulo-ocular reflex runs from the balance organs to the eye muscles without waiting for vision, while news that an image has slipped takes about a tenth of a second to become a correction.

options.text: Head movement is followed by vision, which tracks the sign’s motion across the retina step by step, while a phone shaking in the hand moves too irregularly for vision to follow it.
options.why: Vision does report an image slipping across the retina, but that report takes about a tenth of a second to turn into a correction, too slow for a bobbing head. The steady view comes from the balance organs, which do not wait for vision.

options.text: Head movement is canceled by a learned negative image of the jogging rhythm, while a phone shaking in the hand moves in a new way that no negative image has yet been learned for.
options.why: A negative image is the electric fish’s learned cancellation of its own pulses from a sense. Keeping the eyes on a sign is a different job, done by a reflex that turns the eyes against the head’s turn.

options.text: Head movement while jogging is slow enough for visual feedback to correct in time, while a phone shaking in the hand moves faster than any movement of the eyes can follow.
options.why: The head’s movements while running are quick, and visual feedback would lag them. The reflex that steadies the eyes is fast precisely because it uses the balance organs rather than vision.

items.stem: A person starts wearing new glasses that enlarge the image. For the first days, the view slips a little each time the head turns. Why does the vestibulo-ocular reflex not simply correct for the glasses on each turn of the head?

options.text: It turns the eyes by its current setting without checking the result, so a change in the optics has to be met by recalibrating it.
options.why: Correct. The reflex is fast because it does not wait for vision, and for the same reason it cannot correct itself on the fly. When the eyes, the head, or the optics change, its setting has to be relearned, and that recalibration needs the cerebellum.

options.text: It checks its result against vision on every turn, but the new glasses blur the image too much for that check to detect any of the slip.
options.why: The reflex does not check its result as it goes; that is what makes it fast. The slip is detected, but it is used to recalibrate the reflex over hours to days, not to correct each turn.

options.text: It is driven by a copy of the command to turn the head, and the new glasses change nothing about that command, so nothing signals a problem.
options.why: The reflex is driven by the balance organs sensing the head’s turn, not by a copy of a command. And the slip the glasses produce is exactly the signal that something is wrong.

options.text: It is fixed for life by the length of its short path from ear to eye, so it cannot change, and the person learns to make slower turns of the head.
options.why: The reflex is not fixed. With magnifying lenses it grows stronger until the slip disappears, a recalibration that needs the cerebellum.

items.stem: Animals that lack the part of the cerebellum serving the vestibulo-ocular reflex are fitted with magnifying lenses. What happens?

options.text: They cannot adapt the reflex to the lenses, so the image keeps slipping across the retina whenever the head turns.
options.why: Correct. Recalibrating the reflex needs the cerebellum. Without the part that serves the reflex, the old setting stays, and the enlarged image keeps slipping.

options.text: They adapt the reflex to the lenses faster than intact animals do, since the brainstem circuits are left to learn alone.
options.why: The cerebellum is required for the learning, so removing it does not speed adaptation. The lasting change may involve brainstem circuits too, but they do not learn it without the cerebellum.

options.text: They lose the reflex entirely, so the eyes no longer turn against the head at all when the head turns.
options.why: The reflex’s shortest path runs from the balance organs through the brainstem to the eye muscles, with the cerebellum on a side loop. What is lost is the ability to recalibrate the reflex, not the reflex.

options.text: They adapt the reflex normally, since the image’s slip reaches the eye muscles directly from the retina.
options.why: The slip is carried as an error to the cerebellum by climbing fibers, not to the eye muscles. Without the part of the cerebellum that serves the reflex, that error cannot be used to recalibrate it.

items.stem: A student reasons: “Animals lacking the part of the cerebellum that serves the vestibulo-ocular reflex cannot adapt it to magnifying lenses, so the reflex’s new setting must be stored in the cerebellum”. What is the problem with this reasoning?

options.text: A structure needed for learning is not thereby shown to hold the change; where the change is stored is debated, and brainstem circuits seem involved too.
options.why: Correct. The cerebellum is required for the learning, but where the lasting change is stored is debated. It appears to involve both the cerebellum and the brainstem circuits it controls. Needed for learning does not mean the place where the result is kept.

options.text: Nothing is wrong with it, since a structure that learning cannot happen without is, by that very fact, the place where the learned change is kept.
options.why: That inference goes beyond the evidence. A structure can be needed for learning while the lasting change sits partly elsewhere, and here the change appears to involve brainstem circuits as well as the cerebellum.

options.text: The lenses never change the reflex at all; the animals learn instead to move their heads more slowly, so nothing new is stored anywhere.
options.why: The reflex itself does change. With magnifying lenses it grows stronger until the slip disappears, and the new setting persists for a while after the lenses come off.

options.text: The change is stored in the eye muscles themselves, which grow stronger or weaker as the reflex is recalibrated over the days of wearing the lenses.
options.why: Eye muscles do weaken with age or injury, which is one reason recalibration is needed. But the lasting change appears to involve the cerebellum and the brainstem circuits it controls, and exactly where it is kept is debated.

items.stem: Two groups of patients throw at a target through prism goggles. One group, with damage to the inferior olive, throws accurately but adapts to the prisms slowly or not at all. The other, with other damage to the cerebellum, throws clumsily but still adapts. What can be concluded from the two patterns together?

options.text: Learning a mapping and using it are separable, since each ability can be lost while the remaining one is kept.
options.why: Correct. Olive damage spared accurate throwing and impaired adaptation; other cerebellar damage did the reverse. Since each ability survives without the other, learning a mapping and using it can be told apart.

options.text: The olive stores the mapping from sight to throw, since damage to it leaves the old mapping in place.
options.why: The olive is needed for the learning, as the source of the climbing fibers. But from the olive’s role in learning alone, we cannot tell where the change is stored, which is still debated.

options.text: The cerebellum plays no part in throwing, since the second group could still adapt despite damage to it.
options.why: The second group threw clumsily, so the cerebellum matters for using the mapping. What that group kept was the ability to change it.

options.text: Learning a mapping and using it share one mechanism, since both groups threw worse through the prisms than people without damage.
options.why: Both groups were impaired through the prisms, but in opposite ways. One could use the mapping and not change it; the other could change it and not use it well. That double pattern is what separates the two abilities.

items.stem: The inferior olive is the source of the climbing fibers. Suppose a person with damage to the olive is given glasses that magnify the image. What should we expect of the person’s vestibulo-ocular reflex?

options.text: It would still steady the eyes much as before, but would fail to recalibrate to the glasses, so the image would keep slipping when the head turns.
options.why: Correct. Climbing fibers carry the image’s slip to the cerebellum as the error that drives recalibration. Damage to their source should spare using the reflex and impair changing it, the same split the olive patients showed when throwing through prisms. This is a prediction from that account, not a reported result.

options.text: It would stop steadying the eyes at all, since the climbing fibers form part of the three-neuron path from the balance organs to the eye muscles.
options.why: The three-neuron path runs from the balance organs through the brainstem to the eye muscles; climbing fibers are not part of it. They carry the error used to recalibrate the reflex, not the signal that drives it.

options.text: It would recalibrate to the glasses as usual, since the image’s slip reaches the cerebellum through the balance organs rather than the climbing fibers.
options.why: The balance organs report the head’s turn, not the image’s slip, which only the eye can detect. The slip reaches the cerebellum as an error carried by climbing fibers.

options.text: It would recalibrate faster than usual, since without errors from the olive the cerebellum would adjust to the glasses from vision alone.
options.why: The slip is the error that recalibration learns from. Taking away the fibers that deliver it would slow the learning or stop it, as it did for the olive patients throwing through prisms.

items.stem: Some neurons in the cerebellum respond when an experimenter turns an animal’s head, and stay quiet when the animal makes the same head movement itself. What idea does this pattern fit?

options.text: The cerebellum may predict the sensory effect of a self-made movement and subtract it, leaving a response only to imposed movement.
options.why: Correct. An influential idea is that the cerebellum predicts the self-caused part of a signal and subtracts it, which would explain neurons that ignore self-made head movements. It remains an idea, and whether the cerebellum learns forward models, inverse models, or both is open.

options.text: The balance organs stop sensing rotation whenever the animal turns its own head, so the neurons receive no signal to answer.
options.why: The balance organs sense rotation of the head whoever causes it; that is why they can be used to measure an animal’s own movement. The difference lies in what the neurons do with the signal, not in the sensors.

options.text: The cerebellum has been shown to learn inverse models, working out the command that each wanted head movement requires.
options.why: Whether the cerebellum learns forward models, inverse models, or both is still open. And an inverse model works out a command from a wanted outcome, while this pattern concerns canceling a movement’s sensory effect.

options.text: The neurons receive input only from vision, which sees the scene sweep past when the experimenter turns the head, and not otherwise.
options.why: The eyes receive the same input during a head turn whether the turn is imposed or self-made, so input from vision alone could not separate the two. The pattern fits a prediction of the self-caused part being subtracted.

items.stem: A pufferfish with one eye rotated and the other covered swims in tight circles, because the motion it expects from its own turns and the motion its eye reports add instead of canceling. The circling continues after the fish’s cerebellum is removed. What follows from this result?

options.text: Cancellation of self-caused signals is not confined to the cerebellum; here it most likely depends on the tectum receiving the rotated eye.
options.why: Correct. If the comparison lived only in the cerebellum, removing it should have ended the circling. It did not, so cancellation of self-caused signals happens elsewhere too, most likely in the tectum, the map of the space around the animal.

options.text: The cerebellum compares the expected motion with what the rotated eye reports, since the circling comes from a mismatch computed there.
options.why: A comparison done only by the cerebellum could not survive the removal of the cerebellum. The circling continued, so the comparison does not depend on the cerebellum alone.

options.text: The circling is driven by the balance organs, since sensing the turn directly needs neither a copy of the command nor a cerebellum.
options.why: The pufferfish also kept circling after both of its balance organs were removed, which is why its expectation was traced to a copy of the command. The balance organs cannot be what drives the circling.

options.text: The rotated eye has recalibrated to its new position, so the circling no longer reflects any comparison of expected and actual motion.
options.why: A recalibrated eye would have ended the circling. The fish kept circling, so the mismatch between expected and actual motion was still there.

items.stem: Canceling self-caused signals is linked both to the electric fish’s cerebellum-like structure and to the cerebellum itself. How does the evidence for the two compare?

options.text: In the electric fish, a learned negative image has been seen forming and canceling its own input; in the cerebellum, prediction and subtraction remain an influential but open idea.
options.why: Correct. The electric fish is the clearest case anywhere of a learned prediction subtracted from a sense: the negative image appears after minutes of pairing and fades when pairing stops. In the cerebellum, neurons that ignore self-made head movements fit the idea of prediction and subtraction without settling it.

options.text: In the cerebellum, a learned negative image of head movement has been seen forming and canceling; in the electric fish, prediction and subtraction remain an influential but open idea.
options.why: This reverses the evidence. The negative image was found in the electric fish. The cerebellum’s neurons that ignore self-made head movements are consistent with prediction and subtraction, which remains an idea.

options.text: In both, cancellation has been shown to work by dimming the sense during movement, so neither needs to learn any prediction of the animal’s own signals.
options.why: Dimming is a separate way of handling self-caused signals, suited to brief, simple ones, as when a fish’s lateral line is turned down while it swims. The electric fish learns a prediction shaped to its own input and subtracts it.

options.text: In both, cancellation has been shown to need the cerebellum, since removing the cerebellum stopped the pufferfish with a rotated eye from swimming in circles.
options.why: The pufferfish kept circling after its cerebellum was removed. So cancellation is not confined to the cerebellum, and in that fish it most likely depended on the tectum.

items.stem: A person begins wearing glasses that magnify the image. In a short paragraph, explain why the vestibulo-ocular reflex at first lets the view slip when the head turns. Then say what signal marks the reflex as now wrong, how that signal reaches the cerebellum, what the recalibration needs, and what is still uncertain about where the change is kept.
items.answer: The reflex turns the eyes against the head’s turn by its current setting, driven by the balance organs, and it does not check its result as it goes. With a magnified image, the old setting turns the eyes too little, so the image slips across the retina with each turn. That slip is the error. Climbing fibers carry it to the cerebellum, each delivering it to one output cell. Recalibrating the reflex needs the cerebellum, since animals without the part that serves the reflex cannot adapt it to magnifying lenses. Where the lasting change is stored is debated. It appears to involve both the cerebellum and the brainstem circuits the cerebellum controls.
rubric: Says the reflex does not check its result as it goes (it runs from the balance organs without waiting for vision), so its old setting is wrong for the new optics.
Names the image’s slip across the retina as the error signal.
Says climbing fibers carry the slip to the cerebellum as that error.
Says the recalibration needs the cerebellum.
Says where the lasting change is stored is debated, or that it seems to involve both the cerebellum and brainstem circuits, without placing it in the cerebellum alone.

items.stem: What is a negative image?

options.text: A learned signal, opposite in shape to the input an animal’s own action is expected to cause, that cancels that input when the two are added.
options.why: Correct. In the electric fish, the discharge command comes to produce a pattern that is the expected self-caused input turned upside down. Added to the real input, it cancels the fish’s own pulse and leaves anything else, such as the faint signal of prey.

options.text: A copy of a movement command, kept so that the expected sensory consequences of the movement can be compared with what the senses report.
options.why: That is an efference copy. In the electric fish, the command is one of the signals that drives the negative image, but the negative image is the learned, inverted pattern itself.

options.text: An error in the opposite direction that follows the removal of a distortion the nervous system has adapted to, showing that a mapping changed.
options.why: That is an aftereffect, such as the opposite miss when prism goggles come off. A negative image cancels a self-caused input while that input is arriving.

options.text: A turning down of a sense while the animal moves, so that brief and simple self-caused signals are weakened along with everything else.
options.why: That is dimming, used for brief, simple self-caused signals, as when a fish’s lateral line is turned down while it swims. A negative image cancels only the predicted self-caused part and leaves the rest.

items.stem: In a paralyzed electric fish, a pulse of sensory input was paired with each of the fish’s commands to discharge. The input at first excited cells in a cerebellum-like structure in the hindbrain. After two to ten minutes of pairing, what did the command alone produce in those cells?

options.text: The opposite of the pattern the input had produced, which cancels the expected input when the two are added.
options.why: Correct. That opposite pattern is a negative image of the expected input. Driven by the command, it cancels the self-caused part of the input and leaves anything else, such as the faint signal of prey.

options.text: The same pattern the input had produced, a copy that lets the cell respond to the pulse before the pulse arrives.
options.why: A matching copy is what a simple association between command and input would produce. What formed instead was the opposite pattern, which is what lets the fish’s own pulse cancel out rather than be doubled.

options.text: No response at all, because repeated pairing had switched the cells off for as long as the fish kept discharging.
options.why: Switching the response off would be dimming, and it would silence prey signals too. The command came to produce an active, inverted pattern, and when pairing stopped that pattern faded over minutes.

options.text: A response that grew with each pairing, as Hebb’s rule strengthens inputs that arrive just before the cell fires.
options.why: The rule in these fish is Hebb’s rule reversed. An input arriving just before the cell fires is weakened, so the pattern that builds up opposes the input rather than amplifying it.

items.stem: Why must the electric fish’s negative image be learned, rather than fixed once and for all?

options.text: The fish’s own pulse feels different in different water and near different objects, so the pattern to cancel keeps changing.
options.why: Correct. The same discharge produces a different self-caused input depending on the water and on nearby objects. A fixed negative image would fail to cancel it, so the image has to be learned and kept up to date.

options.text: The fish’s prey changes from place to place, so the pattern to cancel has to keep up with whatever the fish is hunting.
options.why: Prey is exactly what the negative image must leave alone. It cancels only what is predictable from the fish’s own commands, and the fish’s own pulse is what varies with water and objects.

options.text: The fish’s discharge commands are different every time, so no fixed pattern could ever be linked to them in advance.
options.why: The commands are what the negative image is tied to, and they recur in a regular way, which is what makes the self-caused input predictable. What varies is how the resulting pulse feels in different surroundings.

options.text: The fish’s passive sense is dimmed during every discharge, and learning is what lifts the dimming once the pulse has passed.
options.why: Dimming is a different way of handling self-caused signals, and it would hide prey along with the pulse. The negative image cancels the pulse instead, and it must be learned because the pulse feels different in different water and near different objects.

items.stem: An elephantnose fish that has long hunted in one muddy pool swims into a pool with different water, where its own pulses feel different to its passive electric sense. What should happen over the next minutes?

options.text: At first, part of its own pulse goes uncanceled, until a new negative image is learned that cancels the pulse again.
options.why: Correct. A negative image tuned to the old water no longer matches the new input, so a residue remains. That leftover drives the learning, and a matching negative image builds up within minutes, as it did in the original pairing experiment.

options.text: Its old negative image goes on canceling the pulses exactly as before, since the commands that drive it are unchanged.
options.why: The commands are the same, but the input they cause is not. A negative image shaped for the old water would leave part of the new input uncanceled, which is exactly why the image has to be learned.

options.text: It stops producing a negative image altogether, since a learned signal cannot adjust once the fish is somewhere new.
options.why: Being learned is what lets the negative image adjust. The anti-Hebbian rule keeps changing the weights while anything predictable is left over.

options.text: Its passive sense is dimmed for as long as it stays in the new pool, since cancellation works only in familiar water.
options.why: Dimming is a different strategy, suited to brief, simple signals, and it would hide prey along with the fish’s own pulse. The electric fish relearns the cancellation instead.

items.stem: In the electric fish’s cancellation circuit, how does the rule for changing a connection compare with Hebb’s rule?

options.text: It is Hebb’s rule reversed: an input arriving just before the cell fires is weakened, and inputs at other times are strengthened.
options.why: Correct. Because the change runs opposite to Hebb’s, whatever reliably drives the cell at a predictable moment ends up opposed. That is why it is called an anti-Hebbian rule, and why anything predictable cancels.

options.text: It is Hebb’s rule unchanged: an input arriving just before the cell fires is strengthened, so whatever drives the cell is reinforced.
options.why: That is the direction of Hebb’s rule, from Module 5. Run in the fish, it would amplify the self-caused input rather than cancel it.

options.text: It is Hebb’s rule with an error added: an input is strengthened only when a climbing fiber signals that the cell fired wrongly.
options.why: An error delivered by a climbing fiber is what drives the cerebellum’s recalibration of the steadying reflex. In the electric fish, no separate error is needed; the cell’s own leftover response does the teaching.

options.text: It is Hebb’s rule switched off: no connection changes while the fish discharges, so its own pulse is never learned at all.
options.why: Learning goes on while the fish discharges; the negative image forms within two to ten minutes of pairing input with the discharge commands. Turning a sense down during movement is dimming, a different strategy.

items.stem: Suppose that each time an electric fish discharges, its own pulse reliably lowers the firing of a cell in its cancellation circuit for a moment. Under the fish’s anti-Hebbian rule, what happens over repeated discharges?

options.text: Command-linked inputs arriving in the dip are seldom followed by firing, so they are strengthened until they fill the dip in.
options.why: Correct. The rule changes connections in both directions: an input arriving just before the cell fires is weakened, and inputs at other times are strengthened. So a predictable rise is opposed by weakening and a predictable dip by strengthening, and anything predictable cancels.

options.text: Nothing changes, since the rule only weakens inputs that arrive just before the cell fires, and here the cell fires less.
options.why: The rule also strengthens inputs that arrive at other times. That second half is what lets it cancel a predictable drop in firing, not only a predictable rise.

options.text: The dip deepens, since the rule weakens the command-linked inputs whenever the fish discharges, whatever the cell does.
options.why: Weakening applies to inputs arriving just before the cell fires. At the moment of the dip the cell is quiet, so the command-linked inputs then are strengthened, which fills the dip in.

options.text: The dip is left in place, since self-caused input can be canceled only when it raises firing, and a drop passes through like prey.
options.why: Because the changes go both ways, anything predictable cancels, whether it raises the cell’s firing or lowers it. What survives is what the fish’s own commands do not predict, such as prey.

items.stem: When a South American knifefish bends its tail, the electrical input along its body changes ten to a hundred times more than a small prey animal changes it. How can the fish still detect prey while it swims?

options.text: A circuit like the elephantnose fish’s learns the input each tail bend predictably causes and subtracts it, leaving the prey’s faint signal.
options.why: Correct. Movement is canceled the same way as the fish’s own pulses. Signals that reliably predict the tail’s effect, including the position of the body, can drive the learned cancellation, and the prey signal survives because nothing the fish does predicts it.

options.text: Its electric sense is switched off during each tail bend, so that prey can be detected only in the brief pauses between one bend and the next.
options.why: Switching a sense off during movement is dimming, which would leave the fish unable to sense prey every time it swam. The knifefish cancels the predicted effect of the bend and keeps the rest.

options.text: It relies on vision while swimming, since an electric sense swamped by the animal’s own movement cannot be corrected by any circuit.
options.why: The electric sense goes on working during swimming because the effects of the tail bends are canceled. Cancellation is what lets a sense swamped by self-caused signals still report the world.

options.text: It holds its tail rigid while hunting, so that no self-caused change in its electrical input arises for the prey signal to compete with.
options.why: The knifefish does bend its tail as it swims, and a circuit similar to the elephantnose fish’s cancels the electrical effects of those bends.

items.stem: In the electric fish’s cancellation circuit, the weights keep changing over the first minutes of pairing input with discharge commands. What brings the changes to an end?

options.text: The negative image comes to cancel the self-caused input, so no predictable leftover remains in the cell’s response to teach it.
options.why: Correct. The teacher is the cell’s own leftover response. Something predictable that has not yet been canceled keeps adjusting the weights, and once it is canceled there is nothing predictable left to drive change.

options.text: A climbing fiber stops delivering an error once the fish’s own pulse no longer reaches the passive electric sense it was flooding.
options.why: Climbing fibers deliver errors in the cerebellum’s calibration of the steadying reflex. In the electric fish the cell’s own leftover response does the teaching, and the fish’s pulse still reaches the sense; it is canceled there.

options.text: The prey signal is detected, and detecting it switches the learning off until the next time the fish sends a discharge command.
options.why: Prey signals are what the negative image leaves alone, because nothing in the fish’s commands predicts them. They do not switch learning on or off.

options.text: The pairing of input with the command stops, which fixes the negative image in place, unchanged, for as long as the fish lives.
options.why: When pairing stops, the negative image does not stay fixed; it fades over minutes. So stopping the pairing changes the weights too, rather than freezing them.

items.stem: Two circuits learn to adjust a response: the cerebellum recalibrating the vestibulo-ocular reflex, and the electric fish’s cerebellum-like structure learning to cancel its own pulses. How do their teaching signals differ?

options.text: In the reflex, a climbing fiber delivers the image’s slip as an error to one output cell; in the fish, the cell’s own leftover response does the teaching.
options.why: Correct. The cerebellum’s calibration depends on an error arriving on a separate input, the climbing fiber. In the fish, whatever predictable signal is left in the cell’s response keeps adjusting the weights until it is canceled, so no separate error line is needed.

options.text: In the reflex, the cell’s own leftover response does the teaching; in the fish, a climbing fiber delivers the prey’s signal as an error to one output cell.
options.why: This reverses the two. Climbing fibers carry the image’s slip in the reflex; the fish’s cells are taught by their own leftover response, and the prey signal is what the cancellation leaves intact.

options.text: In the reflex, a copy of the command to turn the head does the teaching; in the fish, a copy of the command to discharge does the teaching.
options.why: In the fish, the discharge command and other signals that predict the input drive the negative image; their weights are what change, so they are not the teacher. In the reflex, the teacher is the slip, carried by climbing fibers.

options.text: In the reflex, the teaching signal comes from the balance organs; in the fish, it comes from the prey, whose signal has to be kept rather than canceled.
options.why: The balance organs drive the reflex itself, not its recalibration, which is taught by the image’s slip. And the prey signal is not a teacher; it survives because the fish’s own commands do not predict it.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain how the anti-Hebbian rule lets an electric fish’s cancellation circuit build a negative image of its own pulses. Say why the result cancels self-caused input whether that input raises or lowers a cell’s firing. Then say what keeps the weights changing, and what makes them stop.
items.answer: Under the anti-Hebbian rule, which is Hebb’s rule reversed, an input that arrives just before the cell fires is weakened, and inputs at other times are strengthened. The fish’s discharge commands, and other signals that predict its pulse, arrive reliably along with the self-caused input. Where that input raises the cell’s firing, the predicting inputs arrive just before firing and are weakened. Where it lowers firing, the predicting inputs arrive while the cell is quiet and are strengthened. Either way the command comes to produce the opposite of the self-caused input, a negative image, so anything predictable cancels. The teacher is the cell’s own leftover response: whatever predictable signal is not yet canceled keeps adjusting the weights, and once it is canceled the changes stop. Prey survives, because nothing the fish does predicts it.
rubric: States the rule: an input arriving just before the cell fires is weakened, and inputs at other times are strengthened (Hebb’s rule reversed).
Says the inputs whose weights change are those that predict the pulse, such as the discharge command, so the command comes to produce the opposite of the self-caused input.
Explains that because the changes go both ways, a predictable rise and a predictable drop in firing are both canceled.
Says the teacher is the cell’s own leftover response, and the weights stop changing once nothing predictable is left.

items.stem: The small fish in a stream where eels hunt feels moving water with its lateral line. How strong is the case that, while swimming, it subtracts its own wake from its lateral line, and so can feel an eel’s?

options.text: It is an inference, from cancellation reported on thinner evidence in a fish with no electric sense, and from how many fish have the circuit.
options.why: Correct. The step from those reports to this fish is an inference, labeled as one, not a finding. If it is right, the fish can feel the eel’s wake because its own has been subtracted.

options.text: It is a finding: recordings from this kind of fish show a negative image of its wake forming in its lateral line within minutes of swimming.
options.why: No such recording of this fish is described. The electric fish is where a negative image was seen forming; for the lateral line of a fish without an electric sense, the evidence is a report on thinner grounds.

options.text: It is ruled out: fish without an electric sense lack cerebellum-like structures, so they can only dim the lateral line and never subtract.
options.why: The lateral line feeds cerebellum-like structures in the hindbrain, and cancellation like the electric fish’s has been reported for the lateral line of a fish with no electric sense. Subtraction is likely, not ruled out.

options.text: It is a certainty: any fish that dims its lateral line while it swims must also be subtracting its own wake, by that very same act.
options.why: Dimming does not entail subtracting. They are separate ways of handling self-caused signals, and this fish’s use of the second is the part that remains an inference.

items.stem: A fish’s lateral line is turned down by nerves while it swims. Why would this dimming alone not let a swimming fish feel the faint wake of an eel nearby, while subtracting a learned prediction of its own wake could?

options.text: Dimming weakens all that the sense receives, the eel’s wake included, while subtraction removes only the part the fish’s own movement predicts.
options.why: Correct. Dimming suits brief, simple self-caused signals, but it turns down the world’s signals along with the animal’s own. For a complex, long-lasting signal like a swimming fish’s wake, predicting and subtracting removes the self-caused part and leaves the eel’s.

options.text: Dimming works only on signals that come from outside the fish, while subtraction works only on the signals that the fish causes by moving itself.
options.why: Both strategies are aimed at self-caused signals. The difference is selectivity: dimming turns down the whole sense, while subtraction takes away only what the fish’s own movement predicts.

options.text: Dimming acts too slowly to keep up with each beat of the tail, while subtraction acts at once because it needs no learning at all.
options.why: Subtraction is the strategy that needs learning, since the prediction has to match the self-caused input and keep matching it. Dimming is the simpler strategy, and it works well for brief, simple signals.

options.text: Dimming leaves the fish’s own wake untouched, while subtraction weakens every signal the lateral line receives during swimming.
options.why: This reverses the two. Dimming is the strategy that turns everything down; subtraction is the selective one.

items.stem: A listener recognizes a friend’s voice when it is shouted across a gym, whispered nearby, or muffled through a wall, but cannot recognize it over a badly garbled phone line. What does this pattern illustrate about recognizing what things are?

options.text: Recognition is tolerant rather than perfectly invariant: it survives much of the variation sound’s physics produces, but not all.
options.why: Correct. Each sense faces the recognition problem of Module 7 under its own physics. Loudness, muffling, and the echoes of a room all change a sound, and brains manage that variation with tolerance rather than perfect invariance, so recognition gives out somewhere.

options.text: Recognition is perfectly invariant: once a voice has been learned, it is recognized across any change the sound can undergo.
options.why: With perfect invariance, the voice would be recognized over the garbled line too. What brains achieve is tolerance: recognition survives a great deal of change, but not every change.

options.text: Recognition depends on locating the voice: a sound is recognized only when the two ears agree on where it came from.
options.why: Locating a sound uses comparisons between the two ears, a separate job from recognizing what made it. A voice muffled through a wall is recognized without its location being clear.

options.text: Recognition depends on combining senses: a voice is recognized only when sight of the speaker confirms what the ears report.
options.why: Combining senses means judging whether signals from two senses share a cause, and weighting each by its reliability. The listener here recognizes the voice with no sight of the speaker at all.

items.stem: A fly lands on the back of a person’s right hand twice: once with the arm stretched overhead, once with the hand resting on a desk. Both times the same touch receptors in the skin are pressed. What can those receptors alone signal about the fly’s position, and what more is needed to locate the fly in the room?
tags: combining with where the sheet pointed

options.text: They signal where on the body the fly landed; locating it in the room also needs where the hand was at the time, as proprioception reports.
options.why: Correct. A position on a receptor sheet means nothing about the world until it is combined with where the sheet was pointing. For vision that means where the eye was aimed; for touch, where the limb was, which proprioception reports.

options.text: They signal where in the room the fly landed, since a receptor sheet’s layout gives location in the world directly, with nothing more needed.
options.why: The layout of the skin gives where on the body, just as the retina gives direction relative to the eye. Neither gives a position in the world until it is combined with where the sheet was.

options.text: They signal nothing about location, since touch receptors report only pressure, so the fly has to be located by sight instead.
options.why: Touch receptors are laid out across the skin, so which ones are pressed says where on the body the touch fell, much as where light falls on the retina gives its direction relative to the eye.

options.text: They signal where on the body the fly landed; locating it in the room also needs a comparison of the signals from the two hands.
options.why: Comparing two sensors is how hearing gets direction, from two ears that receive the same sound. A fly on one hand presses only that hand, so the other hand has nothing to compare.

items.stem: An animal produces two kinds of self-caused signal. One is a single brief click with each step it takes. The other is a complex hum that changes shape over many seconds while it flies. Which way of separating its own doings from the world’s best suits each?

options.text: Dimming the sense suits the brief click; predicting and subtracting suits the complex, long-lasting hum.
options.why: Correct. Dimming works well for brief, simple self-caused signals. For complex, long-lasting ones, turning the sense down would silence the world for too long, so the nervous system predicts the specific self-caused signal and subtracts it.

options.text: Predicting and subtracting suits the brief click; dimming the sense suits the complex, long-lasting hum.
options.why: This reverses the two. A brief, simple signal can be handled by turning the sense down for a moment; a complex, long-lasting one calls for a prediction shaped to it.

options.text: Dimming the sense suits both, since any self-caused signal is best handled by turning the sense down.
options.why: Dimming a long, complex signal would turn the sense down for as long as the animal flies, taking every signal from the world down with it.

options.text: Predicting and subtracting suits neither, since a prediction can be learned only for signals that never change.
options.why: Predictions are learned continually from mismatch precisely so that they can follow signals that change, as the electric fish’s negative image follows its pulse into new water.

items.stem: A prediction of what a movement will do to the senses helps separate self-caused signals from the world’s. What second use does the same prediction have?

options.text: It lets the animal act on an estimate of where its body is now, more current than the senses’ last, already old, report.
options.why: Correct. The senses report what has already happened. A prediction of a command’s consequences can stand in for news that has not yet arrived, so the animal can act on information that would otherwise be too old.

options.text: It lets the animal measure its own movement directly, with sensors in the inner ear that respond to rotation and acceleration.
options.why: That is measuring movement with the vestibular system, a separate way of telling self from world. It reports the movement as it happens rather than predicting it.

options.text: It lets the animal locate sounds in space, by comparing the moments at which one sound reaches each of its two ears.
options.why: That is how hearing recovers direction, from the interaural time difference. It concerns where things are, not the animal’s own movement.

options.text: It lets the animal recognize objects from new angles, by matching each new view against the views it has already stored.
options.why: That is the views account of recognition, which concerns what things are. The prediction in question is about the animal’s own movement.

items.stem: Every sense faces a version of the ill-posed problem. In what sense is that problem managed rather than solved?

options.text: Perception commits to what its signals pin down reliably, fills in with assumptions that usually hold, and corrects itself from errors.
options.why: Correct. The signals do not settle a single answer, so the problem is never solved outright. Perception delivers what is good enough to act on: reliable judgments of which point is nearer rather than exact distances, assumptions such as light from above, and correction from mismatch.

options.text: Perception records the world as it is, so that with enough signals combined, each ill-posed problem eventually gets its single true answer.
options.why: Perception is not a recording of the world. Even with every cue available, people misjudge exact distances, so more signals do not turn an ill-posed problem into a solved one.

options.text: Perception reports only what the signals settle beyond doubt, adding nothing to them, so whatever it does report is never mistaken.
options.why: Perception adds assumptions that are usually true, which is how depth cues work at all. Those assumptions sometimes mislead, as when patterned wallpaper fuses at the wrong pairing and seems to float at the wrong distance.

options.text: Perception relies on one sense at a time, so that an ambiguity in one sense is never mixed up with an ambiguity in another sense.
options.why: Senses are combined, and one can resolve an ambiguity in another, as the canals of the inner ear settle whether the head tilted or accelerated.

items.stem: Listeners hear the pitch of a lowest frequency that has been removed from a sound made of its whole-number multiples. Viewers see a shaded disc as a bump or a dent depending on which way its shading runs. What do the two cases have in common?

options.text: In both, the percept goes beyond the signal, filled in by an assumption about the world that is usually true.
options.why: Correct. No component at the missing frequency reaches the ear, and nothing in a flat disc settles which way the light falls. Each percept rests on how the world usually is: sources that vibrate regularly, light that comes from above. That is part of why perception is not a recording of the world.

options.text: In both, the percept is a faithful recording of the signal, picked up by receptors laid out to detect it.
options.why: Hearing a frequency that is not in the wave, or a bump that is not in a flat picture, is the opposite of a recording. Perception adds assumptions that are usually true to what its signals carry.

options.text: In both, the percept comes from comparing two sensors, the two ears for the pitch and the two eyes for the depth.
options.why: Comparing two sensors is how hearing gets direction and how stereo vision gets depth. The missing pitch is inferred from the components in the sound itself, and shading is a cue present in a single image.

options.text: In both, the percept is an aftereffect, left over after the senses have adapted to a distortion that was then removed.
options.why: An aftereffect is an error in the opposite direction after an adapted-to distortion is removed, the sign of a stored mapping that changed. Both percepts here appear at once, with no adaptation.

items.stem: A fox hunting at night hears a mouse rustle in dry leaves and turns its head toward the sound. In a short paragraph, explain two things the fox has to do with what it hears. It has to recognize the rustle as a mouse across the ways such sounds vary. It also has to find where the mouse is in the world, not only relative to its head. Then explain why what the fox perceives is something other than a recording of the sound reaching its ears.
tags: combining with where the sheet pointed
items.answer: A mouse’s rustle varies with how loud it is, which leaves it passes through, and the echoes around it, so the fox has to recognize the mouse across the variation that sound’s physics produces. Like every sense, hearing manages this with tolerance, surviving much of the variation but not all of it, rather than with perfect invariance. The cochlea is laid out by frequency, not by direction, so direction has to be computed by comparing the two ears, in timing and in level. That comparison gives direction relative to the head. It means nothing about where the mouse is in the world until it is combined with where the head was pointing. Finally, the percept is not a recording. Perception settles for what its signals constrain well, adds assumptions that are usually true about how sound sources behave, and corrects itself from errors. The ill-posed problem of recovering a source from one summed wave is managed well enough to strike at, not solved.
rubric: Says recognizing the mouse means handling variation that sound’s physics produces, such as loudness, muffling, or echoes, and that this is managed with tolerance rather than perfect invariance.
Says hearing computes direction by comparing the two ears, since its receptor sheet is laid out by frequency rather than direction.
Says the direction found is relative to the head, and has to be combined with where the head was pointing to give a place in the world.
Says perception is not a recording: it settles for what the signals constrain well, adds usually-true assumptions, and corrects itself from errors.
Says the ill-posed problem is managed well enough to act on, not solved.

items.stem: With Version B: trained on shifted, turned and resized copies switched on, the percent of altered drawings each version of the drawing network labels correctly, over 200 drawings, is printed. On upside-down drawings, Version B did far better than Version A. What did the printed figures show for Mirror it and Squash it flat?

options.text: Both versions labeled most mirrored drawings correctly, and Version B labeled fewer squashed drawings correctly than Version A did.
options.why: Correct. Mirroring left both versions near 90%, because most drawings look much the same flipped from side to side. Squashing flat is not one of the changes Version B was trained on. Version B labeled about 45% of squashed drawings correctly, against Version A’s 68%. Training on altered copies gave tolerance to the alterations that were trained, and on squashing it left Version B worse off than the version trained with no altered copies at all.

options.text: Version B labeled more mirrored and more squashed drawings correctly than Version A did, as it had for upside-down drawings.
options.why: This is what follows if training on altered copies gave tolerance in general. Version B gained on the turns it was trained on. On squashed drawings, an alteration absent from its training, it fell well below Version A, and on mirrored drawings it did not gain.

options.text: Both versions labeled most squashed drawings correctly, and Version B labeled far fewer mirrored drawings correctly than Version A did.
options.why: This swaps the two changes. Mirroring was the one both versions handled, near 90%, since most drawings are close to symmetric from side to side. Squashing flat was the one on which Version B fell well below Version A.

options.text: Version A labeled few mirrored drawings correctly, and Version B, trained on turned copies, labeled most of the mirrored drawings correctly.
options.why: A mirror image is not a turn, so training on turned copies would not cover it in any case. And no cover was needed: Version A labeled about 94% of mirrored drawings correctly, since most drawings look much the same flipped from side to side.

items.stem: After the twelve erased drawings are committed, the drawing network’s percent right in the larger test is shown, over 200 held-out drawings for each eraser, Mid-line and At the joints, with 35%, 50%, and 65% of the ink removed. In a few sentences, say whether the network showed a gap between the erasers in the direction people show, what happened at the heavier deletions, and why this result cannot by itself show that the network handles parts differently from people.
items.answer: The network showed no gap in the direction people show. With 35% of the ink removed the two erasers came out about level, and at 50% and 65% the network did a little better with the gaps at the joints than with the gaps mid-line, though both scores fell as more ink went. People, by contrast, named line drawings whose parts stayed recoverable and failed almost completely when the gaps hid where the parts join. But the joint eraser only approximates the deletions people saw. In those drawings the remaining lines were arranged to run smoothly across the joints, while the eraser only removes ink there. The parts may still be recoverable from what is left, so the missing gap might come from the drawings rather than from the network.
rubric: Reports no gap in the people’s direction: the network did not find mid-line gaps clearly easier than joint gaps.
Reports that at the heavier deletions the network did slightly better with joint gaps than with mid-line gaps.
States people’s result: drawings with recoverable parts were named, and drawings with hidden joins were failed almost completely.
Says the joint eraser does not make the remaining lines run smoothly across the joints, so the parts may still be recoverable.
Concludes that the missing gap may reflect the erased drawings rather than the network, so the comparison with people is not a clean test.

items.stem: In the ten built pairs, each drawing sits beside a version with one group of strokes moved, such as a mushroom with its cap under the stem. After the answers for the ten pairs are committed, the drawing network’s label for each version is shown. On how many of the ten pairs did the network keep its label when the part moved?

options.text: Six of the ten, with both mushrooms keeping their original label when the cap was moved under the stem.
options.why: Correct. The label stayed on six of the ten, both mushrooms included at a probability near 1, and changed on four, such as a coffee cup labeled a bucket. In the reading, networks are described as confusing a moved version with its original easily, and people as rarely doing so. Giving the moved version its original’s label is that confusion, so on most of the pairs this network behaved like the networks described in the reading.

options.text: Six of the ten, with both mushrooms among the four pairs whose label changed to another category.
options.why: The count is right, but the mushrooms went the other way. With the cap under the stem, both kept the label mushroom with a probability near 1. The four that changed included a coffee cup labeled a bucket and an ice cream labeled a chair.

options.text: All ten, with every moved version, both mushrooms included, keeping the label its original received.
options.why: Moving a part leaves every stroke in place, so a network might be expected to keep every label. Most labels did stay, but four of the ten moved versions got a new one, such as an umbrella labeled a floor lamp.

options.text: Two of the ten, with both mushrooms among the eight pairs whose label changed to another category.
options.why: That is closer to how people behave, since they rarely confuse an object with a version in which one part has moved. The network kept its label on six of the ten, both mushrooms included.

items.stem: After the built pairs are committed, two matches at the drawing network’s last layer are also shown for each pair: one between the original and its moved version, and one between two ordinary drawings of the same category. Across the ten pairs, how did the two matches compare?

options.text: For about half the pairs, the moved version matched its original more closely than two ordinary drawings of the category matched each other.
options.why: Correct. In five of the ten pairs the original and its moved version were closer at the last layer than two ordinary drawings of the same thing, some by a wide margin, such as 0.90 against 0.27. For those pairs, moving a part made less difference to the network than the ordinary variation between two people’s drawings. In the other five the moved version matched no better, and in two pairs much worse.

options.text: For most of the pairs, the moved version matched its original far less closely than two ordinary drawings of the category matched each other.
options.why: This is what a network sensitive to how parts are arranged would show, as people are. It held for a few pairs, two of them clearly, but in five of the ten the moved version matched its original more closely than two ordinary drawings did.

options.text: For most of the pairs, the two matches came out about equal, since the last layer reflects the category and not how the parts are arranged.
options.why: The two matches came out about equal in only one or two pairs. The moved pairs ranged from almost no match to a very close one, while the ordinary pairs mostly sat between about 0.2 and 0.45.

options.text: For most of the pairs, the moved version matched its original almost perfectly, since it was made from exactly the same strokes as the original.
options.why: The strokes are the same, but only one pair came near 0.9, and several moved versions matched their originals less closely than two ordinary drawings matched each other.

items.stem: In the larger test on 800 held-out photographs, the Standard photo network, trained only on clean photographs, labeled about 87% of clean photographs correctly. With noise A at its starting strength, a fifth of the pixels replaced with black or white, how did Standard and Trained on noise A do?

options.text: Standard labeled about 16% correctly and Trained on noise A about 68%, a lead of some fifty points.
options.why: Correct. Replacing a fifth of the pixels took Standard from about 87% to about 16%, not far above the chance level of one in sixteen. Trained on noise A held about 68%, ten points under its own score on clean photographs. Training on the noise gave tolerance to it, and the network trained without it lost most of its accuracy.

options.text: Standard labeled about 45% correctly and Trained on noise A about 80%, a lead of some thirty-five points.
options.why: These numbers echo a reported test in which a network trained on one noise beat people on it, 80% against 46%. That test set a network against people, not two networks against each other. Here Standard fell to about 16%, and Trained on noise A held about 68%.

options.text: Standard labeled about 70% correctly and Trained on noise A about 85%, a lead of some fifteen points.
