options.why: With four in five pixels left as they were, a modest drop is a natural expectation. Standard fell much further, to about 16%. Trained on noise A, at about 68%, also fell below its own 78% on clean photographs.

options.text: Standard labeled about 6% correctly, the chance level, and Trained on noise A about 78%, its clean score.
options.why: Standard fell close to chance but stayed above it, at about 16% against about 6%. And Trained on noise A did not hold its clean score: it labeled about 68% correctly, ten points under its 78% on clean photographs.

items.stem: The three photo networks are identical except for what they were trained on. In the larger test on 800 held-out clean photographs, how did Trained on noise A compare with Standard, which was trained on clean photographs alone?

options.text: It labeled noticeably fewer of them correctly, about 78% against 87%, though it still labeled most of them correctly.
options.why: Correct. Standard labeled about 87% of clean photographs correctly and Trained on noise A about 78%. Training on one alteration gave tolerance to that alteration, and the network trained that way lost some ground on undistorted photographs. Trained on blurred and sharp, within a point or so of Standard, showed no such loss.

options.text: It labeled about as many of them correctly, since training on noisy copies adds tolerance to noise and takes nothing away elsewhere.
options.why: It is natural to assume that adding an alteration to training leaves performance on clean images as it was. Here it did not: Trained on noise A labeled about 78% of clean photographs correctly against Standard’s 87%.

options.text: It labeled noticeably more of them correctly, since training on noisy copies made it lean on sturdier features of every photograph.
options.why: Sturdier features are the hope behind training on altered copies. On clean photographs, though, the noise-trained network did worse than Standard, about 78% against 87%, not better.

options.text: It labeled far fewer of them correctly, close to chance, since a network trained only on noisy photographs cannot label clean ones.
options.why: Its training noise came at many strengths, and it still labeled about 78% of clean photographs correctly. The loss against Standard was about ten points, not a collapse.

items.stem: Networks trained on a mixture of sharp and blurry images have been reported to resist noise better than networks trained on sharp images alone. In the larger test, with noise A at its starting strength of 0.20, how did Trained on blurred and sharp compare with Standard?

options.text: It did about as poorly as Standard, both labeling under a fifth correctly, so blurred training gave it no advantage on this noise.
options.why: Correct. At noise A 0.20, Standard labeled about 16% correctly and Trained on blurred and sharp about 14%, against about 68% for Trained on noise A. In the reading, networks trained on sharp and blurry images are described as resisting noise better. The photo network trained that way in this lab did not: it matched Standard on clean photographs and gained nothing against noise A at this strength.

options.text: It did nearly as well as Trained on noise A, both labeling about two thirds correctly, since blurred training gives resistance to noise.
options.why: That is the pattern the reported blur-trained networks would suggest. This one did not show it: about 14% at noise A 0.20, against about 68% for the network trained on noise A itself.

options.text: It did somewhat better than Standard, about halfway between Standard and Trained on noise A, since blur gives a partial resistance to noise.
options.why: A partial gain is a reasonable hedge, but none appeared. Trained on blurred and sharp labeled about 14% correctly at noise A 0.20, with Standard at about 16%.

options.text: It did far worse than Standard, close to none correct, since blurred training leaves it without the fine detail that shows between the noisy pixels.
options.why: It did a little worse than Standard, about 14% against 16%, but not far worse, and well above none. The two networks fared about the same.

items.stem: In the larger test on drawings, the three photo networks, none of which had ever been shown a drawing, labeled 800 held-out drawings of their sixteen categories. How did they do?

options.text: Each labeled roughly a quarter to a third correctly, well above chance at one in sixteen but far below the drawing network.
options.why: Correct. Standard labeled about 25%, Trained on noise A about 30%, and Trained on blurred and sharp about 27%, against 92% for the drawing network and 6% for chance. A drawing has none of the surface texture photo networks lean on, yet its outline carried enough shape for them to do far better than chance.

options.text: Each labeled close to one in sixteen correctly, no better than chance, since a drawing has none of the texture photo networks lean on.
options.why: The missing texture is a good reason to expect failure, and it did hold the photo networks far below the drawing network. But they labeled a quarter to a third correctly, four or five times chance.

options.text: Each labeled most of them correctly, close to the drawing network, since the outline of an object carries its shape whatever it is drawn on.
options.why: Outline shape carried them some of the way, but not most of it. The photo networks labeled a quarter to a third correctly, against the drawing network’s 92%.

options.text: Each labeled about half correctly, with Trained on blurred and sharp well ahead of the others, since it relies on shape more often.
options.why: Blurred training was expected to help with drawings, but its lead over Standard was only about two points, and none of the three reached a third.
